Ukraine has hit seven of Russian online retailer Wildberries' 10 biggest warehouses, military says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:51:57 UTC
20:51:57 KST

A month-long Ukrainian attack campaign against Russia's largest online retailer has knocked out seven of its ten biggest logistics hubs, according to Kyiv's defence ministry and the Institute for the Study of War.
Ukraine's Ministry of Defence said at the weekend that Kyiv's forces had hit Wildberries' single largest warehouse, a 250,000-square-metre complex at the Koledino industrial park in Podolsk in the Moscow region, around 420 kilometres from the border.
Seven logistics hubs belonging to Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, have now been struck and knocked out of action since the campaign began in July.
Wildberries confirmed the strike had sparked a fire and forced it to reroute its supply chains, just as Ukrainian forces also struck a second depot in nearby Domodedovo on the same night.
Kyiv’s campaign underlines Ukraine’s capacity to reach deep inside Russia nearly four and a half years into Moscow's full-scale invasion.
Kyiv’s campaign against Wildberries
Kyiv has justified the strikes by arguing Wildberries helps arm the Russian military, supplying drone components and navigation equipment alongside its consumer goods.
The US-based Institute for the Study of War said that Kyiv’s campaign is squeezing Russia's economy while exposing a deeper vulnerability.
"Moscow simply does not have enough air-defence coverage to shield every piece of infrastructure in its rear, even ten of its most valuable commercial sites," the ISW assessment concluded.
The campaign began on the weekend of 18 July, when drones hit sites in Elektrostal, east of Moscow, and the Tambov region, and has since fanned out from the capital and St Petersburg to southern Russia and as far as Yekaterinburg in the Urals, over 2,000 km from Ukrainian territory.
Roughly 20 Wildberries facilities have now been struck, according to the Associated Press.
Toll for Russia’s economy
Wildberries is often compared to Amazon for its size and importance to Russia's economy.
To understand the scale of the business, Wildberries reports an annual turnover of between €70–75 billion, a figure that various estimates put at just over 2% of Russia’s GDP.
The market place is handling roughly half the country's online orders and serving several hundred thousand sellers across eleven time zones, a role that expanded further after Western brands exited the market following the invasion.
This is why the fallout is rippling well beyond Wildberries itself.
Ukrainian officials said the goal is to disrupt military supply lines, stir domestic frustration and trigger a wider financial squeeze by pressuring banks such as VTB and Sberbank, which extended roughly €13 billion in loans to a company now struggling to keep them serviced.

Who is Khalil Al-Hayya, the Hamas leader who met Kushner in Cairo?

Unknown Publisher

Who is Khalil Al-Hayya, the Hamas leader who met Kushner in Cairo?
- Khalil Al-Hayya is Hamas' overall leader since July, surviving multiple Israeli attacks that killed many of his family members and other Hamas leaders.
- He met US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, marking a shift in US policy by engaging Hamas to negotiate ceasefire and hostage release deals.
- Hayya defends Hamas' actions as resistance, demands Palestinian statehood, and claims the 2023 Gaza war shattered Israel's strategic deterrence, putting the Palestinian issue on the global agenda.
AI generated
Khalil Al-Hayya, the Hamas chief who met US envoy Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, in Cairo on Aug 16, emerged as a pivotal figure in the Palestinian militant group during the Gaza war as Israel killed its other leaders.
Named Hamas’ overall leader in July, Hayya narrowly escaped assassination himself in a 2025 Israeli air strike in Qatar that killed his son and aides.
The Cairo meeting marked Hayya’s second with Kushner. In October 2025, he led a Hamas delegation in negotiations with Kushner and US envoy Steve Witkoff, helping to clinch a deal that led to a ceasefire and the release of remaining hostages seized in the Hamas-led attacks on Israel in 2023.
The meetings have marked a departure from Washington’s longstanding policy of shunning Hamas, which the US designates as a terrorist group.
Hayya served as part of a five-member council that ran the group from 2024 after Israel killed Hamas leader Yahya Al-Sinwar – one of the masterminds of the Oct 7, 2023 attacks that ignited the Gaza war.
On his watch, Hamas agreed in July to lay down its weapons under a Trump-backed plan linking its disarmament to Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza – a once unimaginable declaration from a group that was pummelled by Israel during the war.
Hamas has rejected the word “disarmament”, instead saying it has agreed to hand over its weapons to be stored under the control of a US-backed Palestinian technocratic government.
Israel has rejected the plan, which also foresees Gaza being rebuilt, saying it will not withdraw until Hamas is fully disarmed.
A Hamas veteran
Born in the Gaza Strip in 1960, Hayya joined the Sunni Islamist Muslim Brotherhood movement from which Hamas emerged in 1987. He has a PhD in Islamic Studies.
He rose through the Hamas ranks alongside figures such as Sinwar – serving as his deputy for Gaza – and Ismail Haniyeh, another former Hamas leader who was assassinated by Israel in Tehran in 2024.
The Doha air strike was not Hayya’s first narrow escape.
In 2007, an Israeli air strike hit his family home in Gaza City’s Shejaia quarter, killing several of his relatives. Hayya was not there at the time.
In 2008, his son Hamza was killed in an Israeli attack in Gaza. During a war between Hamas and Israel in 2014, the house of Hayya’s eldest son, Osama, was bombed, killing him, his wife and three of their children.
Azzam Al-Hayya, another of his sons, was killed by an Israeli air strike in Gaza City in May while Hayya was engaged in talks with mediators.
Azzam was the twin brother of Hammam Al-Hayya – the son killed in the Doha strike.
Hayya left Gaza in 2021, basing himself in Qatar along with other members of Hamas’ exiled political leadership.
From Doha, he served as Hamas’ point person with Arab and Islamic states, among other roles.
Among Hamas watchers, Hayya is seen as part of a camp that deepened the group’s ties to Shi’ite Muslim Iran, which provided the group with arms and finance before the Gaza war.
Hayya was closely involved in numerous rounds of indirect negotiations with Israel during the Gaza war before a ceasefire deal was finally reached.
Exchanging condolences with Witkoff
Trump granted Witkoff and Kushner permission to speak directly to Hamas as he sought to secure an end to the war and the release of the remaining hostages.
Their Oct 8, 2025, meeting with the Hayya-led delegation was the highest-profile encounter yet between the US and Hamas.
Witkoff said he had expressed condolences to Hayya during their meeting for the loss of his son Hammam in Israel’s Doha air strike.
“I told him that I had lost a son, and that we were both members of a really bad club, parents who have buried children,” Witkoff told CBS News’ 60 Minutes programme.
Hayya has said he and Witkoff exchanged “humane words” over the loss of their sons.
He also set out core Hamas demands.
“We told them ... what we want. We want stability, we want a Palestinian entity, we want a Palestinian state in accordance with international law and relevant resolutions. We want to live in peace so that the region can stabilise, and without that, the region will not stabilise,” he told Al Jazeera in an interview.
Defending right to ‘resistance’
Hamas’ 1988 founding charter called for the destruction of Israel, although Hamas leaders have at times offered a long-term truce with Israel in return for a viable Palestinian state on all Palestinian territory occupied by Israel in the 1967 war.
Israel regards this as a ruse.
Hayya has been cited as saying the Oct 7 attack had been meant as a limited operation to capture “a number of soldiers” to swap for jailed Palestinians.
“But the Zionist army unit completely collapsed,” he said in comments published by the Hamas-linked Palestinian Information Center in 2024, referring to Israel’s military.
Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people in the Oct 7 attack on Israel, and abducted another 251. Israel’s retaliatory offensive killed more than 73,000 people, according to Gazan health authorities.
Despite the devastation caused by Israel’s Gaza offensive, Hayya said in a December 2025 speech that “the resistance” had shown “the enemy can be defeated” and that the myth of Israeli “strategic deterrence” had been shattered.
He has also said the Palestinian issue has been put back on the international agenda. REUTERS

Russia's most-used mapping service has digitally hidden a military missile site near Finland by copying a fake forest over it on satellite imagery, Finnish public broadcaster Yle reported. Western map services still show the same position, and a Finnish military analyst called the concealment careless and self-defeating. The clumsy edit points to Moscow's growing fear of Ukrainian drones.
What Yandex tried to erase
The concealed site sits beside the Kronstadt naval base, on Kotlin Island off St. Petersburg in the Gulf of Finland. Editing software copied trees from another image and laid them over the missile position. Until now, Russia mostly blurred sensitive locations rather than deleting them, but this edit tries to hide the target's existence outright. The same battery still appears on Google, Apple, and Microsoft satellite maps. In the covered zone, Russia has previously kept Bastion anti-ship missiles and their radar and reconnaissance systems.
A cover-up that gives itself away
Marko Eklund, a military expert and former Finnish intelligence officer, called the secrecy pointless. Western and Ukrainian analysts read their own satellite images, not Yandex, so the edit protects nothing in practice. He believes an administrative order drove it, and that the work was done sloppily. Anyone who knows what to look for can spot the seams and repeating patterns.
Kronstadt, Russia’s major naval Base after Black Sea Fleet losses, gets hit by Ukrainian drones (VIDEO)
A pattern set by Ukraine's drones
Russia's map cover-ups have tracked Ukraine's deep strikes. A Moscow court ordered Yandex to mask an oil refinery in Ryazan in 2024 after repeated Ukrainian strikes, and a Nordic-Baltic investigation later counted 119 blurred sites near Russia's northwestern border. Blurring shows up at once, while cloned forest hides the tampering itself.
Kronstadt gives Russia one of its main Baltic Fleet bases, and Ukraine's drones have already reached it. In early June, they set a Russian missile corvette ablaze in dry dock there.

Films about &quot;Braty Hadiukininy&quot;, Kharlan and Horska: the winners of &quot;Tysyachovesna&quot; have been determined

Films about "Braty Hadiukininy", Kharlan and Horska: the winners of "Tysyachovesna" have been determined
Kyiv • UNN
The Ministry of Culture recommended 546 projects for victory in the "Tysyachovesna-2026" program. Among them are films about Olga Kharlan, Serhii Kuzminskyi, and a Christmas comedy.
Feature films about fencer Olga Kharlan, musician and frontman of the rock band "Braty Hadiukiny" Serhii Kuzminskyi, artist Alla Horska, choreographer Pavlo Virskyi, and director Yurii Illienko, as well as the Christmas comedy "Vertep v khatu," have been included among the winners of the state program supporting Ukrainian culture, "Tysyachovesna-2026." This was reported by UNN , citing the Ministry of Culture of Ukraine.
It is known that, following the final pitching session, 546 projects were recommended for support, including the films mentioned above.
Details
The final presentation of "Tysyachovesna" took place in Ivano-Frankivsk and lasted five days. In total, participants presented 1,215 projects and spent 320 hours defending them.
Following the selection, 546 projects in six areas were recommended for support:
-  77 — in the field of visual arts; 
-  133 — in performing arts; 
-  144 — in contemporary music;  
-  70 documentaries and series; 
-  92 feature films and series; 
-  30 animation projects and content for children. 
Among the feature projects recommended for support is the film "The Fencer: The Main Bout," dedicated to Olympic champion Olga Kharlan. The film is intended to tell the story of her sporting and personal journey — from her first steps in fencing to competing at the Olympic Games in Paris. One of the key episodes is to be the story of the Ukrainian athlete's refusal to shake hands with her Russian opponent.
Another project, "Alla Horska," will tell the story of the life of Ukrainian sixtier artist, public figure, and human rights movement participant Alla Horska.
The film "Virskyi" is dedicated to Ukrainian choreographer Pavlo Virskyi. According to the creators' concept, the film will tell the story of the establishment of a Ukrainian dance ensemble amid Stalinist repressions and the Second World War, opposition to Soviet censorship, and the struggle to preserve Ukrainian identity.
The project "The Golden Lion on Ivan Kupala," about director Yurii Illienko, was also included on the list. The events of the film will unfold in the 1960s, when Soviet censorship banned his work and the director sought to take Ukrainian poetic cinema beyond the borders of the USSR.
The project "Vsio Chotko!" will tell the story of Serhii Kuzminskyi, the frontman of the iconic Ukrainian band "Braty Hadiukiny." Through his biography, the creators plan to show the formation of Ukrainian counterculture and the search for personal freedom.
The Christmas comedy "Vertep v khatu" was also among the winners. At the center of the plot are petty con artists who pose as participants in a nativity play in order to gain entry to wealthy homes. Becoming acquainted with Ukrainian Christmas traditions and people gradually changes the characters.
Context
"Tysyachovesna" is a state initiative supporting Ukrainian culture, launched at the initiative of President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Up to UAH 4 billion has been allocated for its implementation.
In total, the organizers received 2,634 applications. More than 180 Ukrainian and foreign experts were involved in the evaluation. The projects were assessed, in particular, on the quality and creativity of the idea, the feasibility of implementation, the professionalism of the team, the justification of the budget, international potential, and the share of co-financing.
More than 20% of the program's participants were debutants.
The results in the area of "Audiovisual Shows and Videos for Social Media" are still being determined separately. For this area, the second stage of the competition is the final one, and the results are to be published additionally.
The Ministry of Culture also announced plans to continue "Tysyachovesna" in 2027 and expand the program with new areas — video games and books.
Previously
In June 2026, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that there was historic interest in the "Tysyachovesna" program. More than 2,600 applications were submitted for the competition, and more than 150 experts evaluated the projects.

Türkiye’s Marlin unmanned vessel gains smart mine-laying capability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:49:08 UTC
20:49:08 KST

Türkiye’s unmanned surface vehicle (USV), the Marlin, gained significant mine-laying capacity, powered by Malaman smart sea mines.
The Marlin was the first USV to enter the Turkish Navy’s inventory. It was developed through a partnership between Sefine Shipyard and defence firm Aselsan under the coordination of the Turkish Defence Industries Agency (SSB).
The integration of homegrown Malaman sea mines into the Marlin marked a significant milestone in naval mine-laying capabilities. The smart mines were developed by Sefine Shipyard, research centre SISAM and KocDefense.
One year of coordinated efforts resulted in critical capabilities for laying mines using unmanned systems in line with the operational needs of the Turkish Navy.
Validation, testing completed
The design and production phases for the mine-laying system were completed, while autonomous and remote-controlled mine-laying algorithms and mission planning interfaces were integrated into the platform.
Sefine Shipyard completed the validation and testing of these systems, during which the Marlin USV successfully conducted a mine-laying mission as planned in both autonomous and remote-controlled modes.
The deployment of this capability solidifies Türkiye’s position among the few countries that can lay mines using USVs.
The Marlin’s modular architecture and multipurpose mission structure were further enhanced, providing speed, low risk, operational flexibility and high stealth for future naval operations, which are expected to multiply the Turkish Navy’s force.

Italy's working-life expectancy just 33 years, 2nd lowest in EU says CNA
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
13:48:58 CEST
20:48:58 KST

Italy's working-life expectancy is
just 33 years, the second lowest in the EU, think tank CNA said
Monday.
                                    
                                       
				Italy is one of the European countries where people live
longest, but also one of those with the fewest years spent in
the labour market.
                                    
                                       
				In 2025, the expected working life expectancy stood at 33 years,
the second lowest figure in the European Union after Romania and
a full four and a half years less than the EU average of 37.5
years.
                                    
                                       
				The CNA notes this, explaining that the improvement compared to
2024 is minimal: just over two months, compared to a three-month
increase recorded in the European average. Last year, the
Italian indicator was 32.8 years, while the EU average was 37.2.
                                    
                                       
				The gap with the major European economies remains considerable,
explains the CNA.
                                    
                                       
				The expected working lifespan reaches 40.2 years in Germany,
37.5 in France, and 36.8 in Spain.
                                    
                                       
				In the Netherlands, it reaches a staggering 44 years—eleven more
than in Italy.
                                    
                                       
				The most critical figure concerns women, notes the CNA: in
Italy, the expected working lifespan is just 28.4 years,
compared to 35.4 years on average in Europe. The gap between men
and women is 8.9 years, the highest in the EU.
                                    
                                       
				This result is consistent with a female employment rate of 58%,
almost thirteen points below the EU average, and the widest
gender employment gap among Member States.
                                    
                                       
				The indicator does not measure retirement age or the number of
years actually worked by those in continuous employment,
explains the CNA: it estimates the years a 15-year-old can
expect to spend in the labor force, either employed or
unemployed, based on current demographic conditions and
participation levels.
                                    
                                       
				The Italian result - observes the CNA - therefore reflects above
all the late entry of young people, discontinuous careers and
low female participation.

‘The most terrifying 11 hours of my life’: What really happens when you cross Russia’s border? Meduza’s readers share their stories.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:48:39 UTC
20:48:39 KST

‘The most terrifying 11 hours of my life’: What really happens when you cross Russia’s border? Meduza’s readers share their stories.
Crossing Russia’s border has become an increasingly fraught experience in recent years, whether you’re returning home or leaving the country. Last week, Meduza asked Russian readers to share their experiences crossing the border. While we expected to hear mostly from Russians living abroad, we also received dozens of accounts from people who still live in Russia and travel overseas. Not every crossing involved questioning or delays — some readers told us they passed through without incident. Here’s what they had to say.
Anton
I live in Russia but travel abroad for vacations. Border guards have questioned me twice in the past two years — the system flags me for additional screening, and both times were unpleasant. I live in Russia 11 months out of every 12, so it’s incredibly disappointing that this keeps happening. Why can I travel to any country in the world and get let in without a problem, but get interrogated when I come home?
Dmitry
In the four years since I left, I’ve been to Russia three times, to set up my business and visit my parents. Crossing the border went smoothly all three times, without incident or extra interrogation. They always ask on what grounds I live in Europe, and I show my residence permit. Surprisingly — and unfortunately — I have nothing unpleasant to report, except that every time, I feel like a tourist in my own country.
Anatoly
I travel once a year, for a couple of months. Every time I arrive, they ask the same questions: why, where to, where from, what do you do. My tip: bring your internal passport. They always ask for it, and things go faster if you have it. Nothing ever happened at departure — until the last time I left.
In August, they didn’t stop at [questioning me] at the booth — [the border guard] took me to a room and interrogated me for half an hour: who I am, what I do, where I live, with whom, where my relatives are, hand over your phone (I gave him a clean one), who I talk to, do I have anyone in Ukraine? I decided I would not go back to Russia again.
Zhenechka
My last entry was in the fall of 2024, when I waited 11 hours to be screened. I was lucky my laptop stayed with my wife, who had time to wipe it clean while I called her from other people’s phones. Those were the most terrifying 11 hours of my life — primal fear brings on all kinds of thoughts, and I had chat histories and payment records [that could get someone prosecuted].
Arkady
I traveled [to Russia] once, in December 2025 — the only [time] since I moved to Israel in 2022. I came for New Year’s, to visit friends, walk around familiar places, and pick up some belongings.
I prepared thoroughly for the trip. I have no history of detentions or prosecution in Russia, but I do have plenty of posts, photos, and donation records (to Meduza, for example!) that I wouldn’t want Russian authorities to see. I’m also transgender and have a nervous system disorder, which creates extra problems at any checkpoint — tremors and nervous reactions mean I get searched for drugs more often. In Israel, it took a 20-minute body scan for officers to find the organs needed for my passport, which was pretty funny, but fairly safe.
For the trip, I took my brother’s old phone and installed Russian apps I used to use — Yandex Mail, Russian Railways, 2GIS, and so on. I loaded some music for the trip, downloaded wallpaper pictures and plane tickets, made sure I had no Ukrainian contacts, searched for random things on Google, and poked around on YouTube to build up a search history — just to have one — and went.
The plane landed at Domodedovo at seven in the morning, and I spent the next five hours at the airport going through checks of every kind. At passport control, they asked a lot of strange questions: what were you doing in Poland? Is this your passport? You’ve changed so much — my Russian and Israeli passports have photos from before and after HRT — but the personal data matched, since I’d managed to change it before the repressive laws took effect, which made things easier.
After passport control, they took me to a security checkpoint, where I sat for four hours in a fenced-off pen of chairs. Officers called people by last name from there into an office for questioning and a phone search. My conversation with the border guard went something like this:
“Where are all your messaging apps? How do you communicate, by phone calls?”
“Yeah.”
“Where’s your social media?”
“I don’t use it.”
“You’re sure you don’t have a second phone?”
“I’m sure.”
“And if I find one?”
“You won’t.”
Then another officer came in and said, “Just take it to Igor, let him run it through his [some abbreviation, I don’t remember], it’ll take five minutes.” They carried my phone off to another office to “run it through” some kind of plug-in device.
I sat in the pen without my phone or passports, talking with the people around me — most of those waiting for screening had some connection to Ukraine or lacked Russian citizenship. I remember a mother and her adult daughter who had left Crimea in 2010; the mother carried Ukrainian and Israeli documents, while the daughter had only Israeli ones. “They ask why we don’t have Russian passports since we’re from Crimea. But we left before Crimea became Russian, and try explaining that to them now.”
Some people there travel on business every year and go through these checks every single time. […] After four hours of waiting, they returned my phone and passports and told me I could go. Next came a baggage search that took another hour — they emptied my backpack and suitcase completely, filmed the process on a department camera, and inspected every single item. […] After that, I was finally let out of the airport.
Anatoly
For family reasons, I’ve visited Russia six times since November 2025. Each time, I expected some kind of problem at the border, but nothing serious ever happened.
The real problem is the car line to enter Russia — the fastest crossing took about four hours, the longest about 17.
They checked my phone only once, and since I don’t bring my work phone, no additional questions came up. Maybe I’ve just been lucky, but I’ve had no problems with border guards over all these trips. Given that the country is at war, checks like this strike me as understandable, even a necessary security measure. But things could have been much worse.
Ksenia
I fly once a year to visit family, and it usually goes smoothly. But in October 2025, I was pulled in for questioning that lasted four hours. They went through all my things, checked my phone, and took my fingerprints. The interrogation covered who I talk to, who my relatives are, whether I know anyone in Ukraine, and so on. They asked about social media but didn’t check it. It worked out — but I won’t be going again.
Oleg
I come to Russia twice a year to visit relatives — and to buy medicine, tea, and so on. I usually have to answer unpleasant questions: where did you come from, what were you doing there, with whom, what’s your job, where do you permanently live.
The last time, in July, I landed at a regional airport and wasn’t let through because officers didn’t like my answer of “tourism” after a six-month absence from Russia. After waiting 10–15 minutes, I was called into an office for a talk. A different officer let me explain everything fairly quickly, and they didn’t try to look at my phone. It’s also annoying that customs officers X-ray luggage on arrival, and in some places there’s a full customs search on departure as well.
Anna
I mostly live in Russia, but I go to Italy for a month every year to see relatives there. There are other trips sometimes too, but the experience is roughly the same overall. I get through passport control fine, but I’ve noticed more questions lately — and I’ve heard from others that questioning has increased in general, especially for men (purpose of the trip, return tickets, and so on).
The last time — and this wasn’t even at the border, just going through the green channel exit at Pulkovo — they asked a lot of questions: purpose of the trip, how many days I’d flown for, where I’d originally flown in from. Fine. But then they suddenly asked how many euros I’d entered the country with and how much I had left, including how much I’d spent on purchases. I said “definitely under 500 euros in purchases,” and then they asked how much I’d entered with — the difference came out to around 250–300 euros. The young border guard said, “the math doesn’t quite add up, but fine,” and let me through.
I guess I’ll need to keep my receipts so the math works out next time. Before this, there were no questions of this kind, and in general I was rarely questioned at all.
Andrey
I come to Russia once a year to see my parents, and every time I depart from Moscow, the electronic passport control system flags me for additional screening by a border service officer. That’s when the real ordeal begins. Already in line, it’s clear many other passengers are in the same situation — they’re leaving Russia on one-way tickets.
The border guard’s own behavior adds to the tension: he scans the passport on several computers, cross-checks the data against every available database, keeps swiveling in his chair, and every so often stares intently at me, as if gauging my reaction. The atmosphere is so tense that you can’t help feeling he’s hunting for the smallest detail that might look suspicious.
Compared with passport control in other countries, the wariness and suspicion toward passengers here feels especially acute.
Anton
I travel once or twice a year to see my family, always arriving and departing through Moscow.
Fortunately, I’ve never had any problems — no questions, ever.
Alexander
I live in Russia and travel abroad a couple of times a year. I was tried for discrediting the military in 2023 and fined 40,000 rubles. In the fall of 2025, I flew to Paris and passed through passport control with no problems.
In August 2026, I decided to fly from Mineralnye Vody to Armenia for three days, just to walk around. Going through passport control there, a female officer told me to wait for additional screening and kept my passport. I was called into an office, where two officers asked me to unlock my phone and hand it over, which I did. One scrolled through it while the other asked questions: why are you flying, what’s your job, who are your parents, which countries have you visited since 2014, have you ever been convicted, do you have access to state secrets?
Inside, I was panicking that they were scrolling through my phone — personal messages, browser history — but I didn’t let it show. They wrote down my phone’s IMEI number and asked me to sign a paper agreeing to take a polygraph test whenever summoned. They said that if I didn’t sign, I’d stay there another three hours and miss my flight, so I signed. Then they told me to wait outside but kept my phone. As I understand it, they copied all the data off it to study later — or maybe installed something of their own on it too. Who knows.
On the way back to Russia three days later, there was no interrogation, but they again took my unlocked phone and carried it off to an office for about 40 minutes.
Khaidar
After I moved to Germany, I wanted to keep visiting my parents. In Russia, they usually just asked where I’d come from and where I was going. [Then they would say]: have a good trip!
In April 2025, they took my passport and examined it: Why Foreign Ministry of Russia? I live and work in Berlin! They took the passport and [said]: wait. The whole busload of us waited eight hours! Then came the interrogation: How did you get your passport? What’s your attitude toward the war in Ukraine? Toward Putin? Toward [the] Crocus [City Hall terrorist attack] (I’m Muslim)? Do you pray? And a phone check.
Ivan
I’ve lived in Germany for seven years now but go to Russia about once a year to see my parents. I’d never had problems at the border, so I didn’t prepare much — I didn’t wipe my phone or delete any messages, figuring I had nothing to hide. This time, after passport control, they asked me to wait. An officer came over and asked if I had a second phone. I said no.
“What about old phones?”
I said there was an old iPhone with a cracked screen lying at home.
He asked:
“Where exactly at home?”
At first I thought it was just a routine question, so I said it was in a desk drawer. They took me to a separate room and asked me to unlock my current phone. The officer scrolled through the photos for quite a while. There was nothing special there: trips, food, friends, screenshots. Then he stopped on a photo of me standing next to trash bins in Berlin.
“Why did you take a photo with trash bins?”
I explained that a friend had just happened to photograph me on the way home.
“Just happened?”
He asked me to open the photo’s date. Then the geolocation. Then he zoomed in on one of the bins. There was a sticker on it that said, “No to war.”
I hadn’t even noticed that sticker before. The officer asked:
“Do you agree with what it says?”
I said I sort my trash. He asked again:
“What do you mean?”
I had to explain the German waste-sorting system. After that, the conversation somehow shifted to plastic for a long while. He asked why bottle caps are now attached to the bottles and whether that annoys me. I said it sometimes does. He wrote something down. Then they found a photo of breakfast. There was bread, cheese, coffee, and a jar of jam.
“What kind of jam?”
I said French.
“Why French?”
I said it was on sale. He asked me to open my banking app and find the jam purchase. We couldn’t find the purchase, because my girlfriend had bought the jam. Then the officer asked for my girlfriend’s last name. I told him.
“Is she a German citizen?”
“Yes.”
“Why does she buy you French jam?”
I no longer knew what the right answer was, so I said:
“Because we live together.”
After this he first looked at me very closely.
“So you have a shared household?”
I said, probably, yes. He wrote something down again. Next they opened Telegram. Among the recent messages was a conversation with my mom. Mom had written: “Everything’s ready for your arrival.” The officer asked:
“Ready for what, exactly?”
I said the room.
“What room?”
“My old room.”
“Why is it still yours if you’ve lived in Germany for seven years?”
I said that’s just what my parents call it. He asked me to call my mom.
Mom picked up and immediately asked:
“Did you get through?”
The officer raised his eyebrows.
“Get through what?”
Mom explained she meant the border. Then, for some reason, she added:
“We’ve already put the potatoes on.”
The officer asked:
“Why did you put potatoes on?”
Mom said:
“To boil.”
After that, he asked to put the call on speaker and spent about 10 minutes talking with my mom about how many potatoes she’d bought, exactly where, and why she’d decided to boil them before I even arrived.
At one point, mom asked:
“Young man, would you like some potatoes?”
Pavel
[I go to Russia] once every six months to a year. There have never been problems on entry — border guards usually let me through quickly and rarely ask questions, maybe because my arriving flights are from Yerevan or Istanbul. There are usually more questions on departure, about the purpose of the trip and how long it’s for, but even those feel like they’re asked out of boredom.
The only unpleasant experience was in 2022, when they made me turn out all my pockets and flipped through all my books and notebooks looking for cash. Otherwise, everything always goes smoothly. The most interesting moment: border guards once asked to see my foreign diploma, just out of curiosity.
Yekaterina
I come once a year to visit my mom and see friends. This summer I traveled alone with two children (ages 3 and 7) through the Estonian border, at the Koidula crossing. To get there, we took a ferry from Helsinki to Tallinn and spent the night there. In the morning we took a commuter train and rode four hours to Koidula. This used to be probably the most deserted border crossing, located somewhere in the middle of nowhere.
But at the start of summer, hours were cut at the other Estonian crossing point, Narva (where people almost always stand in line for a whole day or longer), and apparently some people decided to look for other routes. So by the time we got to the border, there was already a line, though it seemed small — you have to walk about a kilometer from the train station along the road and then through the bushes, and everyone tries to hurry there right away, so it turns into this sad race of people with suitcases and rolling bags.
The line moved gradually, and the Estonian border guards and customs officers at Koidula are pretty nice, friendly people. But then a double-decker bus arrived, and all its passengers — about 50 people, probably — were let ahead of the line. Still, credit to the Estonians: everyone got through in about an hour, probably. We got through without any problems too, and started moving toward the Russian checkpoint.
And then, around a bend, we saw a strange crowd of people gathered in front of a closed gate. It turned out the Russian border guards didn’t want people crowding up there, because of that bus we’d seen, plus an earlier one, and they were checking them for an extremely long time. So people were standing in front of this ridiculous gate in the heat, waiting. An hour, two hours — some had already been waiting four hours.
It was simply unbearable. Elderly people, families with children in the heat. And about 50 meters (about 164 feet) away was the Russian checkpoint, this nice big building with trees and shade… But no, you wait here. People were outraged, people talked to “the person in charge,” but they weren’t authorized to split up the crowd. It was very hard and upsetting.
Anonymous
I flew from Serbia to Nizhny Novgorod to see my parents, glad they’d introduced direct flights. Next time I’ll fly through Moscow, screw it. They pulled aside almost half the people for questioning. They asked whose Crimea it was, whether I supported the SVO, why I’d left the country, and asked to see my Instagram, Facebook, Telegram. They asked me to explain visible tattoos.
Everything on my phone was clean, and I showed all of it — I had the feeling that if I refused, it would only get worse, but still, the fact of it. They searched my contacts for numbers starting with +380. Then they said “welcome home” with this little smirk. It felt like they just enjoy terrorizing people. I read afterward that this happens a lot in Nizhny Novgorod. The woman behind me in line had children with her.
Klim
Since the war began, I’ve been to Russia four times by plane and twice by car. There was a two-and-a-half-hour interrogation in Zhukovsky about my attitude toward the SVO, an examination of my phone contacts and reading of my Telegram messages, and then they took my phone away entirely for “technical analysis.”
Ivan
I should start by saying that I’m a citizen of Kyrgyzstan, one of the Central Asian republics with especially close political, economic, and cultural ties to Russia. Russian has official status there, Russian media occupies a prominent place, and the republic pursues a fairly accommodating policy toward Russia. Kyrgyzstan has even repeatedly found itself at risk of secondary sanctions because of its trade and economic ties with Russia.
We have relatives living in Russia, so from time to time we visit and stay with them in the Kaliningrad region. I’ve been to Russia in 2021, 2023, and 2025. During the first two trips, nothing came up at the border at all — everything went completely routinely: I said hello, handed over my passport, got a stamp, and moved on to my next flight. But 2025 turned out differently. That was when I first felt, through my own experience, what I had previously only known as other people’s stories about bias against migrants and people from Central Asia.
My mother and I arrived at Sheremetyevo together. At passport control we ended up in different lines. Mine was moving more slowly, hers faster, so at some point I moved closer to her and ended up at the neighboring window. Her turn came. She handed over her passport, the border guard stamped it, and let her through. I submitted my passport right after. My mother stepped a bit further away and waited for me by the exit. The border guard took my passport and said dryly, almost angrily: “Go wait. You’ll be called.” That was it — no explanation of where to go, what to wait for, how long it would take, or why I was even being held. We had no phone connection; connecting to Wi-Fi at Sheremetyevo without verification through a Russian phone number was impossible at the time.
When my mother realized I wasn’t being let through, she asked the border guard not to send her on ahead and to let her stay next to me. He replied irritably: “No. You go ahead, he stays.” The door closed. We ended up on opposite sides of it: without contact, without explanations, in complete uncertainty. What felt especially humiliating was not understanding what I was even guilty of. I hadn’t broken any rules — I had registered in advance with ruID and come to the country on an ordinary private visit, to see relatives. So why was I being treated as if I were some kind of suspect?
Meanwhile, right in front of me, citizens of Russia and Belarus were let through without any trouble, while many people with Central Asian passports and features typical of the region were sent to wait. The border guard’s window was free for a while, so I decided to go up again and ask what I should do, who exactly was supposed to call me, and for what reason. “I already told you: you’ll be called!” he barked. I had to step back. I stood near the passage and waited. After a while, through the general noise, I heard an announcement over the loudspeaker: someone was being called by name to go to a room with a specific number. That’s how I first learned there were special rooms nearby for additional screening.
I went looking for them. People had already gathered near these rooms, most of them from Central Asia. And at that moment it felt especially strange to think about all the talk of customs unions, economic integration, friendship between peoples, and “allied relations.” At the level of official rhetoric, we’re partners and friends. But standing there, I didn’t feel any of that at all. The situation was made worse because we had a connecting flight from Sheremetyevo to Kaliningrad three hours after landing. By that point, only about an hour and 40 minutes remained before departure, and there was still no clarity.
People were called into the rooms one by one. From those waiting, I heard that officers there ask detailed questions about the purpose of the trip, demand that phones be unlocked, and go through their contents. I was never called into one of those rooms myself. But I remember very clearly the feeling of total helplessness — when your passport is somewhere with someone you don’t know, no one explains anything, you can’t reach a loved one, and you don’t even know if you’ll make your next flight.
Time passed. Finally a border service officer came out with a whole stack of passports and started reading off names. After that, they took us back to passport control. About 40 people stood waiting for their names to be called, then went up to the window one at a time. When I was finally let go, about half an hour remained before the flight to Kaliningrad. I ran out into the terminal with two heavy bags. My mother was waiting there, in tears. That moment, I think, stuck with me more than anything else — not the screening itself, not the lost time, not even the fear of missing the flight, but how easily a person can be left in complete uncertainty, separated from a loved one, without anyone bothering to say even a few human words to them.
At that moment I felt a lot of anger. I wanted Russian citizens to one day be met with the same “hospitality” in our country: to have their passports taken without explanation, to have border officers bark at them the same way, to be separated from relatives, sent to wait for who knows what, have their phones checked, and be made to feel like criminals before they’d even done anything.
But setting emotions aside, the problem runs deeper than a simple wish to respond in kind. I understand there’s serious tension in Russia around migration — problems with crime, illegal migration, the integration of newcomers, the work of law enforcement, and flaws in the migration system itself. All of this can and should be debated. But responsibility for state migration policy lies, first and foremost, with the state. And if a system is built over years that simultaneously draws in millions of foreign workers, poorly controls migration flows, allows abuses, and then tries to make up for its own failures with suspicion toward everyone with the “wrong” passport or appearance — that is not a solution to the problem.
An ordinary person legally crossing the border shouldn’t automatically become a suspect just because they were born in Dushanbe, Bishkek, Tashkent, or any other city in Central Asia. A state’s border has every right to be strict. But strictness and humiliation are not the same thing, just as screening and contempt are not the same thing. And security doesn’t require giving up basic human decency.
Anonymous
Over the past two years, I’ve traveled to Russia for family reasons about once every six months. In my case, the red flag for Russian border guards is that I renounced my Russian citizenship. At passport control, I’m always asked about it, both on entry and on exit.
The most unpleasant case was when I was sent for a conversation with an officer from Russia’s Federal Security Service, or FSB. The conversation lasted about 15–20 minutes. They asked me about my reasons for renouncing citizenship, my job, connections to government agencies in my new country of citizenship, whether I’d traveled to Ukraine, and my attitude toward the war.
They tried to look at my phone, but I’d brought a clean one. When the FSB officer realized that, he immediately lost interest in it — though I still had to explain why my phone was clean. Toward the end of the conversation, they even asked how I had a child if I’d never been married…
My advice to people who have renounced Russian citizenship and travel to Russia: always carry a copy of the certificate confirming you renounced citizenship. They may ask for it at passport control.
Dmitry
I travel every six months, mostly crossing the border by car from Belarus through Lithuania into Kaliningrad; I have dual citizenship with visa-free access to the Schengen area. The Belarusians have always conducted fairly perfunctory interviews on entry into Belarus, and on exit there are usually no questions and only a basic search, or none at all.
But in July, entering the Kaliningrad region from the Lithuanian side at Chernyakhovsk, I went through an extremely unpleasant screening — effectively an interrogation with fingerprinting and biometric sample collection and a four-hour interview, during which FSB border service officers read through all my messenger correspondence, went through all my contacts and photos, compiled my entire life story, and took very detailed notes on four typed pages. They probed my political views, asked whether I belonged to any banned movements, in particular the LGBTQ+ movement, asked about my job, and took my boss’s contact information.
I left demoralized and humiliated, fully aware that I would never cross a Russian checkpoint by car again. After that, the 12–19-hour wait at Belarusian customs, with surprisingly friendly staff, doesn’t seem so bad.
P. S. My phone wasn’t always in my line of sight — officers stepped out with it several times — so I can’t guarantee that no third-party software was installed on it.
Nailya
I flew to Russia for two weeks in the second half of May. It was time to renew my internal passport. I’d last been there in December 2021, so this was my first trip since the [full-scale] war began. Before that I used to fly twice a year, even during the pandemic, and nothing abnormal ever happened — it was always calm. This time, too, nothing happened to me.
I flew out of Kazan at the end of May. The room with the border guard booths is very small. There were something like four or five booths, I remember four lines, and people were packed tightly together because there wasn’t much space, the border guards worked slowly, and crowds built up.
Apparently, one line was specifically set aside for “non-Russians.” There was one family, Tajik I think, with a child, age 3 or 4, standing there for about 15 minutes. The man answered questions in fairly good Russian — the room is small, you can hear everything — but then they picked the child up, and the border guard started asking the child something, and the little girl couldn’t answer.
Then the border guard just started stupidly yelling across the whole hall: “Where did you get this certificate? You bought it, didn’t you? She doesn’t even speak Russian. Admit it — did you buy the certificate? How much did you pay, where did you buy it?”
He kept shouting like that for another five minutes, accusing and insulting this family, who were simply frozen with fear, in front of everyone. And no one came over to him, no one told him to stop; all his colleagues and superiors just kept working as if nothing were happening. It became unbearably disgusting and repulsive, both toward my fellow citizens and toward the country as a whole, where civil servants allow themselves to “talk” to people like that. Shameful.
Andrey
I was traveling from Russia to Kazakhstan in June 2025 when I was pulled off the train for additional screening. They demanded I unlock my smartphone — I refused. They held me at the station for almost a full day, beat me, and tortured me. I ended up having to give them access to all my devices. An X-ray eventually showed two broken ribs.
Nastya
I try to go to Russia every year. I love my hometown and my family and loved ones, and it’s very hard for me when I don’t see them for a long time. It’s always a little nerve-wracking, because since the war began I’ve openly spoken out against it on social media. My friends and relatives know my position. So do random people online.
Every time, I prepare my gadgets, wiping chat histories and browser history. I’ve never been checked. But sometimes there are unpleasant questions — unpleasant mainly because of the tone the border guards use. For some reason, women seem especially prone to this. Very hostile looks, as if you’re guilty simply for coming home to visit.
I really want to keep being able to come to Russia, and I’ll keep doing it for as long as I can.
Besides the rudeness and hostile looks from border guards, it’s unsettling when someone from the line gets taken off to a separate office. I’ve seen that happen a couple of times over my five trips.
Sonya
I hadn’t been back since 2022. In 202-something, I flew into my hometown with my young son. We got off the plane and were first in line for passport control. After the standard questions about my residence and permanent residence permits, the female border guard sent me to “sit off to the side.” After that, they questioned me at length about whether I’d had plastic surgery, whether I had a twin sister. They took me into a separate room and, shining a flashlight in my face and enlarging my passport photo, compared every millimeter.
Then they asked whether my son spoke Russian, went up to him, and asked who he was flying with. He was nervous and stayed quiet. They asked him my name, and he used the pet name he calls me at home. After that, yet another — the fourth — customs officer tried to scrutinize me, whispering to a colleague that “there used to be a mole on her cheek, and now there isn’t,” implying the passport wasn’t mine. They suggested I log into Gosuslugi to verify my identity. I refused, offering instead to show my internal passport. Finally, after about an hour and a half, they let us through.

EU plans most far-reaching sanctions on Russia in coming months
EU sanctions must be approved unanimously. Traditional EU packages against Russia have frequently been dogged by lengthy disputes
The European Union intends to significantly expand sanctions against Russia in the coming months over its war in Ukraine, the bloc’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, told a German newspaper.
“EU sanctions have already cost Russia dearly, depriving Russia’s war machine of over €1 trillion (US$1.16 trillion) and for autumn I am putting forward the most far-reaching sanctions listings since the start of the war,” she told Die Welt.
“Once adopted, they would immediately raise the total number of sanctioned Russian entities by a third. The pressure must keep growing until Moscow ends its war,” said Kallas, who leads the European External Action Service (EEAS) – the EU’s diplomatic service.
She did not elaborate on timing or details of the new designations, but EU diplomatic sources later said the EEAS would propose about 1,600 individuals and entities based in Russia and focused on Moscow’s military-industrial complex.
The designations will include travel and transaction bans as well as asset freezes, they added. The EU has already listed nearly 3,000 people and companies.

Türkiye's central government budget posts deficit in July
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:47:14 UTC
20:47:14 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
17 August 2026•Update: 17 August 2026
Türkiye's central government budget posted a deficit in July as expenditures exceeded revenues, the Treasury and Finance Ministry reported on Monday.
Revenues increased by 28.8% to 1.41 trillion Turkish liras ($30.03 billion) in July compared to the same month last year while budget expenditures rose by 59.8% year-on-year to reach 1.79 trillion liras ($38.07 billion) during the month.
The central government budget posted a deficit of 378.1 billion liras ($8.04 billion) in July.
Non-interest expenditures jumped by 48.4% to 1.46 trillion liras ($31.12 billion) compared to July 2025.
The non-interest balance showed a surplus of 110.7 billion liras ($2.3 billion) in July of last year.
Personnel expenses surged by 43.3% to 461.5 billion liras ($9.81 billion) in the same period.
During the January-July period, total budget revenues went up by 37.4% to 9.19 trillion liras ($195.61 billion).
Budget expenditures for the first seven months reached 10.52 trillion liras ($223.7 billion) with a 36.6% increase.
The seven-month budget balance yielded a deficit of 1.32 trillion liras ($28.09 billion).
Tax collections in the January-July period amounted to 7.85 trillion liras ($167.01 billion), reflecting a 37.3% annual rise.
Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek stated on a Turkish social media platform NSosyal that the government maintains fiscal discipline despite the negative impacts of geopolitical developments.
He noted that Türkiye is advancing in line with budget targets despite forgoing significant tax revenues within the scope of the sliding scale system to support disinflation and the effects of balancing domestic demand on revenue performance.
The non-interest budget surplus, a major factor in reducing the debt burden, increased by 228 billion liras ($4.7 billion) year-on-year in the January-July period to reach 470 billion liras ($9.8 billion).
Simsek emphasized that the domestic debt rollover ratio was kept at 87% by considering financing conditions.
The government will continue to direct the fiscal space provided by increased effectiveness in revenue policies and strengthened spending discipline to priority areas to support the disinflation process, he added.

Putin visited Kuril to 'punish' Japan over Ukraine stance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:47:00 UTC
20:47:00 KST

Putin visited Kuril to 'punish' Japan over Ukraine stance
August 17, 2026
The first-ever visit by Russian President Vladimir Putin to one of the disputed Kuril islands off the far northern tip of Japan last week triggered a swift and angry response from Tokyo.
Japan Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in a social media post that Putin's visit was "absolutely unacceptable" while referring to the islands, which it calls the "Northern Territories" as "inherently Japanese territory."
Russia's Foreign Ministry said in response that the islands are an "integral part" of Russia.
The Kuril islands were seized by Soviet troops two weeks after Japan's official surrender ending World War II on August 15, 1945, with the 17,300 Japanese residents forced to leave over the following year.
Putin toured a school, a hospital and industrial facilities on the island of Iturup, which Japan refers to as Etorofu. The visit came just two days before the 81st anniversary of Japan's surrender at the end of World War II.
"This was clearly a message to Japan," said James Brown, a professor of international relations specializing in Russian affairs at the Tokyo campus of Temple University.
"Russia has been angered by Japan's support for Ukraine and for the closer ties that Tokyo has been building with European members of NATO," he told DW.
"So there is a clear desire to punish Japan," he said. "But there is also a domestic element to this … as a visit like this can generate patriotic support among Russians of all political stripes."
Russia and Japan's longstanding territorial row
Successive Japanese governments have consistently taken the position that the islands were illegally annexed, with the dispute so impacting bilateral ties that the two nations have yet to sign a formal peace treaty.
The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 and the subsequent economic hardships gave Japan renewed hope that Moscow could be convinced to return the islands in return for economic assistance or even joint development of the region.
Former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe was arguably the most proactive Japanese leader on the issue, meeting with Putin on a number of occasions in an effort to convince the Russian leader to come around to Japan's way of thinking.
However, all of these diplomatic efforts came to naught, with Russia amending its constitution in 2020 to ban the ceding of any part of Russian territory to a foreign power. Moscow's relations with Japan further deteriorated after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Toshimitsu Shigemura, a professor of politics at Tokyo's Waseda University, told DW that these latest developments are just another nail in the coffin for Japan's ambition concerning the islands.
"Tokyo has already summoned the Russian ambassador and made a formal diplomatic protest, but sanctions are already in place over the Ukraine war and I think it will be difficult for Japan to add more," Shigemura said.
"Japan is importing Russian energy and, because of the situation with Iran, that has become even more important, which leaves Tokyo in a relatively weak position," he added.
Putin tests Japan
Shigemura believes that Putin — potentially in consort with China and North Korea — is attempting to weaken Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi because of the firm line she has taken on security issues in the region. He added that Putin is aware that Takaichi's domestic poll numbers are softening, and likely assesses the Japanese leader will not respond more forcefully than a protest.
Shigemura added that Russia's revised constitution and deepening nationalist sentiment encouraged by state propaganda effectively makes it "impossible" for the islands to be returned to Japanese control.
"Putin may be weak now, but he is cooperating with China and North Korea to challenge Takaichi, who has few options," he said. "And even after Putin has gone, there will be no interest in a new Russian government to return the islands."
Brown agreed, saying that while a few "excitable commentators" in Japan will see Putin's eventual departure from the Kremlin as an opportunity, whomever ends up controlling Russia will be unlikely to align with Japan's territorial interests.
"It did not happen with the collapse of the Soviet Union and all through Russia's subsequent economic difficulties so I don't see any new Russian leader who comes in as countenancing returning the islands," he said.
Edited by: Wesley Rahn

Trump scales down US-S. Korea joint military drills hours from start
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:47:00 UTC
20:47:00 KST

President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military drills with South Korea, calling them “inappropriate and hostile,” just hours before exercises began Monday.
Trump cited his "good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in his latest rebuke to long-standing alliances with Western partners.
South Korean officials said the exercises had begun as planned and that they hoped the personal chemistry between Trump and Kim would bring them back to talks.
North Korea has not responded publicly, though it has previously voiced anger at the regular joint maneuvers, which take place in the South.
The drills began as American allies in East Asia fret over North Korean displays of weapons capabilities and its growing alignment with Russia as well as traditional backer China.
"Based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un, of North Korea, I am not happy with the fact that the United States has, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military Exercises with South Korea," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
"These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful," he added.
He took direct aim at South Korea, writing: "I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, 'No thanks!'"
As it was too late to cancel the drills, Trump said he had ordered Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to "substantially reduce" them.
The 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises are designed to prepare for a possible war with North Korea.
Colonel Ryan Donald, spokesman for the U.S. and South Korean Combined Forces Command, has said they will simulate combat against North Korean troops steeled by their deployment on Russia's side in its invasion of Ukraine.
The maneuvers kicked off as "previously notified and scheduled", South Korea's Defense Ministry said.
Seoul's presidential office said it remained in "close coordination" with Washington over the exercises.
The office "hopes that the friendly relationship between the leaders of the United States and North Korea will lead to meaningful dialogue."
Pyongyang decries the drills as dress rehearsals for an invasion.
It recently test-fired a ballistic missile over the Sea of Japan and warned Friday it could respond to the exercises with a "new level of deterrent."
The U.S. stations about 28,500 troops in South Korea to bolster the country's defenses, a legacy of the 1950-53 Korean War that ended with an armistice rather than a peace treaty.
But Trump's repeated criticism of time-honored alliances has cast doubt on American commitments to security in East Asia.
Asked if China supported new dialogue between the United States and North Korea, Beijing's foreign ministry said on Monday it had "noted the relevant reports."
"Maintaining peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and promoting the political settlement of the peninsular issue are in the common interests of all parties," spokesman Lin Jian said.
In Taiwan, which relies heavily on a long-time security agreement with the United States, President Lai Ching-te said his government would propose record defense spending equivalent to over $35 billion for 2027.
China claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to annex the self-ruled island.
The U.S.-South Korean drills comprise 18,000 South Korean troops and counterparts from U.S. forces, and will focus strongly on drone warfare, GPS disruption and the role of cyberattacks, Colonel Donald had said.
Downsizing the exercise will "damage alliance coordination, slow the process of South Korea taking on greater responsibility for its own defense and weaken deterrence against possible conflicts in Asia," Leif-Eric Easley, a professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul, told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University, told AFP Pyongyang was unlikely to be moved by Trump's announcement.
"The North will only view it as meaningful if the joint exercises are canceled in their entirety rather than scaled back," he said.
Experts say North Korea has expanded its nuclear and missile capabilities since the breakdown of Trump's negotiations with Kim, whom he last met in person in 2019.
Kyiv recently said that up to 50,000 North Korean troops are due to deploy to Russia, although it has provided no evidence or a time frame for the deployment.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, in making the claim, asked Seoul to supply air defense systems to protect against Russian missiles, a request that has gone unanswered by the South.

Warning after Dutch blood donor infected with West Nile virus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:46:24 UTC
20:46:24 KST

Warning after Dutch blood donor infected with West Nile virus
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A case of West Nile virus has been detected in a Dutch blood donor in the first infection of its kind for six years.
The donor, who lives in Utrecht province, is though to have contracted the virus in the Netherlands, as they have not been abroad recently, the public health agency RIVM said.
The virus was confirmed after the patient reported mild symptoms of West Nile fever. Blood bank Sanquin subsequently carried out laboratory tests on a number of samples.
Some 80% of people who contract the virus have no symptoms, but around 1% develop neurological problems, mainly people over 50 with weakened immune systems. In rare cases it can be fatal.
The disease mainly occurs in birds, but can be transmitted to other species, including humans, by mosquitoes. There are no known cases of transmission between humans.
Horse and bird infected
The RIVM said the virus had also been detected in a horse and a bird in different locations in the Netherlands, indicating that mosquitoes that carry the virus are active in the country.
The agency advised people to wear clothes with long sleeves, apply mosquito repellent and use screens or mosquito nets to keep the insects out. It added that the risk of contracting West Nile virus in the Netherlands was small.

EU business registrations drop, bankruptcies rise in Q2
Unknown

11:45:56 UTC
20:45:56 KST

Gökhan Ergöçün
17 August 2026•Update: 17 August 2026
Business registrations in the EU dropped by 0.5%, while bankruptcies climbed by 5.7% in the second quarter of 2026, official data showed.  
The EU's statistical office, Eurostat, reported Monday that business registrations decreased in five out of eight sectors of the business economy during the April-June period.
Industry saw the largest drop in registrations, at 3.6%, followed by accommodation and food services at 3.4% and education and social services at 3.2%.
The number of business registrations increased sharply in the information and communication sector by 8.8%.
The construction sector recorded a 1% increase, while financial services remained stable.
Bankruptcies increased in five out of eight sectors in the second quarter.
The largest increases in bankruptcies were recorded in education and social activities at 21.1%, transport at 11.4% and financial services at 6.8%.
Decreases in bankruptcies were recorded in accommodation and food services at 2.6%, construction at 1.7% and trade at 1.2%.

Italy's working-life expectancy just 33 years, 2nd lowest in EU says CNA
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
13:45:21 CEST
20:45:21 KST

Italy's working-life expectancy is
just 33 years, the second lowest in the EU, think tank CNA said
Monday.
                                    
                                       
				Italy is one of the European countries where people live
longest, but also one of those with the fewest years spent in
the labour market.
                                    
                                       
				In 2025, the expected working life expectancy stood at 33 years,
the second lowest figure in the European Union after Romania and
a full four and a half years less than the EU average of 37.5
years.
                                    
                                       
				The CNA notes this, explaining that the improvement compared to
2024 is minimal: just over two months, compared to a three-month
increase recorded in the European average. Last year, the
Italian indicator was 32.8 years, while the EU average was 37.2.
                                    
                                       
				The gap with the major European economies remains considerable,
explains the CNA.
                                    
                                       
				The expected working lifespan reaches 40.2 years in Germany,
37.5 in France, and 36.8 in Spain.
                                    
                                       
				In the Netherlands, it reaches a staggering 44 years—eleven more
than in Italy.
                                    
                                       
				The most critical figure concerns women, notes the CNA: in
Italy, the expected working lifespan is just 28.4 years,
compared to 35.4 years on average in Europe. The gap between men
and women is 8.9 years, the highest in the EU.
                                    
                                       
				This result is consistent with a female employment rate of 58%,
almost thirteen points below the EU average, and the widest
gender employment gap among Member States.
                                    
                                       
				The indicator does not measure retirement age or the number of
years actually worked by those in continuous employment,
explains the CNA: it estimates the years a 15-year-old can
expect to spend in the labor force, either employed or
unemployed, based on current demographic conditions and
participation levels.
                                    
                                       
				The Italian result - observes the CNA - therefore reflects above
all the late entry of young people, discontinuous careers and
low female participation.

US moves to ramp up naval anti-ballistic missile production
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
12:45:17 BST
20:45:17 KST

Boeing has signed seven-year framework agreements to increase production of key components for the Standard Missile-3, a ship-launched anti-ballistic missile designed to intercept threats outside the Earth’s atmosphere.
The United States is moving to increase production of Standard Missile-3 anti-ballistic missile interceptors, with Boeing signing new seven-year framework agreements covering critical hardware used in both the SM-3 Block IB and Block IIA variants, according to the company.
The agreements with the U.S. Department of War and Raytheon, an RTX business and prime contractor for the missile, are intended to increase Boeing’s output of avionics and ejector assemblies needed for higher production rates of complete SM-3 interceptors. Boeing said the three parties will begin ramping up production ahead of a final multi-year award while negotiations continue under the new framework.
The SM-3 is a ship-launched anti-ballistic missile used as part of the Aegis Ballistic Missile Defense system. Its principal role is to intercept ballistic missiles during the midcourse portion of their flight, when the target can be travelling outside the Earth’s atmosphere. Rather than relying on an explosive warhead, the interceptor uses a kinetic kill vehicle intended to destroy the target through the force of a direct collision.
That makes the SM-3 distinct from shorter-range air-defence weapons intended primarily to engage aircraft, cruise missiles or other threats within the atmosphere. The missile is designed for ballistic missile defence, providing US and allied forces with an exo-atmospheric interception capability from Aegis-equipped warships and related missile-defence infrastructure.
Bob Ciesla, vice president of Boeing Precision Engagement Systems, said, as quoted in a news update: “This gives us a clear demand signal to build and deliver SM-3 interceptors at the levels needed to counter threats.” He added: “The SM-3 is an essential part of the layered air and missile defense architecture that protects the U.S. and its allies worldwide.”
Both the Block IB and Block IIA variants are covered by the new arrangement. The Block IIA is the larger and more capable development of the weapon, designed to provide greater range and engagement capability against ballistic missile threats. Boeing’s role includes producing avionics and ejector assemblies, components that must be available in sufficient numbers if Raytheon is to increase output of complete missiles.
The decision to begin increasing production before completion of the multi-year contract is intended to give industry a clearer demand signal and reduce the delay between a procurement decision and higher delivery rates. Boeing said the framework supports the administration’s effort to strengthen what it calls the “Arsenal of Freedom” and aligns with Pentagon acquisition reforms intended to accelerate the delivery of priority weapons.
The SM-3 agreement also follows an existing arrangement involving Boeing, the Department of War and Lockheed Martin to increase production of seekers for the PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptor.

Guidance: Military low flying: air weapons ranges activity
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
12:43:58 BST
20:43:58 KST

Military low flying: air weapons ranges activity
Notification of extended operating hours and low flying activities for UK air weapons ranges: Donna Nook, Holbeach, Pembrey Sands, Tain and Cape Wrath.
Documents
Details
The above activity is planned range use but in exceptional circumstances there may be additional activity at short notice.
The MOD is aware of the disturbance that can be caused to local residents by activity at the UK Air Weapons Ranges (AWR). Notification of the pre-planned extended operating hours will be published at the earliest opportunity.
It should be noted that when an AWR is closed, the segregated airspace above it no longer has Danger Area status and reverts to Class G airspace, meaning that it becomes freely available to all airspace users (both civilian and military).
The MOD currently uses 5 AWRs for essential operational training:
- Donna Nook and Holbeach in Lincolnshire
- Pembrey Sands in Carmarthenshire
- Tain in Ross-shire
- Cape Wrath in Sutherland.

Horsing around: How Trump's AI George Washington image has symbolically backfired
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:41:41 UTC
20:41:41 KST

Donald Trump's latest AI-generated image, depicting him horse riding alongside George Washington, has backfired as many have pointed out the symbolic blunder of him riding a black horse in the current climate...
Donald Trump is no stranger to bulk posting AI-generated imagery as part of what has been referred to as “memetic warfare” - a tactic which sees him and his administration flood the zone when it comes to AI slop in order to appeal to his base and beyond.
While this social media strategy isn't new, one recently shared image has once again shown that the use of AI can be detrimental when it comes to conveying the proper message. Specifically, how the AI images he posts frequently backfire due to a lack of understanding when it comes to cultural references.
His recent cultural blunder is a symbolic one, which comes with an image he posted yesterday. It sees Trump horse riding with Founding Father and first president of the United States, George Washington.
The self-aggrandising image sees Washington riding a white horse, while Trump is on a black stallion.
While it's not the first time that Trump has hijacked the figure of George Washington, having posted a series of AI images of himself showing Washington around the new White House ballroom, it didn't take long for many to point out the symbolically charged equine error on show.
The cultural connotations of the black horse are numerous, and usually negative. In Henry Fuseli's 1781 masterpiece 'The Nightmare', the ghostly dark horse is a sleep paralysis demon and the embodiment of repressed dread.
In modern symbolism, the black horse can reflect hidden desires and dark secrets, but generally belongs to a series of images mirroring what psychologist Carl Jung called "the shadow self", which includes repressed anger and shame.
Then comes the Biblical reading, as the black horse is a known reference within apocalyptic contexts. The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse in the Book of Revelation all ride different coloured horses. The white horse is pestilence; the red horse represents war; the pale horse is death; and the black horse is famine, representing food scarcity and economic hardship.
Considering Trump's image comes at a time when the price of gas, food and other essentials have soared due to the Iran war, which has now entered its sixth month, the image of him riding a black horse feels accidentally apt - what some have referred to as a "catastrophic self-own".
Social media users pointed out that Trump's handling of the ongoing US affordability crisis is unfortunately reflected in this symbolically loaded image, while others have made references to pop culture and films, with one X user noting: “Does Trump know that bad guys ride the black horse?”
Much like the red lightsaber SNAFU or the irony of portraying himself as Superman or using Spider-Man references, the misused cultural connotations have once again revealed a certain level of cultural illiteracy...
It's not the only black and white slip-up that has sparked alarm this weekend...
Trump posted a black and white 2028 image on Truth Social, which has been perceived as yet another inidication that he will be persuing a third term and is considering being president in 2028 - despite this being unconstitutional due to a two-term limit.
The image, posted with the caption “We are going to win” has reminded people of how Trump began selling red 2028 caps last year.
“I don’t think he’s planning on leaving,” said one X user, while another commented: “America needs to brace for chaos in 2028’s elections. NOT GOOD”.
