The new royals: Trump and US foreign policy in the Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:12:00 UTC
20:12:00 KST

Breadcrumb
The new royals: Trump and US foreign policy in the Middle East
In this second term of the Trump administration, personal ties, backhanders, and flattery have all but replaced formal diplomacy in the Middle East.
The son of Steve Witkoff, US Special Envoy to the Middle East, reportedly leveraged his connections to secure billions of dollars in investments from the Gulf.
Overseas investors, including from Saudi Arabia, account for 99 percent of the $6.16 billion dollars managed by Affinity Partners, the investment fund founded and led by Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and informal advisor, who also participated in delicate regional negotiations over Gaza.
A 49-percent stake in World Liberty Financial, co-founded by several members of the Trump and Witkoff families, was recently acquired for $500 million by UAE National Security Advisor Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed, prompting suspicions of a quid pro quo when the Trump administration later allowed Abu Dhabi to access advanced US-made AI chips.
Trump’s foreign policy in the Middle East seems to be built more on personal connections than on professionalism and institutions.
His administration has hollowed out both the National Security Council (NSC) and the State Department, which were supposed to advise and constrain the president and other agencies. The NSC has been reduced to a few dozen personnel, none of whom seem to have much influence on policy.
The US Agency for International Development (USAID), once an important actor for global humanitarian good and a crucial instrument of US soft power, has been destroyed.
The peripatetic Secretary of State, Marco Rubio - triple-hatted since 2025 as national security adviser, secretary of state, and administrator of what little was left of USAID - seems more concerned with a potential run for the presidency in 2028 than with doing any of these jobs, or being the nation’s top diplomat. Rubio seems to be merely a spokesperson for policies decided elsewhere.
The return of court politics
Trump’s approach mirrors the trappings of Europe’s monarchical age: a courtly clique of family members, loyalists, and wealthy patrons. Scholars have aptly described this personalist style of foreign policy as “neo-royalism.”
The Trump administration treats international affairs not as a series of relations between sovereign governments, but as interactions between a closed circuit of sovereigns, in which only the leaders - and their inner circles - decide the fate of entire peoples.
Perhaps the most vivid example of this approach is seen in how Palestinians are denied agency, their fate referred to a distant “Board of Peace” chaired by the US president, on which a permanent can be purchased for a billion dollars. The lives of ordinary people are no longer seen as part of nations that should be respected; they are consigned to the status of commodities to be traded rather than nations.
Private enterprise, buttressed by state power, now calls the shots. Economic policies on tariffs and technology increasingly correspond to tributes in the form of “investments” that benefit the president’s inner circle. Louis XIV, call your office.
Whoever is in the room with Trump at any given time is now paramount. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, both real estate professionals, are more powerful and influential diplomats than Secretary of State Rubio, but they bring little experience to bear on complicated issues and have failed to draft, define, and implement agreements with real weight to end disastrous conflicts.
The failed ceasefire agreement between Iran and the United States, for example, left out many key details and opened the door to the resumption of hostilities. The Gaza ceasefire agreement, also negotiated by Witkoff and Kushner, remains valid on paper but has allowed Israel free rein to conduct attacks in Gaza that have cost the lives of more than 1200 Palestinians so far.
The humanitarian aid and reconstruction of the Strip promised by the agreement have yet to materialise. But the White House has never formally renounced the plan, and key figures tied to the Board of Peace have continued pushing variations of the "Gaza Riviera" vision, in which the Strip is redeveloped by wealthy outsiders, including the Gulf monarchies and American investors potentially associated with Trump.
Diplomacy for the highest bidder
Across the Middle East, it is this new royalty that decides policy. The Iran war began in February 2026 with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran’s nuclear and military capabilities, but it continues aimlessly today, led by a president who appears to have no goal in mind but personal triumph.
Trump seems to have believed that America’s successful seizure of Venezuela’s president, Nicolás Maduro, was a blueprint for an easy decapitation strike against the Iranian regime. It was not.
Neo-royalism has little time for international law, much less human rights or democracy, which, although seldom the driving force, was in the past at least as a nominal component of US foreign policy.
But not today. The horrors of Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel have given way to what legal experts and scholars have called a genocide in Gaza, with no accountability for the perpetrators. Washington has failed to condemn Israel’s war, let alone stop arms sales to Israel.
The personalised foreign policy of President Trump has displaced the US-led international order, which - with all its flaws and failures - established a blueprint for global relations that helped secure a measure of peace for some seven decades after World War Two.
Multilateral treaty organisations such as NATO and numerous bilateral agreements - unequal and flawed as they may have been - arguably helped stem the tide of global authoritarianism.
Today, the floodgates have been reopened. There is no sense that the United States stands for a stable world order. The tumult in the Middle East is simply one manifestation of that fact.
The president's threats to seize Greenland, the seemingly random application of tariffs to include many of America's closest allies, haphazard military actions such as seizing the Venezuelan president, and air strikes in Nigeria, demonstrate the chaos that one-man rule over US foreign policy has unleashed.
In the Middle East, Trump’s new royalism is likely to provoke a scramble for new alliances and deals - economic, diplomatic, and military - that can help replace Washington’s erstwhile commitment to stability.
That, in turn, is likely to fuel existing regional conflicts and may spur new tensions. Globally, we are living in a new era of uncertainty, fuelled by leaders’ unfettered pursuit of private interest and personal agreements above the public good.
From Washington is a new monthly series from The New Arab and the Arab Center Washington, DC, examining the ideas, interests, and power dynamics driving US policy towards the Arab world
Charles W. Dunne is a non-resident Senior Fellow at the Arab Center Washington, DC
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

Israeli strike kills Lebanese poet and translator who brought French classics to Arab readers
An Israeli airstrike on southern Lebanon killed the Lebanese poet and translator Zeinab Mahdi Nassereddine, her husband and their four children, erasing an entire family in one of the deadliest attacks of a wider Israeli bombardment over the weekend.
The family was killed before dawn on Saturday when a strike hit the house where they were staying in the town of Ansar, in the Nabatieh district of southern Lebanon.
Nassereddine died alongside her husband, Ali al-Hajj Hassan, and their four children, Zahraa, Hassan, Hussein and Abbas.
Their deaths drew particular attention in Lebanon because of Nassereddine's place in the country's literary world. A poet who began publishing in the 1990s, she later became known for translating major works of French literature into Arabic.
But the strike that killed her family was also part of a much broader increase of violence across southern Lebanon by Israel, one that has raised fresh concerns over whether fighting between Israel and Hezbollah could again expand despite diplomatic efforts to contain it.
Lebanon's health ministry said at least 11 people were killed in Israeli strikes across the Nabatieh area in southern Lebanon, including women and children, bringing the total killed in Israeli attacks since 2 March to at least 4,346, with 12,301 others wounded.
Nassereddine came from a family deeply involved in Lebanon's cultural scene. Her father, Mahdi Nassereddine, is a researcher and editor of classical heritage texts, while her brothers are the poet Mohammed Nassereddine and the artist Hussein Nassereddine.
She began writing poetry during the 1990s, publishing some of her earliest work in Nahar al-Shabab, the youth supplement of Lebanon's leading Annahar newspaper.
Her brother Mohammed later recalled that Gebran Tueni, the late Lebanese journalist and newspaper executive, would select some of her poems for prominent placement in the supplement, where she appeared alongside a generation of writers who later became familiar names in Lebanon's cultural press.
Nassereddine eventually devoted much of her work to literary translation from French.
In 2021, Dar al-Rafidain published her Arabic translation of Victor Hugo's "The Hunchback of Notre-Dame". She also translated Alexandre Dumas's "The Three Musketeers", part of a body of work centred on bringing French classics to Arabic readers.
A Lebanese group representing families of children killed in conflict condemned the strike in Ansar on Sunday and urged the government to document the attack and pursue legal avenues for accountability.

Attack on Israeli troops near Ali al-Taher hills

At about 2:30 a.m. on Saturday, an explosive drone struck an Israeli engineering force operating near the hills, seriously wounding an officer and two soldiers, according to Israeli and Lebanese reports.
About half an hour later, Israeli aircraft and artillery began heavily bombarding the hills and surrounding areas before the strikes spread to other parts of the Nabatieh district, including Ansar and Deir al-Zahrani.
Israel claimed the subsequent attacks allegedly targeted Hezbollah commanders and infrastructure in retaliation for the drone strike.
Lebanese accounts said Israeli forces had been attempting to push further towards the hills when the engineering unit was attacked. Israeli reports suggested the soldiers were already conducting an operation in the area when the drone struck them.
The hills, situated between Kfar Tibnit and Nabatieh al-Fawqa and overlooking the city of Nabatieh, have taken on growing military importance. Israel says they contain underground Hezbollah facilities and has been seeking greater access to the area.

‘A better tomorrow’: UK schoolchildren get the chance to rewrite the ending of the Bayeux Tapestry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:09:41 UTC
20:09:41 KST

Nearly 1,000 years after it was made, the Bayeux Tapestry is back in England – and UK schoolchildren are being asked to imagine its missing final scene.
For some British schoolchildren, history homework this autumn is going considerably further than a worksheet on the year 1066.
A new competition is asking primary students across the UK to design and stitch a new final panel for the Bayeux Tapestry, a 70-metre-long embroidered account of the Norman conquest of England with a famously missing final section.
Nobody knows exactly what it originally showed. Rather than trying to reconstruct the lost scenes, however, the children are being asked to imagine what might have come after the conquest, picturing a “better tomorrow” rather than another battle.
What is the Bayeux Tapestry?
Despite its name, the Bayeux Tapestry is an embroidery made of coloured yarn stitched onto linen rather than a woven tapestry.
Semantics aside, its scenes recount the events leading up to William of Normandy’s invasion of England, culminating in his victory at the Battle of Hastings in 1066.
It was likely made in England in the 1070s and may have been commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, William’s half-brother, to decorate the new cathedral in Bayeux, which helps explain the name.
Unlike much of the surviving art from the period, it’s not religious. It instead offers an unusually detailed glimpse of 11th-century life, depicting ships, weapons, horses, buildings, clothing and food alongside its account of the conquest.
The tapestry’s final section has been missing for centuries. No one knows when it disappeared, nor exactly what it showed, although scholars believe it probably depicted William the Conqueror’s coronation.
Finishing the ‘unfinished’ story
Now it’s up to British students to create a new future from ancient history.
The free UK-wide competition, called Beyond the Battle, is open to key stage 2 pupils – roughly aged 7 to 11 – who will work as a class to design and stitch their panels.
Run by Art Explora UK in partnership with English Heritage, the competition will begin in late September this year.
The winning classes will receive a fully funded trip to London to see the original tapestry, as well as a visit to the 1066 Battle of Hastings Abbey and Battlefield, or to another Norman site managed by English Heritage.
Their work will also go on display in a special exhibition, while each winning class will receive a bespoke textile made by artist Jessica Grady.
Runners-up will receive a funded visit to their nearest English Heritage Norman site.
A long journey back to England
The tapestry normally hangs at the Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux in Normandy, but the museum closed in September 2025 for a two-year renovation. Its temporary closure paved the way for the historic loan agreement between France and the UK.
The Bayeux Tapestry will be on display at London’s British Museum from 10 September 2026 until 11 July 2027, in Room 30 of the Sainsbury Exhibitions Gallery. It’s the first time the tapestry has been displayed in the UK since it was made nearly 1,000 years ago.
While it’s in London, objects such as the Sutton Hoo treasures and Lewis chess pieces will travel from the British Museum to museums in Normandy.
Apart from the historic return to England, there’s another historical hook.
Next year marks 1,000 years since William the Conqueror was born in Falaise, and European officials are organising the ‘Year of the Normans’ around the anniversary.
Nearly 1,000 events are being planned across Normandy and seven European territories with a Norman legacy: the UK, Ireland, the Channel Islands, Flanders, southern Italy, Norway and Denmark. The programme will include exhibitions, concerts and medieval-themed festivals – as well as a new tapestry depicting the missing section.
The 25-square-metre tapestry was designed by French artist Hélène Delprat and will be woven by Atelier Tapisserie Guillot d’Aubusson. It depicts William’s coronation and will be shown at Westminster Abbey in 2027 before moving to Falaise.

Is the world experiencing more earthquakes now than before?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:09:18 UTC
20:09:18 KST

Is the world experiencing more earthquakes now than before?
Al Jazeera examines a decade of earthquake data to see how 2026 compares and explains how and where earthquakes strike.
In the past month, three earthquakes of magnitude 7 or above have struck Indonesia, Colombia and Mexico, killing hundreds of people. In June, two powerful quakes seconds apart levelled swaths of northern Venezuela.
The run of disasters has prompted a question asked after every cluster of big earthquakes: Is the Earth shaking more than it used to?
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera examines a decade of earthquake data to see how 2026 compares and explains how and where earthquakes strike.
The 10 largest earthquakes of 2026
According to the United States Geological Survey (USGS), there are about 20,000 earthquakes recorded globally each year, roughly 55 a day. However, most of these are too weak to be noticed by people.
It is when earthquakes reach magnitude 6 and above that large-scale damage tends to occur.
The map below shows 2026’s 10 largest earthquakes. The Philippines recorded the strongest, a magnitude 7.8 off Mindanao in June that killed more than 100 people. Venezuela’s 7.2 and 7.5 quakes, also in June, killed more than 6,300 people. The most recent quakes, in Mexico in July and Colombia and Indonesia in August, were all magnitude 7.4 or higher.
Ten years of earthquakes and where 2026 stands
From 2016 to 2025, the world recorded an average of 133 earthquakes of magnitude 6 or greater each year. They ranged from the lowest number of quakes at 99 in 2024 to the highest of 157 in 2021.
By mid-August this year, 91 earthquakes of magnitude 6 or above had been recorded worldwide, including 11 above magnitude 7. Both those numbers are slightly ahead of the past decade’s pace but still within the normal range. None reached magnitude 8 or 9, the most destructive categories.
What makes an earthquake deadly has less to do with its magnitude than where it hits. Depth, proximity to cities and the strength of local buildings matter more than the number on the Richter scale. The deadliest earthquakes of the past decade were not the largest ones. They were the ones that struck beneath population centres.
Is there such a thing as ‘earthquake season’?
No. Long-term records show that earthquakes occur throughout the year with no consistent seasonal pattern. The US Geological Survey says scientists have never been able to predict when a major earthquake will strike because the tectonic stress that builds along fault lines over decades or centuries cannot be tied to a 12-month cycle.
Aftershocks can continue for months or even years after a major quake.
Instead of predicting individual earthquakes, seismologists calculate the probability that a large quake will hit a given area over a span of years, work that underpins life-saving building codes. They also run early warning systems that alert people once a quake has begun.
How do earthquakes happen?
An earthquake, in the simplest terms, happens when the Earth’s crust shakes.
The Earth’s outer shell is broken into a puzzle of moving pieces called tectonic plates, roughly 100km (62 miles) thick. They sit on hot mantle rock that is solid but slowly flowing, dragging and pushing the plates over millions of years.
The plates are always moving, but their edges often lock together, building stress until the rock gives way along fractures called faults, which can run for hundreds of kilometres. Many faults are well mapped, but others are discovered only when they rupture.
Where do earthquakes happen?
The most seismically active zone in the world, accounting for roughly 90 percent of the world’s earthquakes, is the Pacific Ring of Fire. It forms a belt stretching along the western Americas to the Russian Far East and down to Southeast Asia and New Zealand.
The Ring of Fire includes Japan, the Philippines and Indonesia.
Earthquakes can also strike outside the Ring of Fire. The Alpide belt, stretching from Java through the Himalayas to Turkiye and the Mediterranean, produces 17 percent of the world’s largest quakes, and rarer tremors occur along ancient faults far from any plate boundary.
How are earthquakes measured?
Earthquake size is measured on the moment magnitude scale, which reflects the energy released at an earthquake’s source.
Magnitudes are based on a logarithmic scale, meaning each whole-number increase represents about 10 times more ground shaking and roughly 32 times more energy released.
To put that into context, earthquakes registering a magnitude of 4 to 4.9 are considered light but may still cause some damage.
A magnitude 5 quake produces 10 times more ground shaking than a magnitude 4, releases about 32 times more energy and can cause moderate damage to buildings.
Magnitude 6 quakes are typically considered strong, producing 100 times more ground shaking than a magnitude 4 and releasing about 1,000 times more energy.
Magnitude 7 earthquakes are considered major with the potential to cause significant loss of life and damage to buildings and infrastructure.
Earthquakes registering magnitude 8 or higher are classified as great and can result in near-total destruction across a wide area.
Magnitude, depth, proximity to inhabited areas, soil conditions and the chance of triggering secondary disasters, such as tsunamis and landslides, are just some of the many factors that determine how deadly and destructive an earthquake is.
What are the largest quakes on record?
The most powerful earthquake ever recorded was a magnitude 9.5 quake that struck Valdivia, Chile, on May 22, 1960, generating a Pacific-wide tsunami.
Four years later, a magnitude 9.2 quake struck the Prince William Sound region of Alaska, the second most powerful on record.
On December 26, 2004, a magnitude 9.1 to 9.3 quake off the coast of Sumatra triggered a tsunami that killed about 228,000 people across the Indian Ocean.

NATO no longer deters Russia. A new coalition could
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:07:12 UTC
20:07:12 KST

Russia will keep escalating until Europe shows both the political will and the military capability to stop it, argues Hans Petter Midttun—and NATO can no longer supply either. In an interview with the Guildhall news agency, the former defense attaché to Ukraine makes the case for the Ukraine-anchored coalition he has argued for since long before this interview: Northern Europe together with Ukraine, credible from the day it is declared.
This interview was conducted in Russian by the Guildhall news agency and is republished here in an edited English translation. The subheadings are Euromaidan Press's.
Hans Petter Midttun is a non-resident research fellow at the Centre for Defence Strategies and a former defense attaché to Ukraine.
Why NATO no longer deters Russia
It seems that despite everything the West has done to deter Russia, the Russian threat to the West—particularly to the Baltic states and NATO members in general—is only increasing. What is your diagnosis? Why has the Western deterrence strategy failed, if you agree that it has?
Yes, I absolutely agree, and I have been saying this for quite some time.
To begin with, it is worth questioning your basic formulation—"the West." I have often used the term myself. Almost every time I write about what is happening, I use it. But recently I have begun to question whether it is still accurate.
If we regard the West as a civilization, as a strategic space, then we understand what we are talking about. Usually that means NATO and the European Union. But if we regard it as a political actor, as an entity responsible for deterrence, the situation becomes much more complicated.
For some time now I have questioned the viability of NATO. I am an officer myself, and I have been oriented toward NATO throughout my career. I have always believed in the Alliance. Almost everything I have done over nearly 40 years has been based on NATO doctrine, strategy, and tactics. But since 2022, I have seriously begun to question it. I have written publicly that I doubt the Alliance can survive in its current form. And I have said very clearly that it no longer deters Russia. I can prove it.
Please do.
There are three reasons I have pointed to repeatedly.
The first and most fundamental: if NATO were genuinely deterring Russia, Russia would never have invaded Ukraine. To most people that probably sounds strange, because under NATO's 2010 Strategic Concept, still in force in 2022, NATO was not obliged to defend Ukraine and had not declared any intention to. There was no commitment to Ukraine as such.
But the Strategic Concept stated clearly, under its second core task—crisis management—that in the event of a conflict threatening the security of the Alliance, NATO would use a combination of political and military instruments to manage and resolve it. What is happening in Ukraine is precisely such a conflict. It threatens the security of the Alliance, and the Alliance recognized this many years ago. So before the invasion, Russia must have looked at NATO and concluded it would not act.
The second point: if Russia were deterred, it would not be waging a constantly escalating hybrid war on NATO territory. It is already waging one. And, shamefully, NATO has not even acknowledged the fact. It talks in general terms, but it never calls what is happening what it is: a hybrid war, a campaign to undermine the Alliance. We are not acting on the basis of that reality.
The third point: if Russia were deterred, it would not now be preparing for a potential attack on NATO members.
So there are three very clear indicators that, whatever NATO believes about its own deterrence, Russia does not believe it. And that is what determines whether deterrence works. Deterrence is not determined in Washington or Brussels. It is determined in the Kremlin.
Why the answer cannot come from NATO
We still need to deter Russia from expanding its aggression further, including directly against NATO, which the Kremlin clearly regards as one possible scenario. How should the deterrence strategy be adjusted? What mechanisms need to be created?
Let me take one step back first, because I think it matters. I would argue this cannot be achieved through NATO. NATO will never be able to deter Russia. I would go further: NATO is no longer the solution. It has become part of the problem.
There are several reasons. During the Cold War, NATO took the risk of strategic miscalculation extremely seriously. If the Soviet Union provoked us—by sending a combat aircraft, a warship, or moving ground forces in our direction—NATO always responded. This was done to leave no room for miscalculation and no impression of local weaknesses the Soviet Union could exploit.
After the collapse of the Soviet Union, we stopped acting this way—despite the fact that, for roughly 15 years before the full-scale war, Russia was challenging us, testing us, and doing many of the things the Soviet Union once did. We lost our credibility.
On top of that, a transatlantic divide has opened—a rupture between Europe and the United States. We see an America that is no longer a reliable ally but is becoming more of a strategic opponent. America treats the European Union as an opponent, and that creates an entirely different strategic environment. We are talking about a former ally that threatens to seize NATO territory—Greenland—and talks about annexing Canada. All of it opens a window of opportunity for Russia that it could previously only have dreamed of.
Part of the responsibility lies with Europe too, because we did not take security and defense seriously enough. We did not invest. We are now extremely vulnerable, with critical weaknesses that can be exploited. So we are in a moment of weakness, and Russia understands it. Russia also understands that this window is limited in time, and that is precisely what raises the risk of more serious developments.
The coalition, and which countries would form it
I appreciate the deeper assessment, but that is still diagnosis. What is the treatment? What concrete steps need to be taken, and by whom, to deter Russia again?
I spent so long on the previous question because I wanted to completely destroy the notion that NATO will be the solution. It will not. That means we have to look for something else.
We need some of the qualities NATO had in the 1980s. At the height of the Cold War, the member states—there were 16 then—knew who the adversary was. They all saw it the same way. They understood its strategic goals, its doctrine, its capabilities, its theater of operations. So every state was committed to countering the threat. We invested in defense—Europe spent roughly 3.8 percent of GDP on it—and we had a common strategy. In a sense we were a coalition of the like-minded. That is what I advocate rebuilding.
Trending Now
But it also means that, initially, a significant share of NATO members, and possibly some EU members, would have to remain outside such a structure. If you want a structure built on a common understanding of the threat and unity of purpose, you have to accept that not all states share the same aspirations. That is why I have named a number of countries that should become its founding members, with the ultimate goal of including all of Europe. But we start with a group of the like-minded.
Which countries do you have in mind?
My argument begins here, and it is one of the reasons the coalition is necessary: Ukraine will never become a member of NATO. To be honest, that was already clear five, four, and three years ago. It is a shameful situation. But that is exactly the point. Europe needs strategic autonomy. We have to stand on our own feet and defend Europe ourselves. We can no longer rely on the United States, so we need to build something else.
I believe this coalition should be built around Ukraine and the NB8 countries—the Nordic-Baltic Eight—together with the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Poland, and the Netherlands. Essentially, Northern Europe together with Ukraine. That configuration alone already creates enormous credibility. It would bring together not only Ukraine's battle-hardened armed forces—the Ground Forces, National Guard, Special Operations Forces, air defense, and Unmanned Systems Forces—but also high-tech European air forces, navies, and special operations forces. Almost immediately you have a structure with real credibility, because we share common values and a common understanding of how to fight Russia and how to defeat it. Simply announcing such a coalition would have a deterrent effect.
What you are saying resonates with me. But the Russian threat exists here and now. Building full European strategic autonomy without the United States would take at least five years. What do we do in the meantime? How do we deter Russia now?
I would challenge that. I have heard the argument many times. We are not talking about forces that exist only on paper. The armed forces of the countries I named already exist today, and they are built on the same standards—NATO standards. We do not need to invent new ones. They share a doctrinal foundation and, in many respects, similar strategic approaches. We can use NATO technologies, standards, documents, doctrines, and research—everything the Alliance has already created is available to us. And Ukraine is already largely NATO-compatible. Will such a coalition be as effective today as it could be in five years? No. But Ukraine itself was not as effective five years ago as it is today.
The nuclear question
What about nuclear weapons? Full deterrence of Russia is hard to imagine without a nuclear component.
I would challenge that too. We have all grown accustomed to relying on the idea of nuclear deterrence. I am not saying it does not matter, and some of the states I named do possess a nuclear capability.
But not comparable to Russia's arsenal.
Yes, but it does not quite work that way, and that is the point. Both Russia and the United States have lost wars without using nuclear weapons. The consequences of using them are so catastrophic that the great powers—including China—regard the threshold as extremely high. You could argue Russia might not have attacked Ukraine if Ukraine had kept nuclear weapons. Possibly. But that is in the past. The war is already under way, and after years of it—after Ukraine has crossed practically every one of Russia's so-called red lines—Russia still has not used nuclear weapons against Ukraine.
So we cannot abandon the idea of a coalition simply because it lacks an arsenal comparable to Russia's. On the contrary: we have to recognize that the threshold for use is so high that the probability of actual use is extremely low. Not zero, but extremely low. And we are no longer talking only about deterring Russia. Russia is already at war with Europe and waging war on Ukraine. We are talking about how to end that war, with the tools we have. We cannot do it through NATO. We cannot rely on the United States to do it for us. So either we build something genuinely credible, or we accept that Russia will keep acting against us.
Why it starts with a declaration
You said the cost of using nuclear weapons must be unacceptable to Russia. The same logic can apply to the conventional threat. What concrete steps can we take now to make the cost of further conventional aggression unacceptable to the Kremlin?
The solution is right in front of us. The starting point is what Ukraine itself has said many times: Russia will escalate for as long as we let it, and it responds to nothing but strength. So until we—the West, or the coalition, whichever term you prefer—stand up and demonstrate both the political will and the military capability to act, Russia will keep escalating.
That is why, when you asked about the timeline, I said: if these countries had united yesterday, today, or tomorrow and announced the creation of such a coalition and their intention to fight together, that alone would completely change Russia's strategic assessment.
Today Russia is fighting one country, Ukraine, supported by around 50 partner states. But it is still fighting only one country. If that declaration were made tomorrow, the situation would change radically. Russia already finds it difficult to fight Ukraine; it would face a fundamentally different reality if Ukraine formally joined a coalition with European military powers.
So this is not only about physical capabilities. It is about changing Russia's perception of its strategic environment. And it starts with a declaration.
The next step would be the actual conduct of military operations, if necessary. But it begins with the declaration. That would completely change Russia's strategic calculus.

South Korea Fires Warning Shots After North Korean Troops Cross the DMZ

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

North Korea steps up hacking with AI and deepfakes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:04:26 UTC
20:04:26 KST

- North Korea-linked groups carried out 99 state-sponsored cyberattacks in the first half of 2026, with South Korea targeted 19 times, the most of any country.
- Combined attacks from North Korea, China and Russia totaled 158 incidents, up 7.5 percent from the prior six months, according to S2W.
North Korea-linked hacking groups launched 99 state-sponsored cyberattacks in the first half of 2026, with South Korea absorbing 19 of them, the most of any country, the Korea Times reported, citing a new threat intelligence report from cybersecurity firm S2W.
The figure makes North Korea the most active state-backed threat actor globally over the period, ahead of China’s 33 incidents and Russia’s 26. Combined attacks from all three countries totaled 158 between January and June, up 7.5 percent from 147 in the second half of last year. Most of that growth came in the first quarter, driven by intensified activity from North Korean and Russian groups.
North Korea’s attack volume rose 13.8 percent compared with the previous six months, according to the S2W report. The United States was the second most targeted country by North Korean actors, with eight recorded attacks.
Pyongyang-linked groups concentrated on the cryptocurrency, IT and software development sectors, using fake job postings, code repository infiltration, generative AI and deepfakes to gain access. South Korean cybersecurity firm AhnLab has separately tracked North Korean-linked spear phishing campaigns against South Korean targets this year using malicious LNK and CHM file attachments to deploy backdoors and infostealers.
Russian-linked attacks rose 30 percent to 26 incidents, with 10 aimed at Ukraine. Russian groups also expanded into Eastern Europe, striking Poland and Romania twice each, targeting European government and military organizations alongside their Ukraine-focused activity. The S2W report found Russian operations increasingly combined intelligence gathering with destructive attacks meant to disrupt or destroy systems.
China-linked attacks fell 17.5 percent, from 40 to 33 incidents, with Chinese groups sustaining long-term espionage operations against the telecommunications sector while expanding into Southeast Asia and the Middle East. S2W’s analysis found Chinese operators relied on legitimate cloud APIs, VPNs and network tunneling tools alongside malware to maintain extended access to compromised networks.
Across all three countries, S2W identified 15 unique exploited vulnerabilities used in 19 separate incidents during the first half. North Korean groups relied primarily on social engineering and tricking users into executing malicious files, while Chinese groups exploited vulnerabilities in public-facing servers and network edge devices. Russian groups favored document-based malware along with webmail and network device vulnerabilities. Phishing, exploitation of public server vulnerabilities and abuse of proxy and cloud services were common across all three.
The report projected that infiltration of software development ecosystems, long-term access to telecommunications and infrastructure networks, and destructive operations tied to geopolitical conflicts will continue into the second half of the year. S2W also flagged Iran-linked groups as a risk to South Korean manufacturing, aviation and energy companies through Middle East-based supply chain attacks, saying the threat warrants close monitoring.
A cybersecurity expert cited in the report said organizations need to move beyond fragmented defenses focused solely on email and malware blocking toward integrated security frameworks covering development environments, supply chains, internet-facing assets, cloud systems and AI environments. The expert also called for stronger intrusion detection, immediate rotation of account credentials, and the buildup of immutable backup and recovery systems.

20:04:00 KST

Russian forces shelled and struck front-line and border regions across northern, eastern, and southern Ukraine over the past 24 hours, killing at least eight civilians and wounding more than 40, regional authorities reported on 17 August. Sumy, Donetsk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts reported deaths, while people were wounded in Kharkiv, Kherson, Dnipropetrovsk, Chernihiv, and Odesa Oblasts.
Russia's daily strikes have hit populated areas and civilian infrastructure both near the front line and far behind it. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that 13 regions had come under attack over the past week, with more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided aerial bombs, and 62 missiles, most of them ballistic, launched at Ukraine.
North: FPV drone attacks firefighters’ vehicle
In Sumy Oblast, Russian forces carried out more than 50 strikes on 24 settlements across 11 communities. A drone strike in the Sumy community killed a 75-year-old man and a 72-year-old woman and wounded another civilian, the Sumy military administration said. It also said two more people were wounded in the Seredyna-Buda community. A mass drone attack on Sumy caused large fires and wounded at least one person, Sumy city military administration head Serhii Kryvosheienko said.
In Chernihiv Oblast, a 41-year-old man was wounded in a Geran drone strike on the Kozelets community, Head of the Regional Military Administration Viacheslav Chaus said. He added that Gerbera drones destroyed a hangar and farm equipment in the Kholmy community. In a border village in the Horodnia community, an FPV drone struck a yard, and a second FPV drone hit a firefighters' vehicle that had arrived at the scene. A house later caught fire. A critical infrastructure facility was also hit.
In Kharkiv Oblast, six people were wounded in strikes on Kharkiv and nine other settlements. The heaviest damage was reported in Izium, where 19 houses and four apartment blocks were damaged, head of the Regional Military Administration Oleh Syniehubov said.
East: Russian strikes destroy 30 stalls
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian forces killed two residents of Kramatorsk and wounded 18 people across the region, Head of the Regional Military Administration Vadym Filashkin said. In Sloviansk, round-the-clock strikes damaged critical infrastructure and destroyed 30 stalls at the Lisnyi market, Sloviansk City Military Administration Head Vadym Liakh said.
  In Poltava Oblast, two industrial facilities were hit, causing fires, and drones also attacked another industrial facility in Myrhorod district, Head of the Regional Military Administration Vitalii Diakivnych said. No casualties were reported.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russian forces attacked four districts nearly 20 times from the evening of 16 August, wounding five people, Head of the Regional Military Administration Oleksandr Hanzha said. He added that houses and outbuildings caught fire in Pavlohrad and Nikopol district.
In Zaporizhzhia district, two people were killed and three wounded, Head of the Regional Military Administration Ivan Fedorov said. He also reported 1,217 strikes on 60 settlements across the oblast, including 20 air strikes, about 846 drone attacks, and 350 artillery strikes.
South: strike damages civilian vessel flying the flag of Togo
In Odesa Oblast, a night-time strike on port infrastructure damaged a civilian vessel flying the flag of Togo and wounded four people, one of them seriously, Head of the Regional Military Administration Oleh Kiper said.
In Kherson Oblast, in the early morning, Russian forces killed two residents of the village of Novokayiry in the Mylivska community, – Head of the Kherson Regional State Administration Oleksandr Prokhudin said. Also russian forces attacked 52 settlements, including the regional capital. Six people were wounded, while 11 apartment blocks and 15 private houses were damaged, Prokudin said.
In Mykolaiv Oblast, Russia attacked with Shahed and Gerbera drones, but no casualties were reported, acting Head of the Regional Military Administration Heorhii Reshetilov said. He added that the roof of an agricultural enterprise building was damaged in the Horokhivska community.

Ministry of Finance explained how aviation leasing should be taxed, which led the Economic Security Bureau to open criminal proceedings
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
14:03:41 EEST
20:03:41 KST

Ministry of Finance explained how aviation leasing should be taxed, which led the Economic Security Bureau to open criminal proceedings
Kyiv • UNN
The Ministry of Finance stated that leasing payments for the use of airplanes and helicopters should be taxed in accordance with the Tax Code, which does not provide for the payment of royalties. At the same time, the Economic Security Bureau is investigating cases against five airlines, demanding payment of an additional 15% tax.
The Ministry of Finance of Ukraine confirmed that the taxation of aircraft leasing must be carried out in accordance with the provisions of the Tax Code of Ukraine and international treaties on the avoidance of double taxation, which take precedence over national legislation. Ukrainian tax legislation contains no provisions under which lease payments for aircraft and helicopters would qualify as royalties. However, the Economic Security Bureau applied a different interpretation of these provisions and is investigating criminal cases against at least five Ukrainian airlines, demanding payment of an additional 15% tax on non-residents’ income, UNN writes.
Despite the fact that Ukrainian tax legislation, which has remained unchanged with regard to leasing for decades, and international treaties clearly describe how taxes on helicopter and aircraft leasing should be paid, the Economic Security Bureau decided, at its own discretion, to change this approach. The ESB is investigating cases involving at least five air carriers, including UIA, Constanta Airline, Urga, H3Operations and Skyline, allegedly over the failure to pay an additional 15% tax on non-residents’ income to the Ukrainian budget under aircraft leasing agreements. Investigators equate lease payments with royalties and treat aircraft and helicopters not as means of transport, but as "equipment."
What the Finance Ministry says
"Regarding the taxation of aircraft leasing transactions, we note that the taxation of such transactions is carried out in accordance with the procedure and at the rates established by the Tax Code of Ukraine," the Finance Ministry said in response to an inquiry from UNN.
It is worth noting that the Tax Code of Ukraine contains no provisions requiring the payment of royalties for transactions involving the leasing of air transport from non-residents of Ukraine.
"A resident, (...), who has chosen the simplified taxation system, or another non-resident conducting business through a permanent establishment in Ukraine, who makes any payment of income derived from sources in Ukraine to a non-resident or a person authorized by that non-resident, (...) withhold tax from such income, (...) in their amount and at their expense, payable to the budget at the time of such payment, unless otherwise provided by the provisions of international treaties of Ukraine with the countries of residence of the persons in whose favor the payments are made, which have entered into force. The requirements of this paragraph do not apply to income received by non-residents through their permanent establishments in Ukraine," the Tax Code of Ukraine states.
Ukraine has concluded and ratified treaties on the avoidance of double taxation with dozens of foreign states. These international treaties are applied first and determine whether such income is subject to taxation in Ukraine and at what rate. They either fully exempt the income from additional taxation or significantly reduce the tax. The Finance Ministry emphasizes that these conventions take precedence in application.
"At the same time, pursuant to paragraph 3.2 of Article 3 of the Tax Code of Ukraine, if an international treaty of Ukraine, the binding force of which has been approved by the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine, establishes rules other than those provided for by the Code, the rules of the international treaty shall apply," the ministry said in response to an inquiry from UNN.
ESB cases against airlines
Law enforcement agencies obtained analytical conclusions after, in 2024, the previous team at the State Tax Service published an article proposing that leasing transactions involving transport from non-residents of Ukraine be taxed as royalties. The documents, which according to representatives of the aviation market are similar to one another and appear to have been written "from the same template," formed the basis of the aforementioned criminal cases against air carriers.
Lawyers interviewed by UNN point out that investigators ignore the current international conventions on the avoidance of double taxation ratified by the Verkhovna Rada. According to them, the automatic assessment of an additional 15% tax in Ukraine without taking into account the provisions of a specific convention is, at the very least, debatable.
It is worth noting that, according to the State Tax Service, the airlines underwent tax audits, and only one of them found violations in the taxation of leasing. The remaining tax audits did not reveal any such violations.
"As a result of one audit of companies in the aviation sector, leasing payments were reclassified as royalties. Just one audit," said Viktoriia Kasian, Deputy Director of the Transfer Pricing Department of the State Tax Service of Ukraine.
However, the absence of violations did not prevent the Economic Security Bureau from opening criminal cases against the airlines, believing that they had failed to pay 15% in royalties over the past seven years. At the same time, the list of airlines against which law enforcement agencies have claims over leasing may expand at any moment, since around 40 air carriers use leasing. Thus, the entire civil aviation sector may come under threat.
Representatives of the aviation sector have already publicly stated that they are being pressured by the Economic Security Bureau. In their words, civil aviation has found itself under threat of destruction due to the actions of state regulatory authorities, which could ultimately finish off companies that survived the closure of the airspace and relocation abroad because of the full-scale war. The Ukrainian Air Transport Association appealed to the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Transport and Infrastructure, as well as to the Public Council under the Ministry of Finance, calling for a unified approach to applying tax legislation in the field of aviation leasing to be developed.
Therefore, it is obvious that if the Economic Security Bureau's approach becomes a general rule, airlines may be assessed additional taxes for previous years under agreements that had not previously raised any concerns among tax authorities. For an industry that, following the closure of Ukraine's airspace, is effectively surviving thanks to relocation and operations abroad, this creates the risk of new criminal proceedings and financial claims, as well as withdrawal from the Ukrainian market.

Russia Recruited Nearly 3,000 Africans From 37 Countries For Its War Against Ukraine
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry says at least 2,982 people from 37 African countries have been recruited into Russia’s armed forces, with around 486 killed in the war against Ukraine.
The figures were provided by the ministry in response to a request from Suspilne on August 16.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Foreign Ministry, 35 citizens of 17 African countries are currently being held as prisoners of war in Ukraine. The largest numbers of recruits have reportedly come from Kenya, Egypt, Cameroon, Ghana, Nigeria, Uganda, Algeria, and Mali.
“To recruit Africans, Russian intelligence services employ a wide range of manipulative methods aimed at coercion and deception, including under the pretext of offering civilian employment or education, promising high financial compensation, prospects of obtaining Russian citizenship, or other migration and social benefits,” the ministry said.
In some cases, foreign nationals are pressured into signing military contracts written in Russian under the threat of deportation or imprisonment.
Ukraine is seeking to counter the recruitment campaign through its diplomatic missions in Africa. Ukrainian diplomats regularly inform local officials about cases of Russian recruitment of their citizens and conduct public information campaigns in countries where Ukraine maintains diplomatic representation.
The Foreign Ministry, together with Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, has also launched a dedicated website available in English, French, and Swahili.
According to Suspine, the resource provides verified information about Russian recruitment methods, accounts from people affected by the campaign, analytical materials, practical guidance for potential victims and their families, and channels for reporting suspected recruiters, according to the ministry.
Similar cases have also been reported in other countries. The Peruvian government, for example, has confirmed that 11 of its citizens who joined Russian forces have been killed, while 114 remain missing and three have been captured by Ukrainian forces.
According to Spanish news agency EFE, Peruvian authorities said that among Peruvians recruited into the Russian military were people who are now missing or being held captive by Ukraine.
Overall, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate has identified more than 28,000 foreign nationals serving in the Russian Armed Forces under military contracts, with the number continuing to rise.

Travellers are prioritising cultural immersion over adventure and luxury, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:03:23 UTC
20:03:23 KST

Cultural immersion is overtaking luxury and adventure as a travel priority, while AI and social media reshape how travellers discover and personalise experiences abroad.
Across the globe, cultural immersion is emerging as the leading travel priority, according to the latest research from Skift.
The travel research platform’s Skift State of Travel 2026 report looks at how travel and tourism trends are evolving, including what’s shaping travellers’ experiences abroad.
Its findings show that cultural immersion consistently ranks ahead of adventure and luxury seeking worldwide. In Asia, as many as 50% of travellers were found to be cultural immersion travellers, compared to 32% who prioritised adventure and 30% seeking luxury experiences.
This pattern was also seen in the Middle East and North Africa, North America as well as Europe, with 42%, 39% and 36% of people in each market, being classified as cultural immersion travellers respectively.
Skift’s findings also highlight that in-demand experiences bring together culture with authentic luxury, wellness and nature experiences.
Meanwhile, looking closely at activities, , 71% of respondents said they were most likely to spend on food and culinary experiences, far outranking spends on adventure and nature, arts culture and history, live events and entertainment, health and wellness as well as sports which stood at 48%, 42%, 36%, 36% and 24%, respectively.
At the same time, the report acknowledged 2026 as the “year of intelligence”, a nod to the rise of AI. Its research found that 62% of global travellers are familiar with AI travel-planning tools, while a further 81% of high-income travellers familiar with such tools used them to plan a journey.
Although these developments in technology can make it easy to plan a trip, the report suggests that tech-driven travel is developing side-by-side with a desire for authenticity when it comes to experiences abroad.
Describing authenticity as the “north star” of travel experiences, shifting away from placing a premium on places and instead prioritising specific experiences and emotional attractiveness. According to Skift, experiences are now what dominate travel decision-making, with 43% of travellers from the survey saying experiences are the most important part of travel for them.
“Traveller behaviour is evolving, marked by rising demand for AI-driven personalisation and a shift toward more sustainable choices,” Jean-Jacques Morin, group deputy CEO at Accor, said. “[This is] exemplified by the popularity of ‘dupe destinations’ (less crowded, more affordable alternatives to popular hotspots) and ‘coolcations’ (vacations in cooler climates as travelers seek to avoid extreme heat).”
Social media as a travel-planning tool
Skift’s research also found that social media has evolved from a source of travel inspiration to a full-fledged travel-planning tool.
Some 63% of travellers use social media to get destination ideas and inspiration, while 56% use it to find experiences, restaurants to eat at or things to do, and 45% use it to compare hotels and accommodations.
The research found that travellers also use it for watching travel vlogs or itineraries, searching for deals and promotions, following travel influencers for recommendations as well as reading reviews or watching user-generated content.
Skift also pointed toIShowSpeed’s 12-hour livestream powered by Expedia of his Caribbean tour of Dominica, Guadeloupe, St. Kitts & Nevis and St. Maarten, where a staggering 400 million people tuned in. In the immediate aftermath, searches for St. Maarten had a 70% boost, while Guadeloupe and Dominica searches increased by 50% and 35%, respectively.
But this can be a double-edged sword.
Platforms can help travellers discover lesser-known destinations and experiences, yet, that same virality can quickly turn those hidden gems into the next overcrowded hotspot.
“Social media has destabilised the discovery cycle,” Skift said. “The same platforms that make an unknown destination famous in weeks also make it feel overexposed within months.”
As such, the report added that “oversaturated destinations” introduce fees and visitor caps, which creates damage to the image of tourist hubs. The report added that travellers are instead turning to hidden alternatives with unique experiences, rather than choosing wider-known destinations.

Cooler destinations are drawing tourists — can nature cope?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:03:00 UTC
20:03:00 KST

Cooler destinations are drawing tourists — can nature cope?
August 17, 2026
A ridge with sweeping views across Jotunheimen, a mountain region in southern Norway, seemed like the perfect hiking route for tour operator Georg Sichelschmidt to bring visitors. Then locals informed him it was home to nesting eagles.
The trail remained open. But Sichelschmidt didn't want to disturb the apex predators at home in the massive peaks, dotted with turquoise lakes and glaciers.
"We decided not to use this trail anymore. We had to find another solution," said Sichelschmidt, who runs nature-based tourism company JVB travel.
Norway's right-to-roam rules, known as allemannsretten, give people broad access to nature regardless of land ownership, but also require them to respect it. For Sichelschmidt, who moved from Germany to Norway 16 years ago for its nature, the decision was an easy choice.
But with climate change reshaping summer travel, protecting nature will require far more than individual decisions. According to a 2026 OECD tourism trends report, longer and more intense heat waves across Southern Europe are helping drive interest in cooler destinations. That shift is raising concerns about whether nature in countries like Norway can withstand growing visitor numbers.
Is heat changing the way we travel?
The travel industry has coined the term "coolcation" to promote the shift in summer travel habits. It's too early to know how widespread the trend is, said Daniel Scott, a professor specializing in climate and tourism at Canada's University of Waterloo.
Booking companies, hotels and airlines don't publish data showing how many travelers switch destinations because of heat alone, he said. Still, he added, "we know that people are thinking about it. Some say they are acting on it."
Sichelschmidt said he's seeing the trend firsthand. Partner tour operators offering trips to Mediterranean and the Nordic regions report growing interest in "active" northern vacations, such as hiking and biking, during summer.
"It is difficult to go hiking in France, Spain or Italy in July and August when it is 40 degrees [Celsius, 104 Fahrenheit] plus. The Nordics are a good option to escape from that," he said, adding that Mediterranean travel is shifting to spring and autumn.
More visitors, more pressure on nature
Northern Norway already offers a glimpse of what rising visitor numbers can mean for fragile environments.
Lofoten, with its dramatic cliffs, deep fjords and wild beaches, is home to around 25,000 people. In 2025, it recorded more than 807,000 commercial guest nights, according to Statistics Norway. Increased interest in cooler vacations could add to existing pressure on nature there.
The archipelago is home to hundreds of bird species, including a colony of puffins that could be disturbed by growing visitor numbers. Nesting birds are vulnerable in late summer. But other wildlife can be impacted too, including reindeer during calving season in May and early June, said Elina Hutton, a tourism researcher at UiT The Arctic University of Norway.
Lofoten's coastal heathland, bogs and alpine vegetation are also highly vulnerable to foot traffic. When hikers walk on wet ground, they can damage roots and strip away the thin soil covering mountain bedrock.
Using satellite data, Hutton tracks how growing visitor numbers are affecting trails on Lofoten. Along the route to Kvalvika Beach, an isolated bay only reachable by foot, the worst trails have widened to about 20 meters (65 feet), destroying surrounding vegetation. Northern ecosystems recover slowly from damage.
"That kind of damage is pretty much permanent here," said Hutton, who urges visitors to stick to established trails rather than seeking out "hidden gems" to post on social media.
Managing tourism, not just promoting it
Sichelschmidt believes tour operators can help reduce environmental harm by steering visitors onto well-managed trails, while avoiding the most sensitive areas.
"When we're talking about a large number of people, we need to direct them to where they can go so that the trails can be maintained without destroying nature," he added.
But decisions like Sichelschmidt's to avoid the eagle's nest cannot be left entirely to tour operators. Destinations will have to decide where visitors should go, which areas need greater protection, and how much pressure nature can sustain.
Norway is already experimenting with ways to manage tourism. Under a new law, communities facing particularly high tourism pressure will be allowed to charge a 3% accommodation tax starting in 2027. Hutton said the tax would not reduce visitor numbers but could help in other ways.
"At least it gives us a bit more tools, a bit more money to build better trails, to build better toilets and have better infrastructure to receive this number of tourists," she said.
Some countries are offering ecotourism initiatives that involve visitors in nature conservation work. In the Faroe Islands, for example, the "Closed for Maintenance" initiative invites volunteers to repair trails and maintain natural areas before they reopen to visitors.
Still, destinations, municipalities and tourism businesses need to consider how many visitors they can accommodate and spread tourism evenly throughout the year, Hutton told DW. "It's not good for anybody if we just get more tourists."
Even 'cool' destinations are warming
But as humans continue to burn the fossil fuels heating the planet, the search for reliably cool destinations is becoming harder. Daniel Scott shared preliminary findings from an unpublished study with DW examining how heat risk is changing across Euromonitor's top 100 global city destinations.
The research suggests tourists will increasingly be exposed to higher temperatures and more frequent heat-related risks.
According to the analysis, only nine cities, including Dublin, Auckland and San Francisco, averaged fewer than 10 days per year with temperatures of 32 Celsius (90 Fahrenheit) or higher between 2015 and 2025.
By the 2050s, that number is projected to fall by more than half, highlighting how even traditionally cooler destinations are expected to become significantly warmer.
Hutton finds it concerning to see destinations welcome tourism business opportunities created by Europe's extreme heat. "The same climate change impacts us too in one way or another, and no destination is going to be a winner when the situation evolves like this," she said.
As more vacationers seek cooler weather, Sichelschmidt has decided not to use the term "coolcation" in his company's marketing.
"We don't want to use this situation for promotion," he said. "It's a real situation, but it's sad that we have to talk about it — or that we realize that we are destroying our planet and things change so fast."

Latvia wants €7B from EU to cope with fallout from Russia’s war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:01:00 UTC
20:01:00 KST

RIGA — Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs wants Brussels to hand over €7 billion to help cover the military and economic costs of confronting Russia, as pressure grows over the price of the country’s hard line on Moscow.
The cash, which Riga wants to come on top of other funds earmarked for the country, would amount to almost half of Latvia’s projected €15.1 billion defense bill over the seven-year budget period.
Advertisement
The demand comes at a sensitive moment. Latvia has been one of Europe’s staunchest supporters of Ukraine, sharply increasing defense spending since Moscow's full-scale invasion, even as sanctions and the collapse of bilateral trade have cut deeply into economic links that once ran eastward. But ahead of an Oct. 3 national election, parties arguing that Riga should demand more in return for sanctions and military support are gaining ground.
The European Commission has proposed substantially increasing EU-level defense funding in the 2028-2034 budget, including a €125.2 billion security, defense industry and space pot in the European Competitiveness Fund. That money is designed to finance projects across the bloc rather than provide Latvia with a pre-agreed €7 billion allocation, and the entire budget remains subject to negotiations between EU governments and the European Parliament.
Kulbergs argues that Latvia deserves special consideration because it is borrowing to provide security for countries much farther from the front line. “We are getting our budget deficit to the maximum […] and from that debt we're paying […] the defense of the whole [of] Europe,” the prime minister said at the government chancellery.
Much of Latvia’s military spending ultimately flows back to richer Western European economies, Kulbergs added, pointing to arms purchases from Germany, France, Spain, Sweden and the Netherlands. “We fuel their economies,” he added.
Election pressure
A sharper version of the same argument is emerging on the campaign trail.
Ainārs Šlesers, a veteran populist businessman whose party sits with the far-right Patriots for Europe group in Brussels, says Latvia should demand compensation when it backs EU sanctions on Russia. Šlesers condemns Moscow’s invasion and says support for Ukraine should continue, but argues that Latvia cannot absorb the costs indefinitely.
Advertisement
“We are losing money … we are talking about how to support Ukraine, but we are a victim,” he told POLITICO at his Riga campaign headquarters.
When EU sanctions come up for renewal, Šlesers said Latvia should “get in return support.” Asked whether that could mean withholding Riga’s backing for sanctions, he stopped short of threatening a veto but did not rule it out. “I don't want to talk about [a] veto [now],” he said. “I guess that we [...] will find a peaceful solution.”
Šlesers, who has business ties with Russian oligarchs, said the country needs to eventually restore economic ties with Moscow, and advocated for a quick end to the war. “There are things which we cannot replace because if it's your neighboring country and you're connected historically […] we need to find the right model.”
He argued that whether to hand over territory to Russia should be "a decision by Ukraine" but argued that other countries have lost territory to Russia after conflicts, including Latvia, "to reach [a] peace agreement."
Kulbergs’ center-right party currently leads the polls, but coalition arithmetic could determine how far Latvia’s Russia policy shifts after October.
The far-right, pro-Russia Sovereign Power party, polling second, wants to restore ties with Moscow but is considered off-limits by mainstream parties. Šlesers, polling third, is a more plausible coalition partner — and Kulbergs has left the door open to governing with him.
Advertisement
The center-left Progressives, polling fourth and also hoping to enter government with Kulbergs, warn that bringing Šlesers into the coalition would gradually soften Riga’s line on Russia.
“I’m 100 percent sure Latvia’s foreign policy towards Russia is going to soften over time,” the party’s prime ministerial candidate Andris Šuvajevs told POLITICO outside parliament. He pointed to possible sanctions exemptions for Russian business interests and ministers “speaking in a more friendly tone towards Russia.”
Tough on Russia
Ahead of a new sanctions package due in the fall, Kulbergs called for a total EU visa ban on Russians. EU countries granted more than 630,000 visas to Russian citizens in 2025.
In the last sanctions package, France and Italy resisted a blanket ban on Russian combatants, arguing this issue should be covered by EU visa rules rather than as part of sanctions, while northern and eastern countries pushed for tougher restrictions. The eventual deal created the legal and political basis for barring Russian combatants and ex-combatants who took part in the war — leaving it up to EU countries to decide when the ban would take effect.
“Are we nuts?” said Kulbergs on the delay. “We allow Russian military soldiers to be given visas, the ones killing [Ukrainians] on the field.”
He also urged EU countries to revisit sending Russia’s €210 billion in sovereign assets frozen in Europe to Ukraine, dismissing concerns Moscow could challenge the move after the war.
He called any Kremlin outreach “a useless exercise,” arguing there’s no sign President Vladimir Putin is ready to negotiate and that talks would merely give Russia "breathing time" to make its "next move."
Despite Latvia severing ties with its eastern neighbor, and Kulbergs' hawkish position on relations with Moscow, he said “we have to be open” to reestablishing ties once Russia pays reparations to Ukraine and those responsible for war crimes face justice, pointing to postwar Germany as the example to follow. “Do we isolate Germany because of that? No, it's acceptance of guilt, acceptance of wrongdoing, punishment, and retribution," he said.
After a ceasefire, Kulbergs concluded, "the insecurity of the border will only rise" as the real threat will be a wave of migration as hundreds of thousands of “screwed up” soldiers return from the battlefield seeking a better life and other citizens flee as Moscow's war economy crumbles.

Disabled creatives like me are behind many of your favourite shows – so why has our work support been withdrawn? | Annalisa Dinnella
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:00:53 UTC
20:00:53 KST

When Chris McCausland won Strictly Come Dancing in 2024, he held his trophy aloft and said: “It’s for everyone out there that thought and got told they couldn’t do something. It just shows with opportunity and support and determination, anything can happen.” Later that month, he delivered Channel 4’s Alternative Christmas Message. In it, McCausland warned that Access to Work (AtW), a scheme run by the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), was under threat due to a lack of funding.
AtW provides grants to employers and self-employed workers to cover the cost of reasonable adjustments a disabled person may need in the workplace. Behind McCausland’s jovial reflection on the value of different mince pies was a heartfelt plea to protect this little-known yet vital cog in our national machine.
Like Chris, I cannot do what I do without support. I am visually impaired (I have 5% vision) and I am a television writer. I’ve worked on shows such as Sex Education, Call the Midwife and The Hack. I am currently working on a drama for BBC One about the newspaper editor Harry Evans. My job is my passion, my obsession, my livelihood and a huge part of my identity. But thanks to recent cuts to my AtW support, it has become increasingly difficult, if not impossible, for me to perform.
My grant from AtW is split into two pots: one for taxis (I cannot access public transport independently) and one for a support worker (sighted guide) when needed. In 2025, my grant was cut by 70%, and this year my travel pot was removed entirely. I need to travel. I can’t do my job without attending meetings, rehearsals, writers rooms, sets and post-production facilities. On top of that, I need to network in order to gain future contracts.
AtW didn’t contest these needs – or, indeed, my sight loss – but argued that, as I’m self-employed, I can offset travel expenses against tax. This would reimburse only a fraction of my expenditure. Even more baffling, they also claimed I had failed to submit a contract for “work with ITV”. I had clearly stated that my current job is with the BBC, and had provided a contract and letter from my producer to back this up.
I submitted a reconsideration request and my MP, Ellie Reeves, also contacted the DWP on my behalf. A few weeks later we both received a letter (by post and in small print, which they know I can’t read) informing us that my appeal had been rejected. They restated their earlier claims, including my failure to provide my mythical contract with ITV. So where do I go from here? Nowhere. There is no recourse to appeal against an appeal. I find myself at a legal dead end.
Sadly I am not alone. In the past two years there have been many thousands of stories like mine. When challenged, AtW insists there has been no change in policy and points to a twofold increase in demand over the past five years. It’s true, the system is under strain. Increased demand without a corresponding increase in funding is going to cause a problem; I can’t argue with that. But I can ask: are these cuts by stealth really the best way to solve it?
In 2011, the Sayce report found that for every £1 the DWP put into AtW, it received £1.48 back; it’s obvious this scheme pays for itself. I can certainly prove that I am earning, and paying in tax, a sum far greater than the value of my grant. But must we reduce this argument to numbers on a spreadsheet? I could not make this claim at the beginning of my career. Was I less deserving then? Some claimants have more complex needs than others. Is anyone seriously arguing that their talents should go to waste?
I’m also told this study didn’t take into account the money saved in health and social care. Being employed keeps us fit and well. It keeps the wolves of social isolation from the door. Sadly, it seems no further studies have been conducted. Somewhere along the line, AtW decided to stop collecting data.
When sense-making grants were available, disabled newcomers had the freedom to take the same financial risks as their non-disabled counterparts. Comedians such as McCausland could dart around comedy festivals with their support workers, and many a star was born. Organisations such as Graeae Theatre (our national theatre for disabled people) became lighthouses for talented youngsters – Jack Thorne, the Emmy-winning writer of Adolescence, landed one of his first jobs writing for Graeae’s artistic director, Jenny Sealey (Jenny’s AtW grant was cut this year. After a fierce social media backlash and the support of her MP, it was restored). But in the past year, AtW has become so unworkable that it is already deterring potential talent. Call the switchboard and the recorded voice will tell you that the current waiting time for a new application is nine months.
Those of us campaigning to bring this scandal into public consciousness have spent much time wondering: is this cock-up or conspiracy? Is anyone at the DWP considering the impact on the McCauslands of the future? And what is the new prime minister going to do about it?
If you back us, we will deliver. It’s what Chris was saying when he brandished his glitter ball trophy. A piece of public policy that made money and was a source of national pride has been twisted into something nonsensical, cruel and, quite frankly, shameful. It’s enough to make anyone stop dancing.
- 
  Annalisa Dinnella is a television writer
