Japan tracks four Russian missile boats passing close to its coast off Hokkaido
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:06:48 UTC
17:06:48 KST

Japan's Self-Defense Forces shadowed four Russian missile boats as they passed close to the country's northern coast, the Japanese Joint Staff reported. The warships never entered Japanese waters, yet the move sharpened a diplomatic standoff over islands Russia seized in 1945. Tokyo lodged a protest and summoned Russia's ambassador.
Japan tracked the warships back through the strait
On 14 August, Japan's Maritime Self-Defense Force spotted the four boats near Cape Soya on Hokkaido, heading west. A P-3C patrol aircraft from the 2nd Air Wing watched them and gathered information. The boats stayed 40 kilometers from shore and did not cross into Japanese waters.
The vessels carried hull numbers 916, 946, 971, and 978. Japan had spotted the same four ships on 9 August, 70 kilometers northwest of Rebun Island. They then passed east through the Soya Strait before doubling back.
The transit followed Putin's trip to a contested island
The return passage came days after Vladimir Putin visited Iturup—one of the Kuril Islands—on 13 August. The Soviet Union seized the island in 1945, breaking a neutrality pact it had signed with Japan. Moscow treats the Kuril archipelago as strategically vital and keeps building up forces there. Iturup hosts the Burevestnik military airfield.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called Putin's trip absolutely unacceptable. She said it contradicts Tokyo's stance on the Northern Territories, as Japan calls the islands. Japan's Foreign Ministry summoned Russia's ambassador, Nikolai Nozdrev, and lodged a firm protest. It asked him to pass Tokyo's position to Moscow at once.
What the Molniya-1 missile boats carry
Militarnyi noted that the project 12411M Molniya-1 boats, which NATO calls Tarantul III, come from the Almaz Central Marine Design Bureau. The first entered service in 1981.
They are built to hit surface targets in coastal and near-sea zones. Their main upgrade over earlier versions was four supersonic Moskit anti-ship missiles, replacing the older Termit.
Each boat can reach 41 knots and carries a crew of 40. Its weapons include a 76mm gun, two rapid-fire 30mm mounts, and Igla-1 air-defense missiles.
The four belong to Russia's Pacific Fleet. The oldest, hull 971, entered service in 1990, and the newest, hull 916, in 2003.

====================================================================================================

Exclusive: Brussels keen to monitor UFOs under the radar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:06:04 UTC
17:06:04 KST

Brussels has signalled it is monitoring unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) and has hinted at improving capabilities, according to documents seen by Euronews.
The European Commission seems to have been monitoring unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) under the radar since at least 2023, according to a document from the Commission's defence department seen by Euronews, which pertains to sky and space observations in Malaysia.
"We are getting better at seeing it (UAPs) and better identifying it as our technological capacities improve, but we need to get even better," the letter read, signalling the EU executive is actively monitoring the phenomenon more than officially stated and seems keen to investigate it.
Formerly known as unidentified flying objects (UFOs), the term UAP was introduced by the United States defence department, the Pentagon, in August 2020, when Washington established the UAP Task Force to investigate inexplicable occurrences in restricted airspace.
The topic took on a more serious tone after a New York Times report revealed in 2017 that the US defence department files contained UAP footage from military flights that the US Navy had released.
Euronews also identified a Malaysian father and son — amateur astronomers internationally recognised by space agencies for their discoveries of the surfaces and activities on the moon in 2020 — who reached out to the Commission with a letter titled "UAP captures in the airspace and deep space using our UV infrared telescope" in October 2022.
The family duo sent 37 sky and space footage images to the Commission, including alleged UAPs, and asked President Ursula von der Leyen about their origins.
They noted that "all governments simply have no opinions" of these UAPs when confronted about them, and said they appear to be flying "very near to aircraft and important targets, such as military and nuclear facilities".
"We have also detected various signals from up above through the local networks Wi-Fi frequency," the Malaysian duo wrote.
Since these UAPs were spotted over Malaysia, the Commission would have no authority to investigate the matter, the EU executive responded.
However, the Commission said it would propose to its 27 member states to "increase its ability to detect objects in the space environment around the Earth".
"This is partly to help us better identify the UAPs that you have seen and the many pieces of space debris that endanger the many uses of space," the Commission said.
"We do not claim that in the future this will solve all cases like those you have reported, but maybe some of them."
The Malaysian amateur astronomers also reached out to NASA, the director general of the Malaysian Nuclear Agency, Abdul Rahim Harun, the Malaysian Ministry of Science, Technology & Innovation and the Canadian Defense Ministry. All entities politely shunned the appeal.
Former Canadian MP Larry Maguire, who was also approached individually by the Malaysians, encouraged the pair.
"I suspect that more and more people around the world will be turning their attention to the skies and will be collecting even more data and recordings in the coming year," Maguire wrote in an email in June 2022, seen by Euronews.
"At the end of the day, the skies aren't classified, and as more information is collected, it will lead to more public awareness of the issue."
US landmark Congress hearing
A landmark US Congress UAP hearing, hosted by the House Oversight Committee's National Security Subcommittee, took place on 26 July 2023. The hearing focused on national security implications and explosive allegations of classified government programmes that retrieve and reverse-engineer UAPs, according to the US government.
The change in designation, from UFO to UAP, was meant to kill the stigma associated with UFOs and more exotic theories that have circulated for decades, and to widen the scope of the phenomena.
In the EU, discussions about the topic remain limited and subject to stigma. This starkly contrasts with countries such as the US, which has released several confidential files in recent years. Most recently, it established a UAP Science Council chaired by Avi Loeb, a theoretical physicist who specialises in astrophysics and cosmology at Harvard University.
France is the only EU country with a dedicated, state-funded UAP monitoring and investigation centre: the Study Group and Information on Non-Identified Aerospace Phenomena, more commonly known as GEIPAN.
Since its inception in 1977, GEIPAN has analysed over 3,300 UAP cases. Exactly 106 investigations have been classified as unexplained after thorough analysis. Another 1,014 cases are unresolved due to insufficient data to conduct a proper investigation.
On 29 June, the French Parliament held a major discussion on UAPs. The debate centred on UAP research, work on UAPs by GEIPAN and the French Air and Space Force, and potentially liaising with the US to garner “responses from public authorities”.
“We want to move beyond sensationalism and fantasies and instead address, in a serious and rational way, an issue that is generating significant interest,” French MP Arnaud Saint-Martin, who has a background in aerospace and astronautics, told Le Parisien.
Flight safety concerns
Over the past decades, several EU lawmakers have questioned the Commission about the phenomena, more recently raising flight safety concerns as reports of pilot sightings increase.
These safety concerns gained momentum after several US congressional hearings featured testimony from military pilots describing "unexplainable" flying behaviour that defied the laws of physics.
In 2025 and 2026, MEP Fabio De Masi (Germany/Non-attached) asked the Commission several times to review and update EU aviation reporting systems to introduce a dedicated and standardised reporting category for UAP incidents. This would ensure consistency, data integrity and higher standards of flight safety across EU countries.
The plea has also been raised by pilots who argue that the lack of standardised reporting protocols for UAP encounters hampers data collection and risk mitigation.
They argue that sudden appearances of UAPs may lead to a loss of situational awareness or to emergency manoeuvres, fearing that the phenomena could temporarily cause malfunctions in aircraft sensors and communication systems.
Rob Akkermans, a commercial pilot working for a Dutch airline, spoke to Euronews about his experiences over the past 35 years. The first was in the early 1990s and the last two in 2023 and 2024.
"We, two pilots and four cabin crew members, were on a flight in 2023 from the Middle East to the Netherlands. For over two hours, starting around 19:30 UTC, we witnessed this strange phenomenon, which we found truly remarkable," Akkermans told Euronews, noting that all six crew members viewed the scene from the cockpit.
"It began while we were south of Cyprus. Precisely on a heading of 300 degrees (Magnetic North) — at an elevation of roughly 25 to 30 degrees and at a very high altitude — we saw a light flare up intensely and then slowly fade out. Subsequently, this occurred more frequently, often accompanied by one or two other lights that would also flare up and fade," the Dutchman explained.
"The most bizarre aspect was that one of the three lights would sometimes manoeuvre around the others. It resembled a chase — what air forces call 'dogfighting' — after which two or all three of them would fade out again," he said.
"Initially, we thought it might be a mission over the Balkans, but upon reaching the Balkans, we witnessed the same spectacle — still on the same heading, at the same angle, and at a very high altitude. After approximately 21:30 UTC, the lights suddenly vanished with incredible speed, and we did not see it again," he added.
Akkermans said that the following day, one of his colleagues witnessed the same from his back garden in the Netherlands.
The Dutch pilot said that after his experiences, he felt "a mix of wonder and surprise because what I saw was completely unexplainable," saying that such an experience "never truly leaves you".
But that excitement quickly turned into a distraction during the flight.
"Emotionally, the worrying part to deal with was frustration and concern over the stigma. You are forced to carry this experience in silence, worrying far more about the professional consequences of the taboo than the actual safety risk you just witnessed," he said.
Christiaan van Heijst, 43, a Boeing 747 captain with over 20 years of commercial flying experience, shared with Euronews four experiences he had between 2005 and 2010. Two of them were particularly noteworthy.
His second sighting, in Greece in 2005, probably on the island of Mykonos, was late in the evening.
"After landing at night, we made a 180° turn on the runway, and during the turn we saw a bright light appearing in the sky at extremely high altitude. It moved instantly, disappeared, appeared again, moved roughly the same distance, disappeared again — about three times," the Dutch pilot told Euronews.
"Before it appeared roughly two times that distance and instantly shot off at instant and unbelievable speed, without acceleration: just instant speed and it was gone from sight."
Van Heijst noted that the US Carrier Strike Group 2 with the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier was passing by in the Mediterranean on its way to the Persian Gulf that night for the Second Gulf War.
"This was mentioned in airspace closure (NOTAMS) as well (...) Unknown if these events are connected," van Heijst said.
His fourth sighting took place during a flight with a 737 from Amsterdam to Málaga in the late afternoon of 23 January 2010.
"We noticed a certain object far ahead of us showing a rounded rectangular shape as if we were looking in the rear side of a contrail. But we were flying at 41,000 feet and there is hardly any commercial and/or military traffic above us at these altitudes," van Heijst said.
"While still flying in the north of Spain, we asked Madrid Air Traffic Control if there was any known traffic ahead and above us. They told us there was no traffic at all, and wondered why we asked. So, we told them we saw an object far ahead of us and rather large," he added.
"We were just casually wondering what it was. He immediately asked us to contact the military air traffic control frequency and tell them what we saw. Military air traffic control was prompt, interested and took serious note of all we saw," the Dutch pilot continued.
"Military air traffic control confirmed there was no other traffic at all, all the way down to Morocco — no military activity, no commercial traffic, no weather balloons, nothing. We saw the stationary object all the time for an hour at least, until we descended into the clouds over Málaga, far to the south of the Iberian peninsula," he added.
While van Heijst said he felt "no emotional response to any of those sightings", he emphasised that if something is present in the airspace and authorities are unable to identify it, then "first and foremost it is a safety issue and not science fiction".
Joachim Dekkers is the founder and chairperson of the UAP Coalition Netherlands, a foundation that supports professionals who have encountered UAP. He said the greatest threat to European flight safety is the silence caused by stigma. This means that 90% of pilot sightings go unreported.
"Without a dedicated UAP category in aviation safety systems, flight crews are forced to misclassify critical data. The EU cannot maintain global leadership in aviation safety while ignoring a reality other major powers measure," Dekkers told Euronews.
"We must normalise UAP reporting across member states to guarantee total sovereignty and airspace transparency."
Although no conclusive evidence links UAPs to foreign adversaries, the possibility that some UAPs represent advanced espionage technology, such as drones, cannot be dismissed.
But MEP De Masi countered this argument. He said that neither the EU Commission nor the Council claims to possess specific evidence on the origin of these airspace incursions.
"This is quite astonishing given surveillance of airspace and critical infrastructure. Either our airspace is vulnerable, and we have a major flight safety and security risk, or the EU is misleading public opinion," De Masi told Euronews.
"Either way, it is imperative to create more transparency and remove stigma around the UAP issue and follow international efforts to create better reporting systems. This is not about green little men but the safety of our airspace and the vested interests of the military-industrial complex and national intelligence services," he added.
Reporting gap?
Despite several calls to include a standardised category for UAP reporting, the European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) said it already provides a framework for reporting "any occurrence that may have an impact on aviation safety", including UAPs.
"Pilots and other aviation personnel are encouraged to report anything they consider to represent a potential safety risk, regardless of its nature," EASA told Euronews. The agency dismissed pilots' requests to designate a UAP-specific category, instead of a miscellaneous incidents category.
EASA assesses incidents based on available evidence and the potential impact on aviation safety, the agency said.
"At present, EASA has not identified evidence indicating that reports of UAP represent a systemic aviation safety issue requiring additional measures," it added.
However, some safety advocates suggest EASA's lack of evidence may stem from a reporting gap rather than an absence of events.
In the Netherlands, the Dutch Safety Board has stepped in to accept UAP reports from flight crews under a general category. Germany's Federal Aviation Office has also engaged in scientific research on the topic.
Without a standardised central database, advocates say, these localised insights remain fragmented, leaving the European agency with an incomplete picture of airspace anomalies.
Nuclear power plants
The plot thickens when UAPs are widely reported near nuclear facilities.
A 2015 French economic study confirmed that sightings of unexplained phenomena in France correlate with proximity to atomic sites. One such site is the La Hague reprocessing plant, where large quantities of highly radioactive materials are stored before and after reprocessing.
Similarly, incidents in the UK, such as the 1993 sightings over the Hartlepool nuclear power station and the infamous 1980 Rendlesham Forest incident near the RAF Bentwaters nuclear storage bunkers, have long fuelled public speculation.
UAP sightings have been associated with US nuclear facilities since the 1940s. Military personnel have reported unexplained objects near nuclear missile silos, weapons storage sites and nuclear power plants.
One of the most well-known cases occurred in 1967 at Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, where former US Air Force officers claimed that a UAP was observed near missile silos just before several nuclear missiles became temporarily inoperable.
Similar incidents have been reported at other military installations, including Minot Air Force Base and sites in the southwestern United States.
While many witnesses consider these events significant, no conclusive evidence has been found to establish the origin or nature of the objects involved. The US government is currently investigating UAP reports, but the causes of these incidents remain unresolved.
The paradox of boosting defence capabilities
The EU is currently asking EU countries to increase defence spending, cooperate more closely and invest jointly in European defence capabilities under the bloc's binding industrial and military targets to ensure Europe is defence-ready by the end of the decade.
But when it comes to UAPs, Brussels argues this must be monitored at the national level.
Euronews asked the Commission whether it was considering any information-sharing mechanism between the US and the EU regarding UAPs, or whether it intended to act on its own to monitor and assess them, taking into account possible impacts on flight safety.
"UAP are the responsibility of EU member states, which handle them according to national security and defence priorities," a Commission spokesperson responded.
Akkermans urged the EU to treat UAPs as an aviation safety reality rather than a taboo.
"We need the EASA, the European Commission and the Parliament to formally update our aviation safety frameworks with a standardised UAP reporting category, ending the policy of ignoring or misclassifying data. Right now, the system is forcing us to stay silent," the Dutch pilot said.
For van Heijst, it is crucial to "get rid of the stigma" around the UAP topic since "there is a genuine concern for flight safety".
"This is highlighted by the swarms of (potentially Russian military) drones that invaded European airspace en masse last year. Ignoring these things is in complete contradiction to the high standards of aviation safety in the EU," van Heijst said.

Qantas A380 flew to US and back with maintenance light left in wing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:04:52 UTC
17:04:52 KST

ATSB investigation finds maintenance light was left in Qantas A380 jet wing
In short:
A work light was left inside the wing of a Qantas A380, which flew multiple international trips before it was found.
The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said it was due to a breakdown in processes at Qantas.
What's next?
Qantas has established a working group and changed its tool-control procedures.
A Qantas A380 was cleared to fly passengers return from Sydney to Dallas with a large maintenance light accidentally left inside its wing.
It follows a 2023 incident in which a large tool was left inside a Qantas A380 engine and was not recovered until multiple international trips had been completed.
An Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) investigation found the 33 centimetre light was left behind after maintenance on the aircraft's air conditioning system in Sydney on January 7.
The aircraft then flew to Dallas-Fort Worth and back before maintenance staff realised the light was missing and recovered it from the wing two days later.
The ATSB's final report into the incident found that although the light did not cause any damage to the wing, foreign objects posed a "significant risk to the safe operation of an aircraft".
ATSB chief commissioner Angus Mitchell said the incident was due to a breakdown in tool accountability processes.
"Even well-established processes can be vulnerable when they rely solely on consistent human performance, particularly during maintenance tasks which are often conducted in challenging environments and under operational pressures," he said.
"Tool control systems and procedures must account for this variability with safeguards to detect and recover from errors."
The report said Qantas issued a safety directive to address changes to its tooling control processes and procedures and had also formed a "tooling working group".
Qantas said the light had no impact on the operation of the aircraft and it had voluntarily reported the incident to the ATSB.
"Since the event, we have strengthened our tool-control procedures, including introducing a mandatory pre-clearance check to confirm all tooling is accounted for following maintenance," a spokesperson said.
Second tool left inside Qantas A380
It is the second incident involving a tool being left in one of the airline's super jumbos.
In December 2023, a Qantas A380 flew multiple international trips before a 1.25 metre nylon turning tool was discovered in one of the plane's engines.
An ATSB report found maintenance staff "lost" the "turning tool" in an A380's outboard engine, and it was only discovered after it had been cleared for service, flying multiple trips between Australia and the US.
Last week, Qantas passengers in South Africa were left stranded in Johannesberg for three days after a problem with the nose wheel of an A380 saw their flight to Sydney cancelled.
Qantas sent another flight to bring the stranded passengers home.
CQUniversity aviation expert and associate professor Steven Leib said any unaccounted-for objects found inside an aircraft were "a real safety concern".
"It may not seem like a big deal, leaving a light or leaving a tool, but these are things that could move around during flight, which could jeopardise the safety of the flight," Dr Leib said.
However, he said the two incidents were not enough to suggest Qantas had a systemic problem.
"The discovery of the lost object was made by the accountability system," he said.
"They were able to trace when it was last used, when it was meant to have been returned and what work was being carried out."

Taichung partners with RAI Technology on smart traffic management

08:02:24 UTC
17:02:24 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung announced Monday that it has partnered with RAI Technology to deploy an AI-backed traffic monitoring system in busy areas, according to a city Transportation Bureau press release.
The Transportation Bureau signed a memorandum of understanding with RAI. The bureau said this marks a transition to active detection, real-time notification, and data-backed decision-making.
Transportation Bureau Director Yeh Chao-fu (葉昭甫) said the new system will reduce staff workload, as monitoring was previously done manually to verify accidents and traffic congestion. He noted that going through surveillance footage causes delays as responders await confirmation.
Yeh said the bureau will prioritize the Shin Kong Mitsukoshi-Far Eastern Department Stores shopping area in the Seventh Redevelopment Zone, with AI monitoring along Taiwan Boulevard, Huizhong Road, and Shizheng North 7th Road tracking vehicles near parking lots. When vehicle queues reach a preset threshold, the system will generate a detailed report and notify traffic management staff to determine the appropriate response.
Yeh said the city will then target the entry and exit ramps of Provincial Highway 74 by using cameras at Huanzhong East Road and Taiyuan Road to assess traffic flow. The bureau will use collected statistics to determine the appropriate traffic control measures.
Yeh said the third pilot will take place during the Xinshe Flower Festival, where cameras will be set up at shuttle bus terminals. Once the queue reaches a preset threshold, the system will notify the bureau to respond accordingly.

Taiwan personnel agency rejects proposal to scrap National Travel Card
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:02:00 UTC
17:02:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Cabinet's personnel administration rejected a proposal to end the National Travel Card program, saying it encourages civil servants to take annual leave and protects employee health, CNA reported Monday.
UDN reported that the proposal was posted on the government's Public Policy Network Participation Platform. It called for ending the card program and allowing unused leave to be fully compensated in cash when civil servants cannot take time off because of work demands.
The proposal said the current system requires part of the compensation linked to unused leave to be spent through the National Travel Card. It argued that restrictions on eligible purchases limit how civil servants can use the money.
In response, the personnel administration said it would not adopt the proposal for now. It said replacing the system with cash payments could give civil servants less incentive to take enough time off, per Up Media.
The agency said required leave days help protect employees' physical and mental health. Government figures show civil servants took an average of 11.32 days of annual leave in 2025.
Civil servants entitled to more than 10 days of annual leave are generally required to take at least 10 days. They can receive up to NT$16,000 (US$502) a year through the National Travel Card program, per Liberty Times.
Half of the subsidy can be spent without tourism-related restrictions. The other NT$8,000 must be used for tourism-related spending.
The personnel administration said the card subsidy is a welfare benefit rather than overtime pay or direct compensation for unused leave. Civil servants who cannot use all their annual leave because of work demands can still claim cash compensation for up to 20 unused days beyond the required 10 days.
The Cabinet has approved keeping the current rules from 2026 through 2028. The personnel administration said the program is generally reviewed every three years, per FTV News.
The National Travel Card program began in 2003 to encourage civil servants to take vacations and support domestic tourism. Critics say the program has since moved away from its original purpose.
Former Minister without Portfolio Chang Ching-sen (張景森), opposition lawmakers, and civil servant groups have called for changes to the system. Their proposals include easing spending restrictions, raising the subsidy, or replacing the card with cash payments.
Some civil servants also question whether the card still encourages tourism. They say the subsidy is often spent on hotel vouchers, meals, or everyday goods instead.

China’s passport warfare targets Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:01:57 UTC
17:01:57 KST

China is turning travel documents, overflight permits, visas, and border checkpoints into weapons in a quiet campaign to isolate Taiwan from the world.
In late April, Seychelles, Mauritius, and Madagascar revoked overflight clearances for President Lai Ching-te’s (賴清德) planned flight to Eswatini under pressure from Beijing. Taipei and Mbabane outmaneuvered the blockade when King Mswati III’s aircraft transported the Taiwanese delegation on a much longer route through friendly airspace, landing safely in Eswatini on May 2.
By July, this containment campaign had begun targeting ordinary citizens. The Moroccan Embassy in Tokyo halted mandatory visa confirmation letters for Taiwanese tourists, forcing Taipei to respond with a reciprocal visa suspension against Moroccan nationals.
In August, Ugandan immigration officers at Entebbe International Airport withheld Taiwanese passports and demanded that Taiwanese travelers produce Chinese passports before their documents would be returned.
These shocks reveal a trend toward “passport warfare” — the weaponization of airspace, transit hubs, visas, and checkpoints to isolate Taiwan. This administrative containment mirrors the coercive diplomatic warfare the Chinese Communist Party aggressively conducts against countries that maintain official relations with Taiwan.
By forcing foreign states to deny transit, entry, or basic document recognition to Taiwanese passport holders, Beijing achieves through bureaucratic pressure what it cannot yet enforce through military might. The result directly undermines cross-strait deterrence and assurance.
The Zero-Tariff Cauldron
These travel restrictions reflect clear geopolitical patterns.
Sovereignty fears drive complete transit blockades in Georgia and Moldova, where governments fear legitimizing breakaway regions and have strong reasons to please Beijing. Economic dependencies dictate entry bans in Venezuela and Azerbaijan, while Chinese investment in Morocco’s Tangier Tech Smart City forms part of the broader context for Rabat’s recent visa freeze.
Elsewhere, proxy disputes dictate borders, as Somalia has barred Taiwanese travelers in retaliation for Taipei’s ties with Somaliland.
This African containment stems from a unified economic carrot. On Feb. 14, during the 39th African Union Summit, Chinese leader Xi Jinping announced a unilateral zero-tariff policy for 53 African nations, effective May 1.
Eswatini, Taiwan’s only diplomatic ally in Africa, was the sole African country excluded from Beijing’s duty-free umbrella.
In exchange, African leaders have increasingly aligned their borders and diplomatic language with Beijing. Recent joint declarations with hardline dependents such as Zimbabwe, Equatorial Guinea, Algeria, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo have dropped historical language endorsing a peaceful resolution of cross-strait relations.
By stating only that Taiwan is an inalienable part of Chinese territory and omitting references to peace, these accords grant diplomatic cover to a future military blockade.
Deterrence, Assurance, and Silkworms
International relations theory holds that deterrence relies on raising the costs of aggression, while assurance guarantees that maintaining the status quo preserves security.
Beijing’s passport warfare subverts this balance through consular and airspace deterrence. It creates a gray-zone barrier to prove that standard travel can result in immediate logistical stranding.
This behavior embodies the Chinese idiom 蠶食鯨吞, or “to nibble away like a silkworm before swallowing like a whale.”
Avoiding hot war, Beijing relies on the silkworm’s patience. It pressures civil aviation systems, border authorities, and travel-document databases to make Taiwanese mobility appear abnormal, disputed, and administratively inconvenient.
Squeezing access in isolated hubs gradually conditions the world to accept Taiwan’s isolation. Once this erasure is normalized, the strategy can shift to the whale’s swallow: collapsing status quo assurances and eliminating Taiwan’s international presence entirely.
The Expanding Gray-Zone Grid
This containment has expanded beyond historic non-recognition blocks, combining passport warfare and legal pressure into a unified lawfare campaign.
In South Africa, Pretoria excluded Taiwan from its automated e-visa platform and demanded that Taiwan move its liaison office from Pretoria to Johannesburg, treating travel access and representation as concessions to Beijing.
In China’s own legal system, the CCP has expanded extraterritorial threats. Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council has raised concerns over Article 63 of China’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law, which targets overseas organizations and individuals accused of undermining ethnic unity or promoting separatism.
At the same time, Chinese judicial guidelines on “Taiwan independence” have turned travel through China and China-aligned states into a growing risk for Taiwanese, overseas Taiwanese, and foreign supporters of Taiwan.
Thailand and South Korea have also intensified screening of Taiwanese arrivals under the pretext of fighting transnational fraud, demonstrating how ordinary border enforcement can be turned into broader friction against Taiwanese mobility.
Uganda’s August passport seizures show the campaign’s most blunt form. Ugandan immigration officers at Entebbe withheld Taiwanese passports, demanded Chinese passports, and in earlier cases detained or deported Taiwanese travelers.
Foreign nationals are not immune. Western and other foreign passport holders who renew documents through trade offices or de facto embassies in Taipei can face denial or heightened scrutiny at Chinese checkpoints when “Taipei” appears as the place of issue. In China’s political reading of travel documents, even a neutral administrative field can become a sovereignty trap.
The same pattern appears in paperwork erasure. Serbia and Bolivia process visas for Taiwanese on loose sheets of paper, while Jamaica requires travelers to purchase a separate affidavit of identity to avoid creating an official administrative record on a Taiwanese passport.
The September Entry and Exit Codes
The structural normalization of passport warfare is arriving through China’s sweeping new entry and exit regulation, State Council Decree No. 841, which takes effect Sept. 15.
The 19-article regulation gives Beijing broader administrative tools to refuse entry, cancel transit, restrict exit, demand supporting documents, require electronic data, and impose entry bans on people accused of violating vague border or national-security classifications.
This codifies a weapon-ready architecture for gray-zone border control.
Under the new regulation, border officers and visa authorities can demand documents, materials, and electronic data when verifying a traveler’s identity or stated purpose of travel. False materials or statements can be used to deny entry or exit documents, refuse entry, or impose bans of one to five years.
The system gives Beijing more tools to punish travelers whose identities, documents, political views, or links to Taiwan are deemed irregular.
Because Beijing routinely treats Taiwanese as Chinese citizens under its domestic administrative practices, these measures could be selectively applied to Taiwanese tech workers, academics, businesspeople, activists, and public figures traveling to or from China.
What appears to be a border-management rule is in practice another tool for ideological compliance.
The Democratic Counterstrike
To neutralize this strategy, Taiwan and its allies must establish diplomatic counter-deterrence.
First, democratic partners should impose immediate diplomatic costs on states that target Taiwanese travelers. Taiwan’s July 30 reciprocal visa suspension against Morocco offers a model.
If a state bans Taiwanese transit, withholds passports, or enforces discriminatory entry rules under Beijing’s pressure, the US, EU, Japan, Canada, Australia, and other partners should respond with bureaucratic delays, reciprocal scrutiny, or restrictions on electronic visa access for that country’s officials.
Second, allies must mobilize multilateral aviation protections.
Beijing’s airspace coercion violates the apolitical spirit of the Chicago Convention on International Civil Aviation. Western allies should explicitly extend freedom-of-navigation principles to civil aviation by guaranteeing alternative routes, priority transit, diplomatic escorts, or emergency logistical support for Taiwanese officials facing blockade attempts.
Eswatini’s royal-jet intervention showed that Beijing’s airspace choke points can be broken. The democratic world should systematize that lesson before the next attempted blockade.
Third, allies should establish pre-cleared sovereign whitelisting.
The US, Canada, UK, and Schengen Area should integrate Taiwan into automated, depoliticized biometric corridors such as Global Entry, SmartGate, and similar trusted-traveler systems. Bypassing manual embassy checks protects travelers from localized diplomatic pressure.
This automation is urgent. As the Uganda passport seizures show, Taiwan often lacks local embassies and must route emergency support through remote offices, such as its representative office in Somaliland.
Automated and trusted systems would make Taiwan’s global mobility harder to break, even under China’s incoming Sept. 15 border rules.
A Global Blueprint for Erasure
Passport warfare is an existential threat disguised as paperwork.
The institutional foundations for this global containment were codified during the 2024 Forum on China-Africa Cooperation meeting in Beijing, where every participating African head of state except Eswatini declared support for China’s “national reunification” narrative and “all efforts by the Chinese government” to achieve the goal.
Driven by Beijing’s economic leverage, this language fuels the silkworm’s first nibble, expanding the blockade into a systemic global consular net.
In Southeast Asia, staunch Beijing allies such as Cambodia and Laos have weaponized visa infrastructure by tightening restrictions on Taiwanese nationals while offering broader entry privileges to Chinese citizens.
In South America, China has used expanded visa-waiver frameworks with core trade partners such as Brazil, Argentina, and Peru to encourage compliance with Beijing’s passport and sovereignty demands, increasingly choking off standard entry procedures for Taiwanese travelers.
Normalizing a world where autocrats dictate international transit does not prevent conflict. It accelerates the whale’s final swallow.
If the democratic world fails to break Beijing’s consular blockade today, its own freedom of movement will be held hostage tomorrow.

According to the ordinance, no one should place a smoking product advertisement on the internet, with offenders facing a HK$50,000 (US$6,370) fine upon summary conviction and a further HK$1,500 fine for each day the offence continues.

The attack hit an industrial facility, he added, without giving details.
At the same time, Russian forces launched missile and drone attacks across Ukraine, killing at least four people and wounding 19.
At least two people were killed and four injured in a Russian attack on the southeastern region of Zaporizhia.
At least two people were killed and one person was wounded in Russian shelling on Sumy in northeastern Ukraine, emergency services said.
At least five people were injured in a Russian attack on central Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk region while four were injured after two Russian guided-bomb attacks hit Izyum in the northeastern region of Kharkiv.
Five people were injured in Russian attacks on the southern region of Kherson.
In the Odesa region, also in southern Ukraine, a Russian attack targeted port infrastructure in the Izmail district.
The fires caused by the overnight attack, which damaged a Togo-flagged civilian vessel, have been extinguished, Ukrainian authorities wrote on the Telegram messaging app.
Izmail, close to the Romanian border, is home to Ukraine’s largest port on the Danube River.
Later on Monday, Russia’s Ministry of Defence announced that its forces had captured two more settlements in Ukraine: Novosoloshyne in Zaporizhia and Andriyivska Hromada in the eastern region of Donetsk.
Al Jazeera could not independently confirm the battlefield reports.
The attacks came a day after Russia and Ukraine carried out missile and drone attacks deep inside each other’s territory that killed 19 people in both countries.
With front-line fighting at a near standstill and US-backed talks aimed at ending the conflict frozen, the warring countries have significantly stepped up missile attacks, pushing the civilian death toll to its highest levels since the war’s first months in 2022.
Russia has carried out near-daily missile and drone attacks across Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
It has recently intensified attacks using hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles, exploiting Ukraine’s shortages of air defence weapons after the United States-Israel war against Iran increased pressure on global supplies.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted warehouses belonging to Russia’s biggest online retailer, Wildberries, saying the company sells components for Russian drones and outfits Russian soldiers.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said those attacks along with attacks on oil refineries are aimed at undermining Russia’s war economy.
In July alone, 437 civilians were killed in Ukraine, the highest monthly toll since May 2022, according to a United Nations tally.
Russian authorities reported 79 civilians killed in Ukrainian attacks in July, up from the previous month.

JP Morgan boss Jamie Dimon warns UK chancellor not to hike taxes on banks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
07:55:31 UTC
16:55:31 KST

Jamie Dimon, the boss of the US bank JP Morgan, has urged John Healey not to use his first budget as chancellor to increase taxes on banks’ bumper profits.
Speculation has been growing that a windfall tax could be imposed on UK lenders to fund Andy Burnham’s cost of living agenda, with campaigners estimating such a move could raise £19bn.
Dimon told Healey in a phone conversation that higher levies could hit jobs, citing a fall in finance roles in New York that he blamed on the city’s tax regime.
One person familiar with the conversation said the chief executive of the world’s biggest bank’s comments on tax were not specific to the UK, adding that Dimon was the first among many bank bosses to have an introductory call with the new chancellor, with calls with other chief executives to follow.
The Wall Street billionaire’s remarks, first reported by the Financial Times, were condemned by Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC). He said: “People are sick and tired of being told they have to tighten their belts while profits, dividends and bankers’ bonuses hit record highs.
“The new chancellor has a clear opportunity to show working people he’s on their side by asking banks to pay fair taxes to cut energy bills.”
Dimon has a long track record of criticising Britain’s additional bank taxes, which were imposed after the government bailed out big UK lenders in the 2008 financial crisis. Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, as well as a separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets.
The JP Morgan CEO said in July that raising these taxes further could have “adverse consequences”, telling the Master Investor Podcast: “It would be one more negative on that bucket of things you got to think about.”
Dimon, who was also among the bank bosses who successfully lobbied against higher taxes in Rachel Reeves’ budget last year, announced plans the day after to build a 3m sq ft tower in London’s Canary Wharf district, with the caveat that a “continuing positive business environment in the UK” was required.
In May this year, he said he could scrap plans for the £3bn tower, which is expected to serve as its UK headquarters and house more than half its 23,000 UK workforce, if Keir Starmer were replaced by a new Labour prime minister who was hostile to banks.
Burnham and Healey have not made any specific comments about a bank tax so far. However, they have faced many calls to increase the levy.
Collectively, the UK’s four largest lenders, HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds, reported £29.2bn in profits over the first six months of the year, with almost half, £13.7bn, pledged to investors through dividends and share buy-backs.
The TUC is calling for the government to increase the bank surcharge, claiming a 16% rate would deliver £24bn over the next four years, while 35% would deliver £60bn over the same period.
The campaign group Positive Money has said that figure means they could easily shoulder a tax that could ultimately raise £19bn for government spending plans at the October budget.
The group’s head of advocacy, Simon Youel, said: “Even Margaret Thatcher introduced a windfall tax on banks, recognising that their profits were simply the result of higher interest rates rather than increased efficiency or better service to customers.
“Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves had a chance to recoup banks’ huge windfalls at the last budget, but instead they chose to raise taxes on ordinary people. Hopefully Andy Burnham and John Healey won’t be fooled by the industry’s lobbyists into making the same mistake.”
UK banks together paid an estimated £43.3bn in tax for the financial year that ended in March 2025, according to a report commissioned by the industry body UK Finance.
JP Morgan declined to comment.

Linnahall shooting range in Tallinn could cost millions to make work

Unknown Publisher

Linnahall shooting range in Tallinn could cost millions to make work
Tallinn has offered Linnahall's former ice rink to the Estonian Defense League (EDL) for a temporary shooting range, but experts say repairs could cost millions.
Tallinn Deputy Mayor and EDL member Kristjan Järvan said the city had consulted two shooting range operators before pitching the proposal. He estimated the initial investment needed to convert the space at about €500,000.
"At least 55-meter shooting ranges could be built here, right inside the ice rink," Järvan said.
He argued the project could turn the largely unused concrete structure into a useful defense asset at a relatively modest cost. The Estonian Center for Defense Investments (ECDI) and EDL would ultimately decide whether to pursue it.
"Tallinn just sees this as an additional option we can offer," the deputy mayor added.
Järvan previously said the range would be temporary, operating until the city decides on a longer-term future for the long-neglected venue.
Fellow EDL member and Tondi shooting range owner Tõnis Orumaa said the former ice rink could work particularly well for tactical shooting because its open layout would allow firing in multiple directions.
"You've got a full-sized ice hockey arena, so you could fire across 180 degrees," he explained, adding that in traditional ranges, targets are all in one place at the far end.
But the rink would first have to be cleared out and its leaking roof made watertight, followed by ongoing maintenance costs. Orumaa estimated that renovating the roof alone could cost about €3 million.
Money would stretch further elsewhere
He noted that the EDL's Rapla District, meanwhile, is currently headquartered in a small space, while the Järva District is operating out of the Türi Subdistrict's facilities.
"For that money, we could build three district support centers," Orumaa said.
The same investment could also fund two or three comparable shooting ranges elsewhere in the country instead, he added.
The EDL already has a shooting complex near Tallinn, while the Estonian Defense Forces' (EDF) Central Training Area still offers the best training conditions.
The ice rink at Tallinn's Soviet-era Linnahall venue complex closed in 2009 and has remained unused since then. Whether the EDL wants to take on the building alongside its other priorities remains to be decided

The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has killed 2,325 people since May, according to official data on Sunday, surpassing the toll in the 2018-2020 outbreak to become the deadliest in the country's history.
The Health Ministry's latest situation update showed confirmed cases have reached 4,945, including 2,325 deaths since the outbreak was declared in mid-May.
The 2018-2020 outbreak in Congo killed 2,299 people primarily in eastern North Kivu and Ituri provinces before it was declared over on June 25, 2020.
The latest epidemic has affected six provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele and Tshopo.

This outbreak is the fastest-growing on record, according to the World Health Organization.
To date, no vaccine or specific treatment has been approved against the Bundibugyo virus.

Swiss winegrowers begin harvest in mid-August for first time

Unknown Publisher

Swiss winegrowers begin harvest in mid-August for first time
Switzerland's grape harvest is set to be exceptionally early this year as prolonged drought and high temperatures accelerate ripening. In some regions, picking has already begun, an unprecedented development for mid-August.
“As strange as it may seem, we’re harvesting on August 15,” Aurèle Morf, owner of Cave Saint-Germain in Moutier, canton Jura, told Swiss public radio RTS on Saturday.
Morf said the harvest is running several weeks ahead of normal.
“In 2016, which was a particularly wet year, we finished on November 1. This year, I think we’ll be done by early or mid-September,” he said.
When Morf decided a few years ago to plant vines in Grandval, canton Bern, at an altitude of 620 metres, the idea initially met resistance.
“People said it was too high, that it wasn’t a lakeside location. There were fears the grapes would never ripen,” he recalled with a smile.
Adapting to climate change
Not all winegrowers in French-speaking Switzerland have started harvesting yet, but all are feeling the impact of this summer’s heat and water shortage.
More
Climate change ‘shifting Europe’s wine-growing regions’
In Cornaux, canton Neuchâtel, winegrower Quentin Divernois waters part of his vineyards daily, particularly plots with rocky soils.
“Here, the grapes are plump, unlike on other plots suffering from the drought,” he said. “Without irrigation, these vines would have withered.”
Elsewhere, some vineyards are coping better. In the Vully region, canton Fribourg, Pascal Matthey’s vines benefit from deep roots and deeper soils, making them more resilient to heat and drought.
“The berries are small and there are signs of water stress, which could produce slightly harsher wines,” Matthey said. Yields are also expected to be lower than last year.
The industry has been preparing for a warmer climate for several years. Divernois, for example, is testing different rootstocks to identify varieties that are better able to withstand drought.

Massive wildfires engulfed Greece and Belgium: hundreds evacuated, fatalities reported
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
10:48:58 EEST
16:48:58 KST

Massive wildfires engulfed Greece and Belgium: hundreds evacuated, fatalities reported
Kyiv • UNN
On the Greek island of Salamina, two people died in a fire and more than 500 were evacuated. In Belgium, a fire in the Hautes Fagnes nature reserve engulfed 3,000 hectares, becoming the largest in the country's history.
On the Greek island of Salamina near Athens, two people died amid a wildfire, and hundreds had to be evacuated. Meanwhile, in Belgium, a fire in the High Fens nature reserve became the largest in the country's modern history, UNN reports, citing the Associated Press and Reuters.
Rescuers in both countries continue to battle large-scale wildfires.
Details
A large fire broke out on August 16 on the Greek island of Salamina, located west of Athens near the port of Piraeus. Due to strong winds, the fire spread rapidly and approached residential areas.
Two people have already died as a result of the fire. An elderly couple was found near a house close to the area where the blaze started. At least five people were taken to a local clinic. Residential buildings have also been damaged and destroyed.
The coast guard evacuated more than 500 people, including by sea from coastal areas of the island. Additional vessels were also sent to Salamina and may be deployed if further evacuation becomes necessary. About 260 rescuers were involved in fighting the fire. Volunteers, municipal equipment, and firefighting aircraft are also taking part in the operation. The cause of the fire is currently being established.
Meanwhile, the situation in Belgium remains difficult. A fire in the High Fens nature reserve in the east of the country, near the border with Germany, has affected about 3,000 hectares. It became the largest forest fire in Belgium's modern history. The previous record was set in 2011, when the fire destroyed about 1,400 hectares.
Due to the threat of the flames spreading, about 600 residents and tourists were evacuated from dangerous areas. More than 250 firefighters and other rescuers are involved in fighting the blaze. Belgian services are being assisted by specialists from Germany, as well as aircraft from the Netherlands and Sweden. Belgian military personnel and local farmers with equipment have also been involved in the operation.
Firefighting is complicated by the characteristics of the terrain. A significant part of the High Fens consists of peatlands, where fire can spread through dried-out soil and flare up again in areas that appear to have already been extinguished on the surface.
The eastern front of the fire, which is moving toward Germany, is of particular concern. In Germany's Monschau district, residents of some settlements were urged to leave their homes because of heavy smoke.
Context
The fires in Belgium and Greece are part of a large-scale wave of wildfires in Europe in the summer of 2026. Fires were also recorded in France, Germany, Croatia, the United Kingdom, Spain, and Portugal.
Among the main factors complicating the situation are prolonged periods of heat, a lack of precipitation, and dried-out vegetation.
According to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), as of July 22, about 254,400 hectares of land had burned in the European Union since the beginning of 2026. A total of 1,254 large fires were recorded—more than twice the long-term average for this period.

Belarus’ grain harvest exceeds 8.2m tonnes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
07:46:00 UTC
16:46:00 KST

MINSK, 17 August (BelTA) – Belarusian farmers have threshed 8.2 million tonnes of grain, BelTA learned from the press service of the Belarusian Agriculture and Food Ministry.
As of 17 August 2026, grain harvest including rapeseed amounted to 8.215 million tonnes, which was almost 1.5 million tonnes more than on the same date in 2025, the press service said. 
By region, the progress in the harvest looks as follows: Minsk Oblast – 2,222,000 tonnes, Grodno Oblast – 1,639,000 tonnes, Brest Oblast – 1,632,000 tonnes, Gomel Oblast – 1,027,000 tonnes, Mogilev Oblast – 956,000 tonnes, Vitebsk Oblast – 739,000 tonnes. 
Grain and leguminous crops (including rapeseed, without corn) have been harvested from 2,225,000 hectares or 91% of the areas (2,432,000 hectares in total).
Flax has been pulled across the area of 43,000 hectares, or 99% of the target.
Deliveries under the state procurement order include: 416,000 tonnes of food grain (63% of the target); 105,000 tonnes of rapeseed (105% of the 100,000-tonne target); and 66,000 tonnes of malting barley (77% of the 86,000-tonne target).
Second cut was harvested across an area of 820,000 hectares or 81% of the plan.
Hay production has reached 520,000 tonnes or 73% of the plan. Silage harvest progress stands at 434,000 tonnes. Forage grasses total 3,631,000 tonnes or 36% of the target. Haylage production has reached 11,598,000 tonnes, or 81% of the target. 
 
Fertilizer stocks (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium) for winter planting have been procured at 131% (227,000 tonnes) of the planned requirement.

Europe wildfires: German border town partially evacuated but France blaze stabilised
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
07:44:22 UTC
16:44:22 KST

A historically hot summer on the planet's fastest-warming continent has contributed to the deaths of thousands of people and increased the risk of wildfires, with blazes periodically sweeping through parched landscapes.
Europe is tackling a spate of wildfires spurred by high temperatures and tinder-dry conditions due to a historically hot summer that has already contributed to the deaths of thousands of people.
Scientists blame ever hotter and more frequent heatwaves on human-caused climate change.
Here are the latest developments this Monday morning.
Rain boosts Belgium's fight
Rain started falling in Belgium on Monday to help its fight against the country's biggest modern-day wildfire that has devastated some 3,000 hectares (30 square kilometres) of the High Fens park on the border with Germany.
Some 500 firefighters and troops are battling the blaze that has sent a huge cloud of black smoke across the region into neighbouring Germany and France.
Germany's defence ministry said on Monday that two military water-bombing helicopters would be sent to Belgium.
The German town of Monschau, close to the border, ordered nearly 30 people living in two streets near the frontier to evacuate.
Like much of Europe, Belgium has experienced a new spell of intense heat and drought in recent days.
Temperatures reached as high as 37C in some parts of the country on Friday, creating conditions conducive to wildfire outbreaks.
Greece deaths
Two people died and hundreds were evacuated from popular beaches when two fires broke out on the Greek island of Salamis near Athens, the fire department said.
"Over 570 people were evacuated on coast guard patrol boats and other vessels," a coastguard spokesperson told the AFP news agency.
After largely escaping the heatwave temperatures that blanketed much of Europe, Greece has been hit with several major wildfires since late July, fuelled by strong winds.
Thirty-six blazes have broken out over the past 24 hours around the country, according to the fire department.
Portugal fires
Hundreds of firefighters in Portugal were battling a series of blazes there.
At one near the border with Spain, near the village of Dine, five firefighters sustained minor injuries when their vehicle caught fire, local media reported.
Firefighters were battling several other fires near the Spanish border, including at Boticas and Chavez, said the civil protection agency ANEPC.
Death in Spain
A Spanish soldier died on Sunday while helping efforts to extinguish a major wildfire in Aragon, the northeastern region's leader said, as the authorities deployed the largest firefighting arsenal in the region's history.
French reinforcements were due to help contain the wildfire, which broke out on Monday and has threatened a 1,000-year-old monastery.
Croatia arrests
Croatian police said they had arrested four people suspected of starting some of the wildfires that have swept parts of the Adriatic coast in recent days.
The four are suspected of setting fires that scorched pine forests and olive groves as Croatia battles a wave of blazes fuelled by drought and heat.
France fire stabilised
A fire that burnt 1,700 hectares in the Landes department of southwestern France has been stabilised after three days of ground and air operations.
Local official Gilles Clavreul said the situation was evolving "favourably" as temperatures had dropped, 28C expected in the afternoon compared with 40C when the fire broke out on Thursday, and humidity had risen.
The local prefect said a first group of the 650 people who had evacuated due to the fire would be allowed to return to their homes Sunday evening

At least six people were killed in a Ukrainian rocket attack in the western Belgorod region, local authorities said Monday morning.
In a post on Telegram, Acting Belgorod region Governor Aleksander Shuvaev said four others were wounded in the attack, which took place in the village of Koloskovo, located around 24 kilometers (15 miles) from the border with Ukraine.
Shuvaev said a 14-year-old was among the injured. He said the rocket attack also damaged a “structure” and a vehicle.
In a separate drone strike in the southern Astrakhan region, local authorities said a woman was killed. They said the drones targeted an industrial facility but did not provide further details.
The deadly attacks came a day after Russia and Ukraine exchanged strikes deep inside each other’s territories, killing 19 people on both sides.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 205 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Sunday night and Monday morning.
Several airports in southern Russia introduced temporary flight restrictions amid the overnight attacks.

A German journalist asked Zelensky how Europeans can help kill more Russian soldiers. Russia responded with a criminal case.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
07:43:05 UTC
16:43:05 KST

A German journalist asked Zelensky how Europeans can help kill more Russian soldiers. Russia responded with a criminal case.
Russia has opened a criminal case against Michael Martens, a correspondent for the German newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ), over remarks he made about the killing of Russian servicemen, the Russian state news agency TASS reported, citing a source.
Martens is charged under Part 2 of Article 282 of Russia’s Criminal Code, which criminalizes incitement of hatred or enmity committed in public and carries a maximum penalty of six years in prison.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić held a press conference in Belgrade on August 8, where the FAZ journalist asked a question: “Can you tell us Europeans, what can we concretely do to help you to kill more Russians?” Martens immediately clarified that he meant Russian servicemen specifically.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova called the question “unacceptable and criminal,” while Russia’s embassy in Germany called Martens’ words “disgusting.” The statement also said that German authorities’ failure to condemn the question was “dispiriting.”
Martens later wrote that his question referenced remarks by Winston Churchill. He was apparently referring to the question “Who was killing the most germans, and how we could help them to kill more?” According to British officer Fitzroy Maclean’s recollections, Churchill made the remark while discussing support for Yugoslav partisans during World War II.

Seoul responds to Trump&apos;s decision to scale back military exercises
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
10:39:44 EEST
16:39:44 KST

Seoul responds to Trump's decision to scale back military exercises
Kyiv • UNN
South Korea is reviewing Trump's comments about scaling back joint exercises, hoping for substantive negotiations. Pyongyang has not yet responded, while experts warn of possible high costs.
South Korea has issued a statement on US President Donald Trump's decision to reduce the annual military exercises between the two countries, UNN reports, citing the BBC.
Context
President Donald Trump said that the United States would "substantially reduce" joint military exercises with South Korea, citing his "very good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. He also said on Truth Social that South Korea had recently refused to join the United States in the "denuclearization" of Iran. "These exercises are not only expensive, with a significant portion of the costs paid by the United States of America (as always!), but they also send an absolutely inappropriate and hostile signal," Trump wrote.
Seoul's response
Seoul said it was reviewing Trump's comments, adding that it hoped favorable relations between Washington and Pyongyang could lead to meaningful negotiations. Pyongyang has not yet commented on the situation.
South Korea earlier said that the exercises with the United States would continue "as scheduled".
This came after North Korea conducted tests of ballistic missiles banned by the United Nations this month.
Trump's statement came less than 24 hours after he posted an old photograph of himself and Kim from 2019, writing that they had been good friends, "despite the unfriendly look in this particular photo".
In its statement, South Korea's presidential Blue House said it would continue diplomatic consultations on military cooperation between the United States and Korea related to the Strait of Hormuz, and would also discuss details of joint military exercises with the United States.
Experts suggest that abandoning joint military exercises could result in high costs and relatively little benefit.
Last week, US and South Korean military leaders held a joint press conference at which they announced the "Ulchi Freedom Shield" exercises.
During the press conference, the military leaders also mentioned North Korea's deployment of troops to assist Russia's war against Ukraine.
US military spokesman Ryan Donald said that "our exercises take this threat into account," referring to North Korean soldiers returning from the battlefield. About 28,500 US servicemen are stationed in South Korea.
On Friday, North Korea's Foreign Ministry condemned the joint military exercises as a "rehearsal for an aggressive war".
The joint exercises took place several days after South Korea, the United States and Japan detected North Korea's second missile test in several days.
Pyongyang has accelerated efforts to expand its nuclear and missile programs following the failure in 2019 of Kim's high-profile diplomatic engagements with Trump during his first term in the White House.
He became the first sitting US president to set foot on North Korean territory when he visited it seven years ago.
For Seoul, Trump's post is an ambiguous signal. On the one hand, they had asked Trump to engage with Pyongyang, and the post raises hopes that he may bring Kim back to the negotiating table. But Trump also hints that he is dissatisfied with South Korea's unwillingness to make a direct military or logistical contribution to US military operations against Iran, the publication writes.
He also expressed dissatisfaction with other allies over their unwillingness to intervene in the conflict, including Japan, France and the United Kingdom.
Trump's move to reduce joint military exercises with South Korea is not unprecedented. He completely halted the exercises in 2018 during denuclearization talks with Kim. He said at the time that the annual exercises were "provocative" toward North Korea and that ending the "war games" would save the United States "a tremendous amount of money". The exercises were reduced again in 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic.
What they say in Ukraine
Ukraine has also commented on Trump's decision regarding the exercises.
"At the same time, North Korea is sending military personnel to gain experience in Russia’s war against Ukraine, preparing for a possible escalation on the Korean Peninsula," Andriy Kovalenko, head of the National Security and Defense Council’s Center for Countering Disinformation, said on social media on Monday.

All Malaysia Airlines pilots pass drug tests following Jakarta arrest
The mandatory screening process was ordered after a Malaysian Airlines pilot was arrested in Indonesia on drug trafficking charges
The mandatory screening process was ordered after a Malaysian Airlines pilot was arrested in Indonesia on drug trafficking charges on July 28.
Authorities found 26kg (57lbs) of the mind-altering drug MDMA in his luggage upon his arrival in Jakarta from Kuala Lumpur.
Urine tests also showed the pilot had been under the influence of cocaine and methamphetamine, the customs office said.
MAG said in a statement that as the screening results for all its pilots returned negative, it would proceed to the next phase of the programme, which would screen about 2,840 Malaysia Airlines cabin crew starting from Tuesday and expected to end by September 3.
MAG operates Malaysia Airlines, as well as short-haul carrier Firefly, and haj pilgrimage airline Amal.
