How would cuts to skilled migration, backpacker visas impact the economy?
That's the question from independent Zali Steggall, who wants to know if Treasury has modelled the impact cuts would have on worker shortages.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers takes this one. He says the consistent finding from Treasury and the Productivity Commission is that migrants "are more likely than not to make a big contribution to our economy".
"So our job – the responsibility that we embrace – is to make the most of that economic opportunity, fed by that considered, methodical analysis that we get from all of those places, to make sure we're making the most of this opportunity," he says.
"At the same time as we get net overseas migration down – 45% below its peak, and with some further distance to travel as well."
Minister defends changes to veterans' allied health treatment
Nationals frontbencher Michael McCormack has asked the veterans' affairs minister why he's refused to meet with a delegation of veterans today.
The delegation, he says, has travelled to parliament to raise concerns about the imposition of a $5,000 cap on veteran allied health services.
Veterans' Affairs Minister Matt Keogh says the government is removing the 20-session allied health treatment cycle where veterans have to continually see their GP to get a new referral.
McCormack has stepped up on a point of order on relevance, asking the minister to confine his remarks to the question.
Keogh says the delegation was informed last week that he was unable to meet with them today.
"I have continually said and engaged with many ex-service organisations, we wish to engage with them and the practitioners in allied health services," Keogh says.
'A lot of work' to do on foundational supports: Butler
Independent Sophie Scamps has the second crossbench question of the day.
She wants to know how the government can ensure that no current NDIS participant is exited off the scheme without appropriate foundational supports.
The government's overhaul to the scheme is expected to result in some 300,000 people being kicked off or prevented from accessing the NDIS.
Health Minister Mark Butler says he'll do that by ensuring that foundational supports, as agreed to, are in place by January 2028.
Butler says he's seen implementation plans from all states, with the exception of Queensland, for the rollout of Thriving Kids, a program to support children eight years old and younger.
But for everyone else, Butler acknowledged there was still "a lot of work" to do to get foundational supports up and running.

Liberal MP Garth Hamilton has asked the energy minister how much the Capacity Investment Scheme is costing Australian taxpayers.
Chris Bowen hasn't answered the question and says the scheme is being treated similarly to other schemes, such as the Snowy Hydro 2.0 business case, under the previous Coalition government.
"The point is that these projects that are supported by the Capacity Investment Scheme are all designed to bring cheaper energy to the availability of Australians," Bowen says.
Nationals frontbencher Kevin Hogan has stepped up on a point of order, asking the minister to stick to the question. But Bowen has already concluded his answer.
'Cut the crap': Tehan booted from chamber
Speaker Milton Dick is fully sick of it. He just booted Manager of Opposition Business Dan Tehan from the chamber for defying his ruling.
It all kicked off when Tehan got up to ask when Energy Minister Chris Bowen would "cut the crap" on the cost of the Capacity Investment Scheme. Now, if you've watched any amount of QT, you'll know that kind of language is not in order.
Dick tells him as much and initially lets him try again (despite the plea from independent Zali Steggall that the behaviour is out of order).
Tehan gives it another go, this time replacing the word "crap" with "fecal matter". You can imagine how well that went down.
"That is a direct defiance of what I've just addressed to the house," Dick says, before kicking Tehan out.
"The language must improve. I respect the traditions and conventions of this house. And I want to uphold them. I'm asking all members to do so. For goodness sake."
And in front of the Youth Parliament too!
Chris Bowen defends government's Capacity Investment Scheme
Nationals MP Llew O'Brien has asked the energy minister how much money has been handed to foreign companies under the Capacity Investment Scheme.
The scheme uses government revenue to accelerate and underwrite investment in renewable energy generation and battery storage.
Energy Minister Chris Bowen says the government keeps details of ongoing auctions under wraps so as not to undermine the position of the taxpayer.
Manager of Opposition Business Dan Tehan has jumped up on a point of order, asking the minister to stay relevant to the question.

I think that's a good thing. Those opposite think it's a bad thing."

On the US aircraft carrier "Abraham Lincoln," one of the lowest levels of mental health problems was reported
Kyiv • UNN
US Central Command Commander Admiral Brad Cooper said that the aircraft carrier "Abraham Lincoln" has one of the lowest rates of mental health problems among the 11 aircraft carriers. The deployment has been ongoing for nearly nine months, and the ship is participating in an operation against Iran.
The commander of the U.S. Central Command, Admiral Brad Cooper, said that the U.S. Navy aircraft carrier "Abraham Lincoln" currently has one of the lowest rates of mental health-related incidents among the 11 active U.S. aircraft carriers. CNN reports, writes UNN.
Details
Cooper visited the ship during a 10-day trip to the Middle East amid concerns about the crew’s morale and cases of suicidal thoughts. The carrier’s deployment has lasted nearly nine months.
This does not mean that everything is perfect. Extended service at sea is not for everyone. It is uniquely challenging and difficult, and each of us responds to stressors differently
The aircraft carrier has been on a combat deployment for nearly nine months
The admiral emphasized that mental health requires the same attention as physical and spiritual health.
I have long believed that mental health is another aspect of individual health that requires our attention just as much as physical and spiritual health
He also urged the sailors and Marines to continue their service and wished them a safe return home.
"Abraham Lincoln" arrived in the Middle East in January and is participating in a U.S. military operation against Iran, including the blockade of Iranian ports. Due to its prolonged combat missions, the ship has not been able to regularly visit friendly ports, where crews typically replenish supplies and have an opportunity to rest.

US Attorney General Blanche defends colleague after Trump’s reflecting pool slam
Judging the US Attorney on a single case ‘is not fair’, Blanche said after Trump criticised the way she handled a vandalism allegation
US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Sunday that he backs top Washington prosecutor Jeanine Pirro, who was criticised by US President Donald Trump for the way she handled a case of alleged vandalism at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
“I absolutely support US Attorney Pirro, as does President Trump,” Blanche said on NBC’s Meet the Press programme.
The Trump administration fast-tracked a renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool ahead of the nation’s Fourth of July celebrations, at a cost of about US$14.7 million.
Within weeks an algae bloom developed and material at the bottom of the pool started peeling off. Federal authorities subsequently charged former US Olympian David Hearn and others with vandalism.
In a court filing asking for the case against Hearn to be dismissed, Pirro blamed the Reflecting Pool’s peeling issues on “flawed” work by a contractor and accused the Interior Department of providing incomplete information at first.
Trump subsequently posted that Pirro should revisit her “hastily made decision” to drop the case.
Blanche said he does not fault Trump for being frustrated over the matter, adding that a witness said they observed vandalism.

Iran&apos;s parliament backed a bill criminalizing contacts with hostile media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Iran's parliament backed a bill criminalizing contacts with hostile media
Kyiv • UNN
Iran's parliament approved a bill providing for punishment for contacts with American and Israeli media. Interviews with them will be punishable by imprisonment for 6 months to 2 years.
Iran’s parliament on Sunday approved the general principles of a bill that provides for criminal liability for contacts with media outlets and organizations that the country’s authorities consider hostile. Reuters reports this, citing the Iranian publication Shargh, writes UNN.
Details
The document concerns, in particular, American and Israeli media outlets, as well as organizations funded by the United States or Israel. Interviews or participation in discussions with such media are proposed to be punishable by imprisonment ranging from six months to two years.
At the same time, Osan Salari, a member of the parliament’s Judicial and Legal Commission, said that some provisions of the document had not yet been discussed or approved, so the published details should not be considered final.
The bill will tighten control over contacts with foreigners
Contacts with other foreign media outlets are proposed to be permitted after notifying the Ministry of Intelligence. Communication with foreign embassies and organizations without notification and written permission from the Foreign Ministry may be punishable by fines and restrictions on social rights.
The EU extended sanctions against Iran — Ukraine joined them16.08.26, 09:26 • 21714 views
The document also provides for restrictions on transferring information to foreigners without intelligence-service permission and on scientific cooperation with institutions outside the approved list. For political or legislative proposals carried out under the direction of foreign intelligence services, if they harm Iran’s security or independence, up to 30 years in prison is proposed.
The bill is to be considered article by article, after which it will be submitted to the Guardian Council for consideration. The document can enter into force only after its approval.
Iran has already tightened liability for cooperation with foreign organizations following the 12-day war with Israel in 2025. This month, photojournalist Yalda Moayeri was sentenced to 15 years in prison, including for interviews with media outlets that the authorities consider hostile.

Is BlueScope's US business booming thanks to Trump's tariffs?
If you missed it this morning, manufacturer BlueScope has posted a bumper earnings result — the steel maker has recorded an astonishing 857% increase in its net profit to $802 million.
While the company may be our biggest steel maker here, it's also got a significant operation in the US, with its North Star earnings coming in at $US1.03 billion before interest and tax. (That's up a staggering 101% since last year.)
With those results in mind, BlueScope could be seen as one of the few fans of US President Donald Trump's tariffs.
BlueScope CEO Tania Archibald said the "very strong macro and trade environment" in the US has helped, but there's more to the company's results.
"What I would also say though is that the whole portfolio, when you look at it, has actually done quite well," she told The Business.
"So whilst we have a real standout performance by the North American business, what we also have is record performance in our South-East Asian business, and in Australia, what we have is an incredibly resilient performance given the very low regional prices and spreads that we have, and that's been driven by the large amount of oversupply coming out of China.
"Now that cycle will turn, but [for] the Australian business to be profitable demonstrates the extent of the resilience in that business, so I think it's been a pretty impressive performance all around."
You can catch the full interview tonight on The Business from 8:45pm on ABC News Channel, after the late news on ABC TV, or anytime on ABC iview.

"Coles has not done a trial using this technology," the spokesperson said.

On August 20 last year, James Hardie issued a downbeat first-quarter update and annual earnings downgrade triggering a 34% drop in its share price over the next two days.
Both class actions allege that the fibre cement maker made misleading representations and failed to comply with its disclosure obligations in relation to its fiscal 2026 earnings forecast issued in May and August 2025.
The suit also alleges James Hardie's conduct artificially inflated its share price, causing investors to pay more for the stock than they would have had the company complied with its legal obligations.

Alphabet planning to raise capital via $A bonds
Alphabet, the parent of Google, has mandated investment banks to work on its inaugural Australian dollar bond issue, according to a message sent by one of the book runners and reviewed by Reuters on Monday.
The US tech giant is considering issuing 3-, 5-, 10- and 20-year bonds, it said.
The message did not outline how much Alphabet could raise in the transaction or its plans with the proceeds.
Alphabet did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters.
The 3- and 5-year bonds could be issued with fixed or floating rates, the message said, while the 10- and 20-year bonds would be issued with fixed rates.
Alphabet raised $US25 billion in dollar bonds earlier in August following an almost $US85 billion equity capital raising in June.
Global tech companies are increasingly looking to capital markets to fund their massive AI spending, after having typically relied on their large cash reserves to fund investments.
The firms are expected to spend more than $US730 billion this year primarily on AI, and the outlay is already squeezing cash flows.
Alphabet posted its first ever negative free cash flow in its second-quarter report in late July.
Local currency bonds are becoming increasingly popular among some of the world's biggest issuers as they look to diversify their reliance on dollar bond transactions.
"Kangaroo" bond sales from foreign issuers in Australian dollars are at a record high of around $60 billion ($US42 billion) so far this year, up roughly 40% from 2025, LSEG data tracking internationally placed deals to late July shows.
ANZ, Deutsche Bank, RBC Capital Markets and TD Securities are joint lead managers on the Alphabet transaction, the book runner's message said.

Oil remains stuck below $US90/barrel despite rising tensions - can it last?
The global oil benchmark Brent crude has continued to creep higher this morning but remains stuck under the $US90/barrel level despite no resolution to the US-Iran war and who controls the Strait of Hormuz being in sight.
CBA commodities analyst Vivak Dhar says there are a number of buffers in place that is keeping a lid on prices despite little prospect of an official re opening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Firstly, pipelines bypassing the contested waterway are adding around 5 million barrels/day (mb/d) to global supply, while lower Chinese imports and non-OPEC+ supply from outside the Middle East account for another up to 8mb/d combined.
That's less pressure, but still short of the 20mb/d that flowed through the Strait before the war began.
"Of these supply buffers, the degree that Chinese imports can remain well below levels from last year is the most uncertain assumption," Mr Dhar said.
The IEA recently noted that China's switch to a greater use of EV had cut consumption by around 1.5mb/d alone.
"But a bigger driver of China's ability to reduce imports, especially compared to last year, was China's rapid increase in crude oil stockpiles from October 2024. This effectively means China's crude oil imports rates were inflated last year," Mr Dhar wrote in a research note.
However, on CBA calculations, China would still need to reduce is imports by 2.5 3.0mb/d to keep China's crude oil inventories flat sustainably flat over the longer term.
"Sticking with our conservative view on China's ability to reduce imports, we estimate that the supply buffers outlined above, in aggregate, imply oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz only need to reach 50 60% of pre-war levels to reassert oversupply concerns from the start of the year," Mr Dhar said.
Currently, on US Energy Department estimates the flow of oil through the Strait is at around 45% of its pre-war level.
Overall, Mr Dhar said there are good reasons for Brent crude to stay below $US90/barrel.
"We see $US100/barrel being threatened if US Iran violence escalates and transits through the strait halt sharply, but overall, an oversupply bias that pushes Brent oil futures towards $US80/barrel makes sense.
"We see $US70/barrel being realised if a US Iran deal is reached that allows Iran's oil through the Strait of Hormuz."

Key Event
Japan's GDP growth underwhelms
Japan's economy grew at a slower-than-expected pace in April-June, government data showed on Monday, as lacklustre household spending and business investment partly offset the impact of strong exports.
Gross domestic product rose 1.1% increase in annualised terms, missing a median market estimate of 2.0% growth in a Reuters poll and below an upwardly revised 1.9% expansion in the previous quarter.
"Growth was positive, but the details were somewhat weaker than expected," Meiji Yasuda Research Institute senior Kazutaka Maeda told Reuters.
"Still, given the disappointing results are likely to have been driven by temporary factors, I don't think the latest data would suggest a weakness ahead or affect the timing of the Bank of Japan's next interest rate hike," which is now widely expected as soon as September, he said.
The reading translates into a quarterly rise of 0.3%, compared with the median estimate of a 0.5% increase.
Private consumption, which accounts for more than half of economic output, was flat, falling short of a market estimate of a 0.5% increase, reflecting the effects of tuition-free education measures and higher tobacco prices.
Consumption and wage trends are key factors the BOJ is watching to gauge economic strength and determine the need for additional rate hikes.
Capital spending, a key driver of private demand, fell 1.2% in the second quarter, versus a market forecast for a 0.4% increase.
Key Event
Australians are struggling to navigate the superannuation system and the Age Pension
One of Australia's largest super funds Rest has released new research revealing many Aussies are unsure how to navigate the super system and prepare for retirement.
An online survey of 1,432 Rest members aged 18 and above participated in the research in March and April this year.
- 43% of members say they don't know what steps they need to take to prepare for life after work.
- 61% of members want greater integration between super funds and Centrelink to help simplify access to the Age Pension.
Rest says this data is significant given 2.7 million Australians aged 65 and over rely on either the full or part Age Pension.
Rest also says 1 in 3 Age Pensioners delay their application by more than a year.
Rest Chief Executive Officer, Vicki Doyle, says there is a growing disconnect in Australia's retirement system.
"Superannuation and the Age Pension are meant to work together, but too often people are left trying to bridge the gap between them," she says.
"When people don't know what steps to take as they approach retirement, it's a warning sign that the two biggest parts of Australia's retirement system aren't working together as seamlessly as they should."
From the survey, those aged 46 to 66 were the most likely to describe the retirement system as complex.
"If Australians find the retirement system hardest to navigate at the point they need it most, that's not simply a consumer education issue – it's a system design issue," says Ms Doyle.
"Australians need a retirement system that feels like one connected experience, with simpler pathways and better integration between the services they rely on most."
Other significant findings from the research include women and renters feeling particularly unsure and underprepared when thinking about retirement.
Australia's housing market is widening the gap between socioeconomic class, with a 2025 Grattan Institute Report finding home ownership rates among the country's poorest 40% of 45-54 year olds falling from 68% to 54% between 1981 and 2021.
The report found most older working Australians who rent don't have the funds to keep paying rent in retirement, arguing the Commonwealth Rent Assistance program, which supplements the Age Pension for poorer retirees, is too low.
In the previous two budgets, the government lifted the maximum rate of Rent Assistance by 27%. But the Grattan Institute report says despite this, a single retiree who relies solely on income support can afford to rent 4% of one-bedroom homes in Sydney, 13% in Brisbane, and 14% in Melbourne.
Rest Super says higher housing costs can leave renters more reliant on both superannuation and the Age Pension, while older women remain particularly vulnerable to housing insecurity and homelessness.
"Our retirement system must work for everyone, regardless of gender, housing situation or financial confidence. The system needs to do more of the heavy lifting, otherwise we risk leaving many Australians behind," Ms Doyle said.
"As more Australians retire while renting and rely on both super and the Age Pension, making the system simpler and more connected becomes critically important."

Aussie star Lani Pallister ends American GOAT's 16-year win streak

Lani Pallister hands Katie Ledecky first international 800m defeat at Pan Pacific Swimming Championships
In short:
Lani Pallister has become the first swimmer to beat American Katie Ledecky over 800m at an international swim meet.
Pallister finished her Pan Pacific Swimming Championships with four gold medals — in the 200m, 400m, 800m and 4x200m relay — as Australia won 15 golds overall.
Sam Short also picked up three individual gold medals, breaking the national records of Ian Thorpe and Grant Hackett to sweep the 400m, 800m and 1,500m.
Lani Pallister has toppled swimming legend Katie Ledecky for a second time in 24 hours to complete her stunning Pan Pacific championship campaign with a fourth gold medal.
The 24-year-old Pallister was under world-record pace for much of the race as she won the 800m freestyle final in eight minutes and 6.1 seconds from four-time Olympic champion Ledecky (8:07.26) in the American's signature event.
Ledecky's lone previous defeat in an 800m freestyle final since 2010 came in a small domestic event in February 2024 against Canadian superstar Summer McIntosh, making Pallister the first to beat her over the distance at an international meet.
"Today is the most nervous I've ever felt in my entire life. I was just so locked in and I've been really focused on what I want," Pallister said.
"The 800m is my favourite event. So to have the three titles this week and be just behind Katie in the 1,500 [is great but] … this is the one that I wanted."
Ledecky, who famously signed an autograph for a young Pallister a decade ago, telling her to "dream big", wrote on Instagram that she "can't help but smile about another incredible race with [Pallister]".
Pallister had beaten Ledecky to win the 400m freestyle gold a day earlier and took silver behind her great rival in the 1,500m free, as well as downed McIntosh to win the 200m free gold and also collect gold in the 4x200m free relay.
Australia's Dolphins well and truly flexed their middle- and long-distance muscle at the meet, two years out from the LA Olympics, with Sam Short also emerging with three individual gold medals after winning the men's 1,500m free to go with his 400 and 800 free titles.
Having beaten Ian Thorpe's 1999 Pan Pacs record to win the 400m, he erased another Australian legend's mark in the 1,500m.
His time of 14:33.97 was the sixth-fastest in history, breaking Grant Hackett's Australian record that had stood since 2001, and came a day after German teenager Johannes Liebmann smashed the world record at the European Aquatics Championships.
"I am proud of my consistency," said Short, who also won the 400m, 800m, and 1,500m titles at the Commonwealth Games late last month.
"I've gone five well sub-15-minute swims now, so if I can do that here my average come Olympics, world championships, all I need to do is be my average and be contending for some podium places."
Adding to a strong final day for Australia, Zac Stubblety-Cook went from fourth to first in the 200m breaststroke final, winning in 2:08.09 from American Josh Matheny.
And countryman Jamie Jack won the 50m freestyle gold in a championship record of 21.35 as American Jack Alexy took silver in 21.42.
"It's awesome. That's the best I could ask for," Jack said.
American Kate Douglass lowered her own world record in the 50m free twice, winning the final in 23.19.
Douglass capped a busy night by anchoring the US women to a dominant victory in the 4x100 medley relay in a championship record time of 3:50.43, with Australia second in 3:55.09.
The US men won from Australia in the 4x100 medley relay.
Australia finished the four-day meet with a medal haul of 15 gold, 11 silver and nine bronze, behind only the US haul of 19, 22 and nine.

MINSK, 16 August (BelTA) – Chairman of the Permanent Commission of the House of Representatives on Education, Culture and Science, historian Igor Marzalyuk spoke about the false narratives about the origins of Belarusians promoted in neighboring countries in the latest episode of BelTA’s project True History. Lectures by Igor Marzalyuk.
 
Various theories about the origins of Belarusians are put forward by nationalist movements in neighboring countries. Igor Marzalyuk stressed that there are numerous false concepts that call Belarusian statehood into question. “The doctrine of Great Russian chauvinist nationalists: the Belarusian nation never existed and does not exist; the Belarusian state is a fake created by Polish nationalists and the Bolsheviks. It is nothing more than the territory of Western Russia. The Belarusian language is something repulsive, nonexistent, to be ridiculed. That is the gist of it,” he said.
 
He noted that the doctrine of Polish nationalists turns everything upside down. According to it, the Belarusian nation belongs to the Great Russian one, and Belarusians themselves are exclusively Orthodox. At the same time, Western Belarus, in this concept, is Polish territory occupied by Stalin in collusion with Hitler. “The repressions of 1937–1938 in Belarus were, first and foremost, repressions against Poles and the Polish intelligentsia. The actions of the Home Army during and after the war are presented as heroic resistance by Polish patriots fighting to restore the borders of interwar Poland. Therefore, Western Belarus is not Belarus - it is Poland, suffering under the Belarusian yoke. That is the doctrine of those who share such nationalist, chauvinist Polish views. This is a fairly marginal viewpoint - there are more cunning, more subtle, and more camouflaged ones,” the expert said.
 
Igor Marzalyuk also outlined the key tenets of Ukrainian nationalist doctrine. “Belarus, it turns out, has occupied and is systematically assimilating the ‘Ukrainian’ population of Belarusian Polesie, meaning Brest Oblast and Gomel Oblast. There are supposedly (shocking to say!) 1.5 million Ukrainians living there. And they are all suffering. The emphasis is placed on the fact that, under the terms of the 1918 Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, these territories were ceded to the Ukrainian People’s Republic, and also on the fact that in Brest Oblast, after the Great Patriotic War, Bandera armed formations were active. The Reichskommissariat Ukraine, which was established during the German occupation, indeed covered all of Brest Oblast and a large part of Gomel Oblast. In this way, the Nazi occupiers fulfilled the boldest and most ‘tempting’ dreams of Ukrainian nationalists regarding Belarusian lands. But as we know, nothing came of it,” the historian emphasized.

Brazil: Lula, Bolsonaro return to strongholds to launch runs for president

Brazil: Lula, Bolsonaro return to strongholds to launch runs for president
Candidates Lula and Bolsonaro appeal to Brazil’s women voters with promises to combat rising femicide and gender violence.
Brazil’s two main presidential candidates have inaugurated their campaigns by mustering supporters in their political strongholds ahead of what is expected to be a fierce October election.
President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva spoke with nostalgia to more than 10,000 supporters on Sunday at the Vila Euclides Stadium outside Sao Paulo – a city where he rose to political fame 47 years ago as a metalworkers’ union leader during the country’s 1964-1985 military dictatorship.
The 80-year-old, wearing a hat after a skin cancer diagnosis, insisted Brazil needs more of his policies.
Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, age 45 and one of the sons of former President Jair Bolsonaro, gathered with thousands of voters on Copacabana Beach in Rio de Janeiro. His father, under house arrest following his conviction for an attempted coup, did not attend the rally.
Lula echoed his own earlier comments denouncing foreign interference in Brazil’s politics. His allies have accused the United States government of seeking to boost Flavio Bolsonaro’s bid with measures such as raising tariffs on Brazilian exports and revoking the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to Washington.
Speaking about Brazil’s vast reserves of rare minerals, Lula said, “No one [abroad] will tap our minerals. We are going to tap them for the benefit of the Brazilian people.”
Bolsonaro argued that he is “the only one who can sit with the United States, with China, with Israel, with the Middle East, with India and with Argentina to make the best and biggest trade deals for our nation.”
His party’s convention was attended by Argentina’s President Javier Milei. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and several members of the Trump administration have expressed support for him.
Both top candidates appeal to women voters
Women account for nearly 53 percent of Brazil’s 158 million eligible voters, according to the country’s electoral court.
Both Lula, who is seeking his fourth nonconsecutive term, and right-wing challenger Bolsonaro have used the fight against gender violence to appeal to voters.
Brazil registered nearly 400 femicides (the killing of a female because of her gender) in the first quarter of 2026, the highest number for the period since the country first began tracking the crime 11 years ago, according to Brazil’s Justice and Public Security Ministry’s database.
“Men need to learn from childhood that they are no better than women. We need to be equal,” said Lula, as First Lady Rosangela da Silva stood by his side, nodding. She was one of the event’s main speakers in Sao Bernardo do Campo, where Lula lived for many years.
The rally wasn’t the first time the president has confronted this heavily entrenched crisis. During his Workers’ Party convention to launch his re-election bid in early August, Lula had said that men who commit acts of domestic or gender-based violence must choose between supporting him or hitting a woman, declaring that if they choose violence, “they don’t need to vote for me”.
Lula said he would launch a platform within 10 days, noting that more details are still to come on his gender-responsive policies, including education initiatives and laws to further thwart and punish violence against women.
Femicide laws and legal protections for women in Brazil have only sluggishly improved over time. In 2024, femicide stopped being classified as an aggravated form of homicide and finally became a separate crime, punishable by 20 to 40 years in prison. Still, the grim trend has not abated.
Meanwhile, with his mother and wife by his side, Bolsonaro promised his supporters that he would also work to fight violence against women.
Brazilians will vote in the presidential election on October 4.

In Messina, Italy, four priceless works by Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum

In Messina, Italy, four priceless works by Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum
Kyiv • UNN
On the evening of August 15, four works by Antonello da Messina were stolen from the MuMe museum in Messina, including parts of the San Gregorio polyptych. Investigators are considering the possibility that the theft was commissioned by collectors.
On the evening of August 15, four works by the outstanding 15th-century Italian artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from the MuMe Regional Interdisciplinary Museum of Messina, three of which are parts of the San Gregorio Polyptych. Corriere della Sera reports this, writes UNN.
Details
The perpetrators broke into the museum and forced open the armored display case where part of the polyptych was kept. They took the central panel depicting the Madonna, as well as the two upper panels depicting the Archangel Gabriel and the Annunciation. The thieves left two more panels featuring Saints Benedict and Gregory on a low wall while fleeing.
A double-sided panel by Antonello da Messina depicting the Madonna and Child and Christ in the Pietà was also stolen. The alarm was triggered, and surveillance cameras recorded the events, so investigators are examining the footage to identify those involved in the theft.
Investigators are examining the possibility that the theft was commissioned
According to investigators, the thieves may have been well aware of the location of the exhibits and the museum’s layout. To get inside, they cut through part of the railing near the second entrance, after which they quickly entered the rooms containing Antonello da Messina’s works.
Museum Director Marisa Mercuri called the incident “a very serious loss.” Messina Mayor Federico Basile and Councillor for Culture Enzo Caruso also stated that the robbery was serious.
Investigators are considering the possibility that the theft was planned in advance and carried out on behalf of collectors. Particular attention is being paid to the fact that the perpetrators took specifically the works painted on wood, which would be difficult to select by chance during a rapid robbery.
The San Gregorio Polyptych is considered one of the most important works by Antonello da Messina held in his native Messina. Since 2013, the work has been included in the immovable cultural heritage of the Sicily region. The polyptych suffered significant damage during an unsuccessful 19th-century restoration and the 1908 earthquake, but it was partially restored in subsequent years.

six-tatami garden tea room layers salvaged timber, titanium, and steel in ichihara, japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
20:35:46 UTC
05:35:46 KST

Kurosawa Kawara-ten renovates a timber tea room in Ichihara
In Ichihara, Chiba, Japan, Kurosawa Kawara-tenrenovates a six-tatami tea room within an annex belonging to a former family timber business. The project retains traces of the building’s accumulated history while introducing new elements through a material and formal language that connects the existing structure with its garden setting. For generations, the property was associated with the family’s timber business. A small annex within the garden accommodates a tea room, storage space, and garage, with the six-tatami tea room renovated as a place for resting between farming and gardening activities and for receiving guests. The main house is a traditional timber dwelling surrounded by a professionally designed garden with stone lanterns and carefully positioned rocks.
The annex has a different architectural character. Prefabricated siding and decorative brick were added over time as the property changed, reflecting periods in which the business closed, the family moved to the city, and the building was extended with readily available materials. The renovation retains these layers instead of establishing a strict distinction between old and new. Existing elements are incorporated into the new intervention through changes in form, material, and detailing.
A glazed extension connects the tea room with the garden
A glazed volume is inserted between the tea room and the existing storage and garage, establishing a defined transition within the annex. A gabled canopy extends the line of the existing rain hood, while openings follow the pitch of the roof and bring views of the garden into the interior. The floor is level with the exterior ground, allowing the client’s mother, whose mobility is limited, to move between the interior and garden without encountering a step. The glazed enclosure establishes a separation between the renovated room and the less connected portions of the annex, while the canopy geometry maintains a visual relationship with the existing structure.
Several elements from the tea room’s previous configuration remain in place, including a decorative post, perimeter ledge, and sliding entrance door. Studio Kurosawa Kawara-ten arranges new components around these elements according to principles associated with sukiya architecture, which emphasizes the precise composition of slender structural and architectural lines. Window frames and sills are detailed with distinct hierarchies, while the walls retain their original shinkabe construction. Japanese evergreen oak veneer panels are positioned behind the columns, separated by fine shadow gaps. Through this approach, existing and new lines are brought into a shared architectural composition without emphasizing their different periods of construction.
existing siding and decorative brick retain traces of the building’s later additions
Salvaged timber materials connect the renovation to Ichihara
Material selection is closely tied to the history and location of the property. Japanese evergreen oak used for the exterior and interior wall surfaces was salvaged from trees felled nearby and would otherwise have been discarded. The material introduces locally sourced timber into the renovation while extending its use within the building. A keyaki plank from the tokonoma alcove was also planed and refinished as a shelf, giving an existing component a new function within the renovated room. New cypress beams used in the lean-to are treated with an iron mordant, bringing their color closer to that of the existing timber and reducing the visual distinction between the two. The treatment also references the industrial character of Ichihara’s waterfront, several kilometers away, through the iron content of the mordant. Other materials establish different relationships with time. The canopy is clad in titanium sheet, selected for its ability to maintain its appearance for approximately 60 years, while the exterior columns are made from Corten steel, whose surface develops a controlled layer of rust.
The project avoids establishing a hierarchy between existing and newly introduced materials. Salvaged components and newly sourced materials are selected according to their relationship with the site, its construction history, and its material character. Reuse and repurposing therefore form part of the architectural approach to the building’s continuity. Materials retain traces of their origin, age, and previous use, allowing the renovation to incorporate elements that are specific to the property and its surroundings. The approach also responds to a broader condition affecting Japanese residential architecture. Since the postwar economic boom, the closure of businesses, movement of families to urban areas, and incremental modifications to houses have contributed to a large number of vacant homes. The renovation of the small tea room addresses this condition at the scale of an existing family property, using material provenance and architectural continuity to adapt the building to its current use while retaining its accumulated history.

US-Iran MoU is set to expire: What to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
20:28:21 UTC
05:28:21 KST

US-Iran MoU ends: What happens next?
Both sides accused the other of violating the June agreement shortly after it was signed.
The Memorandum of Understanding aimed at ending fighting between the US and Iran expired on Monday, with little sign that either side is willing to extend the agreement, which both sides have accused the other of violating for weeks.
“We have not yet made a decision to restart negotiations with the United States,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a post on Telegram on Saturday.
Meanwhile, mediators from Qatar and Pakistan continued to exchange messages with Iran. Araghchi added that Iran was working on a separate agreement with Oman to hash out new shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz, but emphasised that this was only possible if a political solution was reached.
On the US side, President Donald Trump told supporters in New York on Friday that the US would soon claim the critically important waterway for itself.
Here’s what you need to know about the expired MoU.
What is the MoU?
The agreement, signed on June 17 by Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, followed rare high-level talks hosted by Pakistan. It was meant to bring an end to more than three months of war that had killed thousands and crippled commercial movement in the Gulf, especially oil and gas exports relied on globally.
Leaving complex issues such as Iran’s nuclear programme to be dealt with later, the agreement sought not only to find an immediate diplomatic solution to halt the war with Tehran, but also to find an end to Israel’s attacks on Lebanon.
Iran and the US, the agreement said, “declare the immediate and permanent termination of military operations” and that a “final deal” would “confirm the permanent termination of the war on all fronts”. The agreement said this “final deal” would be endorsed by the UN Security Council and would be reached in a maximum of 60 days, which could be extended by mutual consent.
The US was to end its naval blockade within 30 days, remove its forces from near Iran after the “final deal” was reached and begin work on a reconstruction and development package for Iran of at least $300bn. Washington also agreed to terminate sanctions against Iran, issue waivers for Iranian oil exports and allow Tehran to access frozen funds. Iran, for its part, was to clear mines from the Strait of Hormuz and allow ships to pass “with no charge” for 60 days.
Tehran also reaffirmed it would not seek nuclear weapons and would negotiate on issues such as enrichment, the details of which would be laid out in a “final deal” to be backed by the UN.
Was the MoU successful?
Although the US and Iranian versions of the agreement differed slightly, much of the dispute since its signing has centred on more basic issues, such as whether it was a ceasefire or a more permanent agreement and what each side was supposed to do.
Whether the entire agreement was still in effect soon became disputed, and by June 27, Trump was calling Iranian strikes in the region “a foolish violation” of the deal. Iran said US strikes “violate Article 1 of the Memorandum of Understanding”.
On July 7, Trump said the agreement was “over,” and the US continued launching attacks on Iran, including on what Tehran called civilian infrastructure, killing at least 50 people. Iranian officials said the US had “violated and suspended” all its commitments and Tehran had “likewise suspended all our own commitments”.
Since then, the US has not fully lifted sanctions on Iran and Trump has scoffed at the idea of paying Iran for reconstruction, suggesting instead that Tehran pay compensation to families of protesters it had killed “over the last 50 years” as well as “all the people they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts”.
Reopening Hormuz has not materialised either, with Iranian and US officials continuing to insist their side controls the strait. Earlier this week, the Pentagon said it had fired on a Panama-flagged cargo vessel in the strait because it “violated the US blockade against Iran.”
“The ceasefire stopped and was rendered obsolete after the US didn’t comply with the terms of the agreement, or the MoU,” Mostafa Khoshcheshm, professor at the University of Applied Sciences in Tehran, told Al Jazeera.
In particular, he added, Tehran views the US as having failed on its promises of releasing Iranian assets, lifting sanctions, removing its naval blockade and having Israel withdraw from southern Lebanon. “Now, formally, on paper, it is said the deadline has ended,” Khoshcheshm said.
What happens next?
Although the MoU expired on Monday, what that means exactly depends on which side you ask.
Iran’s Araghchi said on Friday that what was in the Islamabad MoU was “the end of the war, not a ceasefire”, according to the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA). He added that since the US violated the MoU and continued attacks, “there was no 60-day ceasefire that needed to be extended”.
The recent reshuffle in Iran’s national security apparatus suggests a tougher stance in future talks and less willingness to back down, particularly on control of Hormuz. Earlier this month, for instance, the former head of the IRGC, Mohsen Rezaei, was named as the new head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, its top security body. The move is meant to better synchronise military and civilian operations, analysts have told Al Jazeera.
Rezaei’s appointment, along with other recent leadership changes, “shows Iran believes it has the upper hand”, Khoshcheshm said. Any new talks would likely see Iran coming to the table with more demands, he said, from ending the war on Gaza, to lifting sanctions and a blockade of Yemen, even calling for the denuclearisation of Israel.
Few cards left to play for the US
As for the US, Trump and his administration have escalated rhetoric regarding the strait and economic warfare.
Trump on Friday announced plans to formally claim the waterway for the US.
“After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States,” he said.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also said on Friday that the US would apply measures that have “never been seen” on Iran.
But there are not many levers left for Trump to pull if he wants to exert more pressure on Tehran, Barbara Slavin, distinguished fellow at the Washington, DC-based Stimson Center, told Al Jazeera.
US stocks of interceptor missiles have been depleted, its strategic oil reserves drained and key military hardware, including aircraft carriers, have been kept at sea months longer than planned, meaning the US has few military options left to try. As for economic pressure, Tehran has shown it can inflict economic damage of its own by disrupting traffic transiting Hormuz, Slavin said.
“Iran is playing hardball here, clearly furious at the Trump administration for, in its view, not fulfilling the MoU signed back in June,” Slavin said. “They’re making the international economy and they’re making Donald Trump sweat.”
One way or another, Iran would likely be reimbursed for the war and gain a great deal of control over the Strait of Hormuz, Slavin said. This conflict, she said, “resolves through a deal, probably after our midterm elections, when there will be less of an impact on the vote”.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf told reporters in Tehran on Saturday that the concessions Iran won in the MoU were “a source of pride and victory”.
“I can say with complete conviction that we truly emerged victorious in this war, both militarily and politically,” he said.

Category 1 Hurricane Lala caused flash floods and landslides in Hawaii, destroying several homes, while one person was killed in a car accident. BBC reports, UNN writes.
Details
The Big Island was hit hardest by the disaster, although the hurricane passed it without making landfall. In the coastal communities of Naalehu and Waiohinu, several homes were torn from their foundations, after which search-and-rescue operations began.
Although the storm’s center did not cross the coast, up to 89 cm of rain fell in some areas. Powerful torrents of water rushed down mountain slopes, causing floods and landslides.
Rescue operations continue in Hawaii
Hawaii County reported that the eye of the storm passed approximately 48 km from the South Point of the Big Island. The National Weather Service office in Honolulu received reports of two homes washed away by heavy rains.
What makes this very difficult is that there is fast-moving water, there is debris, there are boulders on the road, and it is dark
About 180 Hawaii National Guard service members were deployed to respond to the effects of the disaster. According to PowerOutage, about 219,000 customers were left without electricity. Three hospitals were operating on backup generators, while 190 flights were delayed because of the bad weather.
The storm continues to pose a threat
After Lala’s wind speed reached 145 km/h, the storm weakened to a tropical storm on Sunday. Winds decreased to approximately 108 km/h, but tropical storm warnings remained in effect for all eight major Hawaiian islands.
Lala is expected to bring an additional 4 to 8 inches of rain to the Big Island and windward Maui, with maximum rainfall totals of 30 to 35 inches
Authorities warned that the threat of additional floods and landslides remained. The last time a powerful hurricane directly struck Hawaii was in 1992, when Category 4 Hurricane Iniki caused six deaths and approximately $3 billion in damage.

Britain’s Amy Hunt wins record fourth gold medal at European championships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
20:23:02 UTC
05:23:02 KST

Britain’s Amy Hunt wins record 4th gold medal at European championships. ‘Mondo’ victorious again
BIRMINGHAM, England (AP) — Amy Hunt won a record fourth gold medal in a single edition of the European championships when Britain clinched victory in the mixed 4x100 relay on Sunday.
Hunt had already won two individual titles — the 100 and 200 — and added a third gold Saturday in the women’s 4x100 relay at Alexander Stadium.
The team of Jeremiah Azu, Dina Asher-Smith, Zharnel Hughes and Hunt won Sunday in a time of 39.97 seconds. Germany was second in 40.11 and Spain third in 40.42.
On the anchor leg, Hunt pulled away from Gina Lückenkemper to cross the line for gold.
“Oh my gosh, I’m over the moon,” Hunt told the BBC. “To finish it off with some of my best friends in the sport ... to do it all together is incredible.”
Asher-Smith won her career eighth European championships gold and became the competition’s most decorated athlete with her 11th medal, moving one ahead of the late Polish sprinter Irena Szewinska.
This was the debut of the mixed 4x100 relay in the European championships.
“It’s good to get to try something new,” Asher-Smith told the BBC, although she added, “I was absolutely terrified.”
Four in a row for Duplantis
Swedish pole vaulter Armand “Mondo” Duplantis earned his fourth consecutive European championship title by clearing 6.15 meters.
Duplantis is the world record holder — he vaulted 6.31 meters in March. That was his 15th world record. He first broke it in 2020 and has eclipsed his mark by 1 centimeter each time since.
The two-time reigning Olympic champion watched on as Greek rival Emmanouil Karalis (6.00) lost momentum after getting over 6.10 but knocking the bar off on his way down. Karalis took his second straight silver at the championships. France’s Baptiste Thiery (5.85) earned bronze.
Italy wins medal table
Bragging rights were on the line in the last event of the week-long championships when Britain and Italy were tied at nine golds each atop the medal table.
The Italians pulled out the victory in the men’s 4x400 relay final, and the home team settled for silver. That means Italy topped the table with 10 golds and an overall 22 medals, three more than Britain’s total.
Italy also topped the medal table two years ago in Rome.
In the penultimate event of the championships, the Dutch women’s 4x400 relay team won gold when star Femke Broeders-Bol held off Britain’s Emily Newnham down the stretch. It was the third straight women’s 4x400 relay championships title and Broeders-Bol’s sixth career gold at the championships.
In the women’s 1,500 final, Britain’s Georgia Hunter Bell improved on her silver medal from two years ago by crossing the line first in 4:07.78.
Larissa Iapichino had added to Italy’s gold tally by winning the women’s long jump, leaping 7.00 meters for the title.
Memorable marathons
Amanal Petros made sure there was no photo finish this time.
The German won the men’s marathon on Sunday morning by a whopping 7 seconds, less than a year after missing out on gold in a photo finish at the world championships in Tokyo.
Petros crossed the finish line in Birmingham in 2 hours, 9 minutes, 11 seconds — breaking the championships record in the process. Italy’s Pietro Riva took silver with his 2:09:18, three seconds better than Israel’s Gashau Ayale.
Last September, the Eritrean-born Petros settled for silver behind Tanzania’s Alphonce Simbu in the closest marathon in world championships history. Both men were officially clocked at 2:09:48, but it was determined that Simbu crossed the line a fraction sooner.
In the women’s marathon Sunday, Finland’s Alisa Vainio dominated the field to finish in 2:22:26, nearly five minutes ahead of silver medalist Lili Anna Vindics-Toth of Hungary. Britain’s Abbie Donnelly took bronze. Vainio broke Christelle Daunay’s championship record from 2014 by almost three minutes.

What foreign drivers need to know about driving in Belarus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
20:23:00 UTC
05:23:00 KST

MINSK, 16 August (BelTA) - The Internal Affairs Ministry of Belarus has outlined what foreign drivers need to know about driving on Belarusian roads, BelTA has learned.
“Foreign citizens temporarily staying or temporarily residing in Belarus are entitled to use their foreign driving licenses. The license must comply with the requirements of the 1968 Convention on Road Traffic, or be issued in one of the official languages of Belarus, or be accompanied by a certified translation,” the ministry said.
Foreigners who have been granted permanent residence and hold a biometric residence permit must obtain a Belarusian driving license within 90 days. This requirement does not apply to Russian citizens holding Russian-style licenses.
Law enforcement officials warned that driving without a license carries administrative liability, and repeated violations within a year may result in criminal prosecution. “Compliance with traffic rules is mandatory for everyone,” the ministry stressed.

African Union rejects foreign interference, parallel governments in Sudan

Adel Abdelrheem and Rania Abushamala
16 August 2026•Update: 16 August 2026
The African Union Peace and Security Council on Sunday rejected foreign interference in Sudan's internal affairs and attempts to establish parallel entities or governments that could undermine the country's unity and sovereignty.
The position was conveyed during a meeting between Sudan's Sovereignty Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and an African Union Peace and Security Council delegation led by Algerian diplomat Mohamed Khaled at the presidential palace in the capital Khartoum, according to a statement from the Transitional Sovereignty Council.
Khaled, the council's rotating chair, described the meeting as "fruitful," saying it addressed several issues related to peace, security and stability in Sudan.
He reiterated the council's condemnation of any foreign interference in Sudan's internal affairs, saying such intervention "fuels the conflict."
Khaled also affirmed the council's rejection of attempts to create parallel entities or governments that could undermine Sudan's unity and sovereignty.
"The only path to achieving lasting peace in Sudan is through dialogue, national reconciliation and reaching a comprehensive political settlement that meets the aspirations of the Sudanese people," he said.
He welcomed steps related to a peace initiative and the government's return to performing its duties from Khartoum, describing the move as "pivotal" to restoring the functioning of state institutions and providing essential services to citizens.
Khaled called on the government and political forces to make the transitional process more inclusive and work toward a national consensus leading to a constitutional system through free and fair elections.
Earlier Sunday, Sudanese Prime Minister Kamil Idris told the council's delegation that a Sudanese-Sudanese dialogue would "begin soon."
Sudan has been engulfed in war since April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) over plans to integrate the latter into the regular military.
The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN estimates.

The Houthis did not immediately comment on the army's statement.
Separately, Yemen's Defense Ministry said Houthi mortar fire caused extensive damage to homes in Taiz.

Yemen has witnessed a relative lull since April 2022 in a war that began nearly 12 years ago between government forces and the Houthis, who have controlled the capital Sanaa and other cities and provinces since September 2014.
Fighting has resumed in several provinces in recent weeks, however, including Marib, Al-Jawf, Al-Dhalea, and Taiz, as the country continues to face one of the world’s worst humanitarian and economic crises.

Historian exposes false theories about the origin of Belarusians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
20:06:00 UTC
05:06:00 KST

MINSK, 16 August (BelTA) - Chairman of the Permanent Commission of the House of Representatives on Education, Culture and Science, historian Igor Marzalyuk spoke about the historically unfounded concepts regarding the origin of Belarusians in the latest episode of BelTA’s project True History. Lectures by Igor Marzalyuk
 
 
 
 
  
 .The expert emphasized that those who attempt to divide the Belarusian nation in order to make it easier to govern have put forward various concepts of ethnogenesis, i.e. the origin of the people. “The academic scientific community views the Belarusian ethnic community as a product of the evolutionary development of the common Slavic and East Slavic community that preceded it. However, the most popular mythologeme in the modern ultranationalist narrative (I am now referring to the Belarusian nationalist ethnic narrative) says that there never was any East Slavic unity. That modern Russians, or Velikorusy, are Slavophone Asian Mongoloids, and that Belarusians are not simply an East Slavic people, but Slavophone Balts. So in their narrative we are Balts that lost the Baltic language. They say ‘we are Balts, not Slavs. Therefore, more true Aryans than all the rest.’ Thus, through such constructs, the Belarusian nation is presented both genetically and historically as a bearer of the Western European tradition. The cultural unity of the Eastern Slavs is ignored. Belarusian neo-Nazis declare paganism as the true national religion ,” Igor Marzalyuk said.
Also, according to the historian, there are modifications of such views, in which the truly Aryan, racially pure peoples are those of historical Rus’. “Their genetic origin is declared to be the heritage of distant Indo-European ancestors, and all problems and failures are attributed to racial mixing with alien harmful elements - Mongoloids, Finno-Ugrians, and all the rest. The common enemy, naturally, for the neo-Nazis who profess such views (whether they are Belarusian, Russian, or Ukrainian) is the Jewry. Such an interpretation is particularly popular among adherents of radical National Socialist traditions and is reflected, among other things, in Black Pagan Metal, heavy rock and folk-rock culture, where Nazism is openly preached in the lyrics. Similar groups have existed in Belarus, Russia, and Ukraine,” the expert noted.
He added that another ultra-radical nationalist version makes an emphasis on anti-Russian themes in Belarusian history: “The Belarusian historical tradition is presented as a permanent struggle of the Belarusian Western European people against Asian Moscow. Accordingly, the following chain is constructed. The wars of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth against Russia are interpreted as a Russian-Belarusian confrontation. The War of 1812 is portrayed as a joint struggle with Napoleon against the Russian enslavers. All uprisings (1794, 1831, 1863–1864), which were attempts to restore the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, are declared simply to be a Belarusian national liberation movement.” 
There are as many myths about national statehood regarding the 20th century. “The BSSR is declared to be a puppet state, which Belarusians supposedly did not create and to which they have no relation. Unlike the BPR (the Belarusian People's Republic). Although, as we know, the BPR did not actually exist as an independent state. The withdrawal of the German occupiers after the revolution in Kaiser Germany [in 1918] from the territory of Belarus is interpreted in the most mythologized tales about our past as the occupation of the BPR by Soviet Russia. Although, again, I emphasize, the BPR as an institution of power, as a state, did not exist,” Igor Marzalyuk noted.
“The most radical versions are associated with attempts to break the traditional historical memory of the Belarusian people, which is based on the tragedy and heroism of the Great Patriotic War. In this historical discourse, they propose ‘new’ terminology - the German-Soviet, or better yet, Soviet-German war. The partisan struggle is denied as a fact of Belarusian history, of Belarusian historical agency. For proponents of such concepts, partisans are bandits. Participants in the partisan movement, in the best traditions of Goebbels’ propaganda, are declared to be bandits and robbers. The war, the occupation, and the confrontation between partisans, underground fighters, and Nazi collaborators are interpreted in terms of a civil war. As if there was no Great Patriotic War, but a civil war. Therefore, those traitors, collaborators who used Belarusian nationalist ideology and actively cooperated with the Hitlerite occupation regime, are declared to be true heroes of the nation and fighters for national independence. To justify their actions during the war, the number of political repressions of the 1930s is grossly inflated compared to what actually took place. Why is this done? For only one reason - to assert that the Stalinist regime was more criminal than the Hitlerite one. Accordingly, those who opposed it are heroes for these people, not traitors,” the historian said.

U.S. Central Command Commander Adm. Brad Cooper on Sunday acknowledged mental health challenges aboard the USS Lincoln after reports that a sailor jumped overboard amid the aircraft carrier's long Middle East deployment.
"Here's an important fact: Of the U.S. Navy's 11 active aircraft carriers, the Lincoln currently has among the lowest number of cases related to mental health," Cooper said in a statement posted to X following his visit to the ship on Saturday. "This doesn't mean that all is perfect. Find any of the nearly 4 million Navy veterans in America today and they will likely tell you that service at sea for long periods isn't for everyone."
Cooper's visit and statement follow reports of widespread morale and mental health issues aboard the Lincoln, which has been deployed for more than eight months. The Navy Times reported last week that several sailors had attempted to go overboard, and Stars and Stripes also reported on widespread mental health issues.
Cooper, the top U.S. commander in the war with Iran, said his visit to the ship was "awe-inspiring" and lauded the crew for "stepping up and making mental health and crew resilience a leadership priority."
President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, however, have sought to downplay reports of deteriorating morale aboard the Lincoln.
Asked by a reporter on Friday whether the Lincoln's deployment has gone on too long, Trump said, "No, no, no" and added, "not nearly long enough." The president also said that the Lincoln would soon be replaced in the region by a different carrier.
Hegseth said that reports are "completely misrepresented."
The USS George Washington is now headed toward the Middle East and is expected to take the place of the Lincoln, MS NOW reported.
Lawmakers, meanwhile, have questioned and criticized the Pentagon over conditions aboard the Lincoln.
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., who serves on the Senate Armed Services and Intelligence Committees, said in a statement on Saturday that there "must be accountability for the reported deteriorating conditions endured by our service members serving in a reckless war started with no justification, no strategy, and no end in sight."
"I demand hearings, accountability, and a clear plan to protect our service members and prioritize American families," she said.

How AI is splitting Australia's education system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
19:55:17 UTC
04:55:17 KST

Why alternative schools are not rushing to bring AI into classrooms
In short:
One of Australia's largest alternative school systems has ruled out developing its own artificial intelligence (AI) tool.
Generative-AI tools have been created for public schools in New South Wales, South Australia and Queensland, with supporters saying it reduces workloads and helps students more study effectively.
But early research has cautioned against an over-reliance on the technology, and the NSW government has now launched a broad review into its impact on student learning.
The head of one of Australia's major alternative school systems has ruled out creating an artificial intelligence (AI) learning tool for its teachers and students.
Generative-AI learning tools have already been created for public schools in New South Wales, South Australia, and Queensland but concerns about the technology's impact on critical thinking are growing.
Steiner Education Australia CEO Andrew Hill said their schools would not be following suit.
"Anything which is going to compromise healthy growth of the brain, we would take a cautionary view towards," Mr Hill said.
Supporters of embedding AI in schools say it reduces teacher workloads and allows senior students to study more effectively.
But early research has suggested an over-reliance on AI reduces independent problem solving and critical thinking skills.
Last week, the NSW government announced it would consider banning take-home assessments as part of a broader review into AI's impact on student learning.
Complicated ethics
Data from the OECD suggests most Australian teachers have at least experimented with AI.
Loading...
In a 2024 education report, two-thirds of Australian teachers reported having used it in their work; the fourth highest proportion among the international organisation's 38 member countries.
Some teachers are boycotting the technology, unable to look past the public criticism that has accompanied the AI boom.
Mark*, a south-east Queensland state primary school teacher, scaled back his use of AI because he felt it brought a cold, lifeless feel to the classroom.
"I used it a bit last year to create things to read from, like an example paragraph to practise reading," he said.
"And then I noticed it has that AI voice. I really started to notice it, and I thought 'this isn't great', I don't want kids to learn how to read through this really sterile way of using language."
A growing number of students are pushing back against the technology too.
In June, high school and university students protested outside the construction site of a new data centre at the Sunshine Coast.
Students who attended cited anxieties around environmental impacts and diminishing future job prospects for young people.
Fears over cognitive 'offloading'
South-east Queensland teacher Lauren* said she was reluctant to role-model a technology that could be impacting her students' ability to think for themselves.
"I teach English and the humanities — those subjects exist to teach critical thinking skills.
"If we're outsourcing that to computers then what are we doing?"
In Queensland, the Department of Education uses a generative AI tool called Corella which is available to teachers and students in years 7-10, although students need parental consent.
A spokesperson for the department said Corella was built around a Socratic teaching method, which guides students "rather than instantly providing them with full, direct responses".
"This encourages critical thinking and problem solving … it is intended to support learning, not replace student thinking, effort or creativity," the spokesperson said.
"The department continues to monitor the rollout of Corella and developments in AI and education across jurisdictions."
The impact of AI on critical thinking skills has been the subject of a growing body of research.
A 2025 UK study which surveyed more than 600 people found young people with high dependence on AI scored lower in critical thinking tests than older people with lower AI dependence.
University of Queensland Education Psychology Professor Jason Lodge said cognitive "offloading" was the biggest risk of embedding AI deeper into schools.
"The brain in many ways is like the body. The harder you work it, the better it gets at doing what it does," he said.
"And AI provides shortcuts that mean some students are not doing the work that's necessary."
But he said those shortcuts could also be beneficial.
"If you're writing something, not necessarily in English class and grammar and spelling is not a key part of the lesson, then maybe it's OK if we're getting an AI tool to help with structuring grammar and correcting spelling," Mr Lodge added.
"There can be very beneficial offloading that allows students and teachers to focus on the more important parts of the lesson."
At the Samford Valley Steiner School, north-west of Brisbane, school director Andrew Curry said designing lessons without intellectual shortcuts had never been more important.
He teaches year 10 students trigonometry by taking surveying instruments called theodolites to measure angles at a nearby creek.
"They're creating a map with traditional techniques," Mr Curry said.
"[It] could be done with drones and AI in probably half the time, but the students wouldn't get all of that richness of learning in that time. They'd just get a map."
Super-powered teachers
Ali Kadri, chief executive of Queensland independent school the Islamic College of Brisbane, said students becoming dependent on AI would not be the fault of the technology.
"It's the fault of how some people are taught or some people teach," he said.
The 45-year-old is also a tech entrepreneur and is designing an in-house AI assistant for the college called Aladin; his answer to the comic book hero Tony Stark's digital sidekick Jarvis.
As well as generating learning materials, Mr Kadri claims Aladin will be able to predict the likely future performance of students based on past grades and attendance.
"If we identify the student is going to do worse than what they've been doing so far, then the machine learning model will trigger an alert … a staff member will then intervene and assign a strategy to address that issue," he said.
"I think it … gives teachers superpowers."
The Islamic College of Brisbane's head of junior secondary Vincent Parry said, although initially a sceptic, he had started to discover where AI could work in the classroom.
He said he was encouraging his students to use AI to simplify explanations they didn't understand, which was particularly helpful for students for whom English was a second language.
"Once you take control of it rather than let it take control of you, it's a very valuable tool," he said.
From teachers to support workers
Looking into the future, Ali Kadri sees a world where AI has changed the teaching profession entirely.
"At this point in time a student does not have to go to a classroom to get their question answered … they can go to an AI model, which is much more knowledgeable and smarter in information that an average teacher would be," he said.
"I think there is a world where education looks like a teacher going into a classroom full of students and instead of delivering content, they'll be mentoring and coaching students while they learn, study and thrive."
Samford Valley Steiner school director Andrew Curry said such a world might improve test scores but wouldn't help students.
"You might get results, but you wouldn't get understanding.
"And the difference is where is your focus? Is your focus on passing a test? On accessing uni? Or is your focus on the student actually understanding the content that's being presented to them?"
*Names withheld for privacy

Zimbabwe and Zambia share the lake, with their border running through its middle.
